pages.title: Chacoan culture: a regional ancestral Pueblo world
pages.intro: Chacoan culture describes a regional pattern of architecture, connections, and practices, with Chaco Canyon as an important centre. It should not be equated automatically with a single ethnic group, language, or uniform political state.

sections.heading: Religion and ritual

paragraphs.text: Great kivas, formal open spaces, sacred landscapes, and orientations toward celestial cycles support Chaco's ceremonial importance. Pueblo descendants describe it as a gathering place for peoples and clans with different traditions. Some researchers interpret roads as ritual or symbolic connections; others also emphasize practical transport. These interpretations do not establish one uniform religion or reveal every ceremony performed in the canyon.

sections.heading: Language: a question left open

paragraphs.text: No single spoken language is established for all Chacoan communities. Keres has been proposed as an important language at Chaco, but that remains a scholarly interpretation. Shared ceremonial imagery or architectural forms cannot independently identify speech. NPS cautions that rock imagery is not a translatable language record, while descendant communities maintain distinct interpretations and connections. Cultural affiliation should not be converted into a one-language census.

sections.heading: Rise, transformation, and migration

paragraphs.text: Monumental building began in the mid-800s, and by about 1050 Chaco had broad ceremonial, administrative, and economic importance. During the 1100s and 1200s construction slowed and regional roles shifted toward other centres. Drought was a substantial challenge, but a single climatic cause does not explain every change. Migration and reorganization continued living histories whose descendants include multiple Pueblo communities and Navajo clans.

pages.title: Chaco Canyon: great houses, community spaces, and engineered roads
pages.intro: Chaco's monumental buildings belong to a regional history of ceremony, exchange, and coordinated construction. Their scale is visible; the precise organization of authority and the functions of particular spaces require interpretation.

sections.heading: Reading the canyon as a connected place

paragraphs.text: NPS places Chaco's prominence between about 850 and 1250 CE. Its multistory public and ceremonial buildings required deliberate design, engineering, and the organization of substantial labor. Architectural sophistication demonstrates coordinated work, but does not by itself identify a particular political system.

A great house is a monumental architectural category, not a population count. Rooms could serve multiple purposes; the number of rooms should not be presented as the number of residents. Compare the excavated spaces of Pueblo Bonito with the largely buried remains of Hungo Pavi before treating their present appearances as an original difference in size or importance.

sections.heading: Principal great houses and the great kiva

rows.name: Pueblo Bonito
rows.architecture: A D-shaped complex that at its height had more than 600 rooms, about 40 kivas, two plazas, and four to five stories in places.
rows.limits: Architectural totals summarize a building that changed through time. They are not a simultaneous resident census, and 'palace' or royal residence is not established by its size.

rows.name: Una Vida
rows.architecture: An early multistory great house with distinctive masonry and a great kiva, near the present visitor center.
rows.limits: Only minor excavation and preservation work has occurred. Much of its form remains buried, so the standing walls understate the original complex.

rows.name: Hungo Pavi
rows.dates: Chacoan great-house period; a precise building sequence is not supplied by the cited visitor page.
rows.architecture: More than 150 rooms, a great kiva, and an enclosed plaza; a stairway survives on the cliff behind it.
rows.limits: Unexcavated remains are largely protected by sand and vegetation. Do not interpret their low profile as a small original structure.

rows.name: Chetro Ketl
rows.dates: Multiple building episodes; exact construction dates are not specified in the cited site page.
rows.architecture: The second-largest Chacoan great house covers more than three acres. Great and elevated kivas accompany an elevated plaza about 12 feet above the canyon floor.
rows.limits: Second- and third-story construction and plaza raising created the visible form over time; do not assume a single building event.

rows.name: Pueblo del Arroyo
rows.dates: About 1065–1150 CE, in two comparatively short phases.
rows.architecture: A great house built in the open near the arroyo rather than against the canyon cliffs; its unusual tri-wall structure is the only example NPS identifies in Chaco Canyon.
rows.limits: The tri-wall form is distinctive, but its presence alone does not demonstrate a specific ethnic identity or political relationship.

rows.name: Casa Rinconada
rows.dates: Part of the Chacoan community landscape; precise dates are not supplied by the cited overview.
rows.architecture: A very large excavated great kiva on the south side of the canyon, among smaller house sites.
rows.limits: Potential astronomical alignments have been proposed. The surrounding buildings also record remodeling and construction over older structures.

rows.name: Wijiji
rows.dates: Early 1100s CE; uniform construction suggests a concentrated building episode around 1110–1115.
rows.architecture: A strongly symmetrical great house with uniform masonry and rooms. Its layout lacks an enclosed plaza and an incorporated great kiva.
rows.limits: Its apparently brief construction contrasts with repeatedly enlarged great houses. Suggestions that it was unfinished remain interpretations.

rows.name: Pueblo Alto and New Alto
rows.dates: Chacoan great-house landscape; exact dates are not established by the cited trail page.
rows.architecture: Mesa-top great houses reached by the Pueblo Alto Trail, in a landscape of roads, ramps, stairways, and broad views across the basin.
rows.limits: Use these sites to study connections between canyon floor and mesa, without treating visibility as proof of centralized control.

sections.heading: What the roads show—and what remains debated

paragraphs.text: Chacoan roads often follow conspicuously straight alignments. NPS describes canyon roads averaging roughly 15 feet wide and outward routes roughly twice that width. Carved stairs and built ramps sometimes carry alignments across cliffs. The Jackson Stairway above Chetro Ketl can be viewed from the Pueblo Alto Trail; it is closed to climbing.

The Great North Road runs from east of Pueblo Alto toward Kutz Canyon; the South Road leaves through South Gap toward the Red Mesa Valley. Many other known alignments are discontinuous. Researchers disagree about whether missing connections eroded away and about the relative importance of pilgrimage, symbolic connections, ordinary movement, and carrying goods. A diagram of the system should distinguish observed segments from reconstructed links.

sections.heading: Before the great houses: a settlement landscape

paragraphs.text: Chaco’s history begins well before the monumental buildings visible in the central canyon. Shabik’eshchee, on Chacra Mesa southeast of Pueblo Bonito, belongs to the survey’s 550–750 CE habitation phase. Its pithouses and shared architecture offer a different scale of community life. A village plan combines evidence accumulated over time; it does not show that every excavated house stood and housed a family in the same year.

The public point marks the named village, with about 200 metres of uncertainty across a dispersed settlement. It does not identify the great kiva or a particular dwelling. This distinction matters when moving between a community history and the construction history of one feature.

rows.name: Shabik’eshchee
rows.architecture: Pithouse village on Chacra Mesa with shared architectural spaces.
rows.limits: The phase is broader than the use of any one house; differing published summaries of the great-kiva date are not collapsed into an exact year.

sections.heading: Small houses beside the monumental canyon

paragraphs.text: The houses south of the wash make everyday settlement visible beside the better-known great houses. Bc 50, Bc 51 and Bc 57 have separate plans and separate chronologies. Bc 50 contains rooms and kivas above earlier remains; its ceramic evidence is centered in the 900s and 1000s. Bc 57 includes evidence from parts of three centuries. Neither sequence establishes continuous residence throughout the whole interval.

Bc 51 provides a useful contrast in dating resolution. Three samples from Room 7 report timber harvested in 967 and 1043. Those years date wood, whereas the broad pottery ranges describe longer episodes of activity. A timber may have been reused. The small-house label describes architecture and scale; it cannot by itself establish household income or political status.

rows.name: Bc 50 / Tseh So
rows.architecture: A 26-room small house with four kivas and underlying earlier remains.
rows.limits: Continuous versus periodic residence remains unresolved.

rows.name: Bc 51, Room 7
rows.architecture: Dated building material within a small-house room.
rows.limits: These are not construction dates for the entire settlement.

rows.name: Bc 57
rows.architecture: Rooms, several enclosed kivas, an exterior kiva and a pithouse.
rows.limits: The public location is calculated from a published distance and direction, with about 50 metres of tolerance.

sections.heading: Great houses were built in stages

paragraphs.text: The surviving plans of Chaco’s great houses combine additions, rebuilding and changed uses. Una Vida’s western roomblock followed an earlier eastern block, and further additions continued toward 1100. Chetro Ketl’s history includes repeated enlargement, superimposed kivas and an infilled colonnade. At Pueblo Alto the arc enclosing the plaza is a probable early-twelfth-century addition. These differences help explain why one construction date cannot stand for an entire great house.

The local sequence extends beyond the central canyon. Pueblo Pintado’s dated timber places substantial building in the later eleventh century; the archive also records numerous smaller surrounding sites. Kin Bineola had early rooms, but most surviving construction appears much later, in 1110–1120. Their distinct histories should remain visible rather than being absorbed into one date for a Chaco system.

rows.name: Una Vida
rows.dates: Western stage from the mid-900s; later additions about 1050–1100
rows.architecture: Successive roomblocks built around an older core.
rows.limits: Approximate stages, not a continuous building campaign.

rows.name: Chetro Ketl
rows.architecture: Repeated expansion and remodeling of the great house.
rows.limits: The general range does not date each altered feature individually.

rows.name: Pueblo Alto
rows.architecture: Rooms enclosed the plaza after earlier work.
rows.limits: The source’s qualification “likely” remains part of the interpretation.

rows.name: Pueblo Pintado
rows.architecture: Eastern great house within a larger settlement community.
rows.limits: Construction samples do not define its full occupation lifespan.

rows.name: Kin Bineola
rows.architecture: Later expansion of an E-shaped great house.
rows.limits: Beam removal limits the surviving dating evidence.

sections.heading: Pueblo Bonito: rebuilding, residence and later reuse

paragraphs.text: Pueblo Bonito is an accumulation of changing buildings. Crown and Wills identify early structures beneath later rooms and a diverse masonry phase around 850–925. A gap in building dates around 975–1040 may include partial abandonment, but continued residence without new construction is possible. The visible plan should not be treated as one completed project.

The archive places some reoccupation in the later twelfth century. Crown and Wills also identify ceramic and architectural evidence of use into the thirteenth. These are different observations from the building peak, and they prevent a regional turning point around 1150 from becoming an automatic local disappearance.

rows.name: Pueblo Bonito
rows.architecture: Repeated construction and altered rooms within the same great-house complex.
rows.limits: A broad habitation envelope contains internal gaps and changes of use.

rows.name: Later Bonito
rows.architecture: Reuse and renovation after the main monumental building sequence.
rows.limits: The scale of residence and a proposed Mesa Verde connection remain uncertain.

sections.heading: Roads: physical traces, regional connections and meanings

paragraphs.text: Chacoan roads include cleared linear traces, stairs and ramps. The Great North Road leaves the Pueblo Alto area and runs toward Kutz Canyon. The South Road passes through South Gap toward communities in the Red Mesa Valley. Preserved stretches can end abruptly or remain disconnected; a line between named places on this map is a schematic explanation, not a reconstruction of every surviving trace.

Roads could enable movement while also making relationships visible. Interpretations include travel, carrying materials, pilgrimage and symbolic connections to places beyond settlements. These purposes are not mutually exclusive. The overview distinguishes a documented road corridor from context-only links to Salmon and Aztec. It does not claim that every northern connection was a continuously surveyed road or that an alignment proves centralized political control.

rows.name: Great North Road
rows.dates: Dates and uses vary by segment
rows.architecture: Cleared corridor, associated features and a northern destination at Kutz Canyon.
rows.limits: The drawn links are schematic and do not supply travel directions.

rows.name: South Road
rows.architecture: Passage through South Gap toward the Red Mesa Valley.
rows.limits: Not drawn here because this proposal does not establish adequately qualified intermediate coordinates.

sections.heading: Unequal status and competing explanations of authority

paragraphs.text: Plog and Heitman interpret unusual mortuary treatment at Pueblo Bonito as evidence that significant social differentiation began earlier than previously proposed. Their argument connects authority with ancestors and cosmology. It is a claim about inequality grounded in a particular body of evidence; the rich burial chamber does not by itself identify a king, a state boundary or the position of every canyon household.

Different models explain how people and resources gathered at great houses. Corporate accounts emphasize household contributions coordinated for communal construction and ritual; pilgrimage accounts emphasize offerings and religious participation. Mattson’s analysis finds substantial ornament manufacture within Pueblo Bonito itself, challenging a simple picture in which small houses supplied all ornaments to great-house elites. Her study supports status differences while changing the proposed organization of production. Cooperation, ritual authority and unequal access can coexist; their balance remains a research question.

rows.name: Room 33 evidence
rows.architecture: A mortuary context used in arguments about ancestry and status.
rows.limits: Human dates are not room-construction dates; medians are not exact burial years.

rows.name: Ornament production
rows.architecture: Tools document manufacture at Pueblo Bonito as well as small houses.
rows.limits: Bonito’s assemblage need not represent every great house.

sections.heading: After Chaco’s regional prominence

paragraphs.text: Change did not require every building or practice to end together. Pueblo del Arroyo acquired a tri-wall structure during the twelfth century, and Pueblo Bonito preserves later use. Buildings could retain significance while residence, investment and wider relationships changed. The regional Four Corners study follows the larger settlement shifts; this local view keeps the different canyon sequences distinct.

Weiner and Ortman compare a Chaco-era community at Kin Nizhoni with later Wiyo’owingeh in the Rio Grande Valley. They propose continuity in landscape and cosmological relationships alongside a shift from elite great-house settings toward communal dwellings and separate shrines. This is a comparison of two communities and an interpretation of social change, not a universal succession or a claim that modern Pueblo communities simply reproduce Chaco’s organization.

rows.name: Pueblo del Arroyo tri-wall
rows.architecture: An unusual addition after the main roomblock, with comparisons at Aztec.
rows.limits: The great-house map point is retained; no individual tri-wall centroid is invented.

pages.title: Hovenweep: springs, towers, and distinct communities
pages.intro: Hovenweep is a collection of separated ancestral places. Its canyon-head buildings connect architecture to springs, farming, and ceremonial life, while Goodman Point belongs to a different setting in the Montezuma Valley.

sections.heading: Six monument units, with Horseshoe and Hackberry distinguished

paragraphs.text: NPS counts six distinct monument units: Square Tower and Cajon in Utah; Holly, Cutthroat Castle, the combined Horseshoe/Hackberry boundary, and Goodman Point in Colorado. Horseshoe and Hackberry are also described as separate groups within their shared boundary. The table distinguishes those two places, producing seven named entries without implying seven separate administrative units.

The towers were made by ancestral Pueblo people. Their forms and placements vary, and their purposes should not be reduced to a single explanation. NPS presents ceremonial, calendrical, protective, storage, and residential possibilities; some descendant-community consultants emphasize rain prayer and relationships among springs, mountains, and water. These attributed interpretations should remain distinct from measured architecture.

rows.name: Square Tower Group
rows.dates: Most visible structures were built and used around 1200–1300 CE.
rows.architecture: Room blocks, towers, and complexes occupy the rims, boulders, slopes, and ledges of Little Ruin Canyon. NPS reports remains of nearly thirty kivas. The named Square Tower stands on a boulder near the canyon head.
rows.limits: Pueblo, Zuni, and Hopi descendants regard this as a continuing sacred place. Its name does not mean that cultural relationships ended when permanent residence shifted elsewhere.

rows.name: Cajon
rows.dates: Structures began in Pueblo I; greatest use about 900–1300 CE.
rows.architecture: A compact concentration of buildings at the southern edge of Cajon Mesa. Its towers and western building interact with seasonal sunlight and shadow in the interpretation presented by NPS.
rows.limits: Rain-prayer and timekeeping interpretations are attributed to tribal consultants, not established as the sole function of every building. The unit is reached through Navajo Nation land; use the designated public approach and parking.

rows.name: Holly
rows.architecture: At the north fork of Keeley Canyon: five single-level masonry structures, three towers, possible kiva depressions, a dam, and a retaining wall. Holly Tower has two rooms and two stories on a large boulder.
rows.limits: The trail-visible petroglyph panel receives light beams around the summer solstice. NPS presents seasonal timekeeping and rain ceremony as interpretations informed by descendant consultants.

rows.name: Cutthroat Castle
rows.dates: Buildings were used across Pueblo I–III, about 750–1300 CE.
rows.architecture: Unlike the rim groups, its buildings lie within and along a drainage. The main three-story, D-shaped building sits on a boulder; nearby are towers, dwellings, and possible kiva depressions.
rows.limits: NPS identifies a probable above-ground kiva with an outer corridor. Neither its circular shape nor the modern name 'castle' proves a single exclusive function.

rows.name: Horseshoe
rows.dates: Evidence of occupation from around 450 CE; prominent stone construction belongs to the later ancestral Pueblo landscape, around and after 1200.
rows.architecture: Horseshoe House is a two-story, double-walled D-shaped building with four rooms around a circular room. A separate tower and room block occupy the point between drainage forks.
rows.limits: The central room is described as kiva-like. Horseshoe shares a protected boundary and trail with Hackberry; they should remain distinguishable as sites.

rows.name: Hackberry
rows.dates: Early use of the springs from around 450 CE; major masonry construction around 1200 and later.
rows.architecture: The largest complex in the monument retains traces of towers, rooms, terrace walls, and check dams near its spring, though comparatively little masonry stands upright.
rows.limits: Low surviving walls do not imply a minor settlement. It remains sacred to descendant communities.

rows.name: Goodman Point
rows.dates: Major thirteenth-century village; the cited NPS overview does not provide an exact construction sequence.
rows.architecture: A large, unexcavated pueblo in the Montezuma Valley, rather than a Cajon Mesa canyon-head tower group. NPS describes public architecture including great kivas, plazas, reservoirs, and enclosing walls in these village remains.
rows.limits: Buried architecture should not be reconstructed as fully known. Goodman Point is geographically and architecturally distinct from the five Cajon Mesa units.

sections.heading: Water and living connections

paragraphs.text: Hovenweep's prominent canyon-head groups are associated with springs and seeps. A spring is a strong reason to locate buildings nearby, but proximity alone does not settle what each tower did. NPS explicitly leaves the purpose of Square Tower open and notes that its adjacent excavated kiva was not connected to it by a tunnel.

NPS asks visitors to remain on defined trails, avoid touching or entering structures, and leave artifacts in place. Outlying units require additional travel and walking; rough roads can become impassable when wet. Route conditions and permitted access should be checked with the monument before visiting.

sections.heading: Read the named buildings before assigning their functions

paragraphs.text: Several distinct buildings surround Little Ruin Canyon in the Square Tower Group. Their varied plans and positions reveal different architectural choices. Modern names such as castle, house, and tower do not establish royal residence, domestic use, or defense; the functions of some structures remain uncertain.

rows.name: Unit Type House
rows.dates: Broadly thirteenth century; no independent construction date verified here.
rows.architecture: A small cluster of living and storage rooms with one Mesa Verde-style kiva.
rows.limits: The building plan suggests a household unit; the number or identity of residents is not a census.

rows.name: Twin Towers
rows.architecture: Separate oval and horseshoe-shaped buildings stand almost against one another; NPS describes sixteen rooms across the pair.
rows.limits: Nearby does not mean connected, and room totals do not establish population.

rows.name: Rim Rock House
rows.architecture: A rectangular, multi-level building with small wall openings and no clear interior residential partitions.
rows.limits: Its name should not be used as evidence of an ordinary dwelling; a distinct function remains uncertain.

sections.heading: A canyon head with three different monuments

paragraphs.text: Hovenweep Castle, Hovenweep House, and Square Tower occupy different positions around the canyon head. Standing walls reveal only part of the earlier complexes: collapsed masonry extended down the slopes. The spring setting is shared, but it does not prove that all three buildings had the same purpose.

rows.name: Hovenweep House
rows.dates: Thirteenth-century architectural horizon; finer sequence unresolved here.
rows.architecture: Bedrock supports the standing part of a larger pueblo. Pecked stone surfaces and small chinking stones illustrate careful masonry.
rows.limits: Fallen walls and possible former plaster complicate comparisons based only on today’s visible height.

rows.name: Hovenweep Castle
rows.dates: Broad architectural phase, with a timber cut in 1277 CE.
rows.architecture: Two D-shaped towers formed part of a larger complex descending into the canyon.
rows.limits: The dated timber is one observation, not the founding date of every room or proof of the structure’s exclusive use.

rows.name: Square Tower
rows.dates: Broadly thirteenth century; its particular building sequence remains unresolved.
rows.architecture: A tower on a sandstone boulder beside a seep, with an adjacent excavated kiva.
rows.limits: NPS reports no connecting tunnel. Two current NPS pages differ over the surviving story count, so no definitive story total is repeated.

sections.heading: Storage and construction in difficult terrain

paragraphs.text: The canyon architecture adapts to bedrock, ledges, boulders, and steep changes in level. Tower Point overlooks two branches; rooms in nearby alcoves provided crop storage. This is evidence of practical planning alongside the ceremonial interpretations presented elsewhere. A broad building horizon cannot resolve the order in which every tower, room, and storage space was added.

rows.name: Tower Point and adjacent storage
rows.architecture: A tower at the branching canyon edge and storage spaces beneath nearby ledges.
rows.limits: The mapped anchor is the public viewpoint beside the named feature, with about 50 m positional tolerance; no granary footprint is claimed.

rows.name: Stronghold House and Eroded Boulder House
rows.dates: Architectural discussion retained; no new exact feature point proposed.
rows.architecture: Stronghold includes part of a larger pueblo; Eroded Boulder House incorporates a natural boulder cavity.
rows.limits: The publicly available GNIS Stronghold coordinate conflicts with the official trail layout. These remain guide context rather than falsely precise new map points.

sections.heading: Chronology beyond the famous towers

paragraphs.text: Holly, Horseshoe, Hackberry, Cajon, and Cutthroat Castle preserve distinct histories of settlement and building. Earlier use of springs at Horseshoe and Hackberry preceded their visible masonry. Goodman Point was a large village in the different setting of the Montezuma Valley, providing a useful comparison with nearby Sand Canyon.

rows.name: Holly and the combined Horseshoe/Hackberry unit
rows.dates: Holly’s primary use broadly 900–1300; major Horseshoe/Hackberry stone building around 1200 and later.
rows.architecture: Several separate settlements connected to water sources rather than one continuous urban block.
rows.limits: Earlier use near a spring does not demonstrate unbroken residence at each later building. Existing group Place objects remain unchanged.

rows.name: The 1277 Castle beam
rows.dates: One cutting date within the late architectural history.
rows.architecture: A piece of roof/construction wood supplies a different kind of date from the general century-scale village chronology.
rows.limits: A timber’s cutting year is not automatically its installation year, a whole-building completion date, or the year residents left.

sections.heading: Ancestral places remain part of living communities

paragraphs.text: NPS presents Hovenweep as an ancestral footprint for living Pueblo, Hopi, and Zuni people. Community consultants relate springs, mountains, rain prayer, and seasonal knowledge to these places. These attributed interpretations belong beside architectural evidence, without being reduced to a single function for every tower. Residential migration does not mean the place lost its relationships or that descendants vanished.

Compare the individual buildings here with the larger public villages at Sand Canyon and Castle Rock, and with the earlier great-house histories of Chaco. The comparison concerns different local building traditions and timelines. It does not require that every tower copied a Chaco plan or that all villages shared one political authority.

pages.title: Mesa Verde: cliff villages within a much longer mesa-top history
pages.intro: The cliff dwellings are one part of Mesa Verde's settlement history. Mesa-top houses, farming communities, reservoirs, and ceremonial buildings reveal a landscape inhabited and repeatedly transformed over centuries.

sections.heading: Individual cliff dwellings

paragraphs.text: NPS dates most cliff-dwelling construction to about 1180–1300 CE. Nearby seep springs helped make alcoves attractive as water supplies became less dependable. These were varied villages with living rooms, granaries, communal spaces, and kivas, fitted to particular rock faces and available space.

rows.name: Cliff Palace
rows.architecture: About 150 rooms and 23 kivas in a large alcove. Shaped sandstone, mortar, chinking stones, timber, and colored plaster formed its buildings.
rows.limits: Its exceptional size and abundant communal space suggest a wider community role; the English name does not identify a royal palace. Room counts are not resident counts.

rows.name: Balcony House
rows.dates: Late cliff-dwelling era; exact site sequence not supplied by this profile.
rows.architecture: 38 rooms and two kivas, with surviving balconies and two main plazas joined by a narrow passage.
rows.limits: The suggestion of two resident social groups is an archaeological interpretation, not an identified ethnic division.

rows.name: Long House
rows.architecture: About 150 rooms, 21 kivas, a central gathering plaza, and carved water basins and drains along the rear of its Wetherill Mesa alcove.
rows.limits: A community-center role for neighboring villages is probable rather than directly documented.

rows.name: Spruce Tree House
rows.architecture: About 130 rooms and eight kivas in a natural alcove; the park's third-largest cliff dwelling.
rows.limits: NPS estimates 60–80 residents independently of room totals. View from designated overlooks; entry is closed because of unstable rock above the site.

rows.name: Step House
rows.dates: Two occupations: pithouses around 700 CE and masonry around 1200 CE.
rows.architecture: Early semi-subterranean houses and a later village of 27 rooms and three kivas share an alcove.
rows.limits: The two architectural episodes are separated by about five centuries, rather than constituting one continuously expanding village.

rows.name: Square Tower House
rows.dates: Late ancestral Pueblo cliff-dwelling landscape; exact dates not established by the cited visitor page.
rows.architecture: The park's tallest surviving structure, plus an intact kiva roof, original plaster and paint, and rock art.
rows.limits: The Mesa Top Loop overlook and restricted ranger-led visits offer different views. This site is separate from Hovenweep's Square Tower Group.

sections.heading: Mesa-top places deserve equal attention

paragraphs.text: Far View shows that the move into alcoves was not universal. Some families continued living on the mesa top while nearby cliff villages were occupied. Fields, houses, water storage, and paths connected these places; a simple progression from mesa-top settlement to complete cliff occupation obscures that coexistence.

rows.name: Far View Community
rows.dates: About 800–1300 CE in the cited place profile.
rows.architecture: Far View House, Pipe Shrine House, Coyote Village, Megalithic House, Far View Tower, and a now-dry reservoir form the visitor circuit through a larger farming landscape.
rows.limits: The six displayed places are a sample of a much wider community. NPS suggests at least 35 occupied villages within half a square mile in the mid-1100s.

rows.name: Badger House Community
rows.dates: A sequence spanning roughly 600 years, including an early pithouse around 650 CE.
rows.architecture: Four interpretive sites: Modified Basketmaker Pithouse, Developmental Pueblo village, Badger House, and Two Raven House, on Wetherill Mesa.
rows.limits: These are sites from a long sequence, not four necessarily contemporary neighborhoods.

rows.name: Cedar Tree Tower and nearby farming terraces
rows.dates: Tower-kiva complexes were chiefly built about 1100–1300 CE.
rows.architecture: A mesa-top tower associated with a kiva. Nearby check dams slowed runoff, trapped soil, and retained moisture for crops.
rows.limits: Tower use is unresolved: ceremonial and communication functions are proposals. The agricultural interpretation of check dams rests on their form and hydrological effect.

rows.name: Sun Temple
rows.dates: Mesa-top construction continued into the 1200s; precise dating is difficult without roof timbers or a substantial domestic assemblage.
rows.architecture: An intentionally D-shaped complex with thick masonry walls, 24 excavated rooms, three circular structures within the main complex, and another detached circular structure.
rows.limits: NPS describes a likely communal or ceremonial building. Whether it was left unfinished or intentionally unroofed, and the details of possible astronomical use, remain open questions.

sections.heading: Mesa-top homes before cliff villages

paragraphs.text: The Pithouse on Mesa Top Loop dates to about 600 CE, centuries before Mesa Verde’s famous late cliff villages. Step House and the earlier Badger House Community preserve other early structures. These separate places reveal a long history of home building across the landscape.

An excavated plan can show how a home was arranged without establishing the first settlement of the whole mesa. The 600 date is an archaeological interpretation expressed approximately. Later masonry villages grew within landscapes that already contained houses, fields, pathways and places remembered by their inhabitants.

rows.name: Mesa Top Loop first-stop Pithouse
rows.architecture: A semi-subterranean home on the mesa top.
rows.limits: A date for this feature, not the first human presence in the region.

sections.heading: Far View: a community rebuilt across centuries

paragraphs.text: Far View includes more than its largest visible house. Pipe Shrine House, Coyote Village and the reservoir are separate public features, close enough to compare at community scale. Buried charcoal under Far View House represents trees cut in the 800s and 900s. Pipe Shrine timbers extend the earlier building sequence into the mid-700s, while Coyote Village preserves successive structures and overlapping walls. The ruins visible today bring several periods into the same view.

The evidence does not advance in one uniform sequence. Pipe Shrine has no reported timber samples from the 1100s in the cited booklet, yet that gap alone cannot establish abandonment. A 1200s timber may mark later remodeling. At Far View Reservoir, pottery and stratigraphy distinguish early walls around 950 from final building around 1200; debates about water storage and additional uses should not erase those construction observations.

rows.name: Far View House
rows.architecture: Earlier activity below visible walls and floors.
rows.limits: Charcoal dates the trees represented, not every standing wall.

rows.name: Pipe Shrine House
rows.architecture: Several building episodes and possible late remodeling.
rows.limits: Sparse records and reused timber complicate the sequence.

rows.name: Coyote Village
rows.architecture: Successive mesa-top structures identified through walls, pottery and wood.
rows.limits: A long sequence does not mean all rooms were contemporary.

rows.name: Far View Reservoir
rows.architecture: Wall-building stages distinguished through ceramics and stratigraphy.
rows.limits: These are not exact years of filling, drainage or continuous use.

sections.heading: The Badger House community: different local histories

paragraphs.text: Badger House is one place within a trail that visits several settlements. Its first occupation, about 900–1100, is separate from the much earlier Basketmaker site already mapped nearby. Two Raven House was used at different times from the 900s into the 1100s. Giving these places separate points prevents the trail’s collective name from turning all of its structures into one village with one lifespan.

The later return to Badger House is especially useful for comparing mesa tops and alcoves. The institutional guide attributes its final roomblock, tower and connected kiva to about 1258. This was a late mesa-top project while cliff settlements existed elsewhere in the park. A tower’s presence does not independently identify warfare: connected rooms, plazas and kivas require interpretation in their local setting.

rows.name: Badger House, earlier residence
rows.architecture: Earlier rooms beneath and beside later construction.
rows.limits: Later building disturbed parts of the earlier remains.

rows.name: Badger House, final project
rows.architecture: Tower, connected kiva and last roomblock.
rows.limits: An institutional attribution; the guide does not include its original dating table.

rows.name: Two Raven House
rows.architecture: Small pueblo, enclosure and kiva-like structure.
rows.limits: A fence may have served as a windbreak or turkey enclosure; it is not labeled defensive.

sections.heading: Mesa tops and alcoves overlapped

paragraphs.text: Cliff Palace, Balcony House, Spruce Tree House and Long House were substantial late communities, but people did not move from every mesa-top settlement to every alcove at the same moment. The late work at Badger House makes that overlap concrete. Sun Point Pueblo adds another mesa-top village with rooms, a tower and a kiva connected by a tunnel.

Sun Point appears from its pottery to have been occupied for only about a decade, according to the interpretive guide. That decade falls somewhere within the broad 1100s–1200s attribution. The wide date range reflects uncertainty about timing rather than two centuries of continuous residence.

rows.name: Sun Point Pueblo
rows.dates: An unresolved short episode within the 1100s–1200s
rows.architecture: Approximately 30 rooms with a tower, kiva and connecting tunnel.
rows.limits: The suggested ten-year occupation has no exact decade in the cited guide.

rows.name: Late Badger House and cliff villages
rows.architecture: Mesa-top building continued alongside alcove settlement.
rows.limits: Overlap does not prove a single organized movement or a shared final year.

sections.heading: Close construction histories inside cliff villages

paragraphs.text: Long House’s overall history is broader than any single room or kiva. Street’s dendroarchaeological study dates Kiva I to three winters, 1270/71–1272/73, using a high proportion of successfully dated samples. This unusually fine sequence helps place labor within the village’s later history. It does not date all of Long House or reveal when every household arrived.

The Balcony House booklet illustrates successive building stages at 1250, 1270, 1275, and 1280. Elsewhere, its text gives an earlier endpoint for intermittent construction. Both accounts describe changes within the cliff village, but their disagreement leaves the final construction sequence uncertain.

rows.name: Long House, Kiva I
rows.architecture: Construction reconstructed from tree-ring samples.
rows.limits: The study’s publisher abstract is explicit; the full specimen-level article was not inspected.

rows.name: Balcony House
rows.architecture: Rooms and spaces added to a changing alcove village.
rows.limits: The booklet’s narrative summary and diagram disagree about the last construction date.

sections.heading: Reading departure without losing continuity

paragraphs.text: The last building dates and the last evidence of residence answer different questions. A timber cut in the 1270s shows construction or repair; it cannot determine the day a household left. Regional depopulation models place changes across many settlements, while these named features retain their particular building and use histories. The regional Four Corners study connects this local evidence to migration and later Pueblo communities.

Mesa Verde remains an ancestral home for living Pueblo peoples. Departures from particular villages were followed by movement, new communities, and continuing relationships with these places. The end of residence in a building is one event within that longer history.

pages.title: Canyons of the Ancients: Lowry, Sand Canyon, and Castle Rock
pages.intro: These public sites represent different moments and forms of ancestral Pueblo settlement in southwestern Colorado. Lowry's longer growth contrasts with the concentrated thirteenth-century histories of Sand Canyon Pueblo and Castle Rock Pueblo.

sections.heading: Three communities, three archaeological records

paragraphs.text: Canyons of the Ancients protects a broad cultural landscape northwest of Mesa Verde and Cortez. Its thousands of recorded places belong to histories extending well beyond the three pueblos shown here. The visitor center and museum provides context before a visit; in the Sand Canyon/Rock Creek management area, travel is restricted to designated routes.

rows.name: Lowry Pueblo
rows.dates: Built over an earlier community around 1060 CE and inhabited for about 165 years. Major additions occurred about 1085–1170.
rows.architecture: Grew from a small settlement to about 40 rooms, eight kivas, and a great kiva. Additions included Kiva B, known for painted decoration.
rows.limits: The final architectural inventory accumulated over time. Forty rooms does not mean forty residents, and Chaco-related architecture alone does not establish direct political control from Chaco.

rows.name: Sand Canyon Pueblo
rows.dates: Construction began in the late 1240s or early 1250s and continued into the late 1270s.
rows.architecture: An estimated 420 rooms, 90 kivas, fourteen towers, a plaza, a great kiva, and a D-shaped bi-wall building. A substantial masonry wall enclosed much of the village around a canyon-head setting.
rows.limits: Counts are estimates for a complex archaeological site. Excavated structures and archived study units are not the same as all structures in the pueblo. A wall had defensive potential, but its presence does not explain every aspect of community life.

rows.name: Castle Rock Pueblo
rows.dates: Occupied from the 1260s into the 1280s; occupation ended abruptly around the mid-1280s.
rows.architecture: A village constructed at the base and on top of a prominent sandstone butte. Crow Canyon interprets the position as probably selected in part for defensibility.
rows.limits: Excavation evidence indicates a violent ending. That event should not be expanded into an unsupported identity for the attackers or a single explanation for all regional migration. Crow Canyon estimates 75–150 residents; this is an estimate, not a census.

sections.heading: What excavation can and cannot establish

paragraphs.text: Sand Canyon's excavated rooms, kivas, refuse, and tree-ring samples support a reconstruction of a lived-in village that grew through additions and collective building projects. Some reused or older timbers predate the main construction sequence; individual early wood dates should not automatically be treated as the date the village was founded.

Castle Rock's abrupt violent ending is a site-specific finding. Lowry's different chronology and Sand Canyon's much larger architectural footprint caution against treating all places in the monument as one synchronous settlement or one uniform community. Dates, room totals, and excavation coverage need to remain attached to the individual site.

sections.heading: Lowry grew through distinct building episodes

paragraphs.text: Lowry developed from its first rooms and kiva around 1060 into a larger room block with communal architecture. The Great Kiva had an initial building phase and later roof construction. These separate episodes reveal investment in the same settlement over generations.

rows.name: Initial Lowry rooms and kiva
rows.architecture: A small pueblo was established above an earlier community.
rows.limits: The source does not date that underlying community precisely enough to create another numerical interval.

rows.name: Room-block additions and Kiva B
rows.architecture: Added rooms and a painted kiva transformed the earlier pueblo.
rows.limits: This broad envelope does not separately date every room; Kiva B uses the existing Lowry map place rather than a fabricated room coordinate.

rows.name: Lowry Great Kiva
rows.dates: Initial work around 1086; later roof/construction evidence 1160–1170 CE.
rows.architecture: A separate large gathering building, approximately 47 feet across.
rows.limits: Latest sampled construction is not the date of the final ceremony. Its function as a gathering place is an interpretation.

sections.heading: Two museum-ground pueblos, different scales of home

paragraphs.text: Dominguez and Escalante are publicly interpreted on the visitor-center and museum grounds near Dolores, outside the main monument tracts. Including them provides a local twelfth-century comparison without moving them inside the monument boundary. Their modern names honor later Spanish visitors; the construction evidence belongs to ancestral Pueblo histories centuries earlier.

rows.name: Dominguez Pueblo
rows.architecture: Small rooms, originally with walls of poles, brush, and earth, faced an earth-walled kiva.
rows.limits: The buried kiva is protected by backfilling. Sources differ in room-count conventions; this guide does not derive a population from them.

rows.name: Escalante: first residence
rows.architecture: A planned building with a central kiva, substantial walls, and architectural affinities with Chaco.
rows.limits: The 1138 boundary is calculated from the published first occupation of about nine years, not an exact independently dated move.

rows.name: Escalante: later returns
rows.dates: Briefly around 1150; a few rooms reused around 1200 CE.
rows.architecture: The same physical building hosted distinct later episodes.
rows.limits: The single approximate display years mark observations of reuse; their durations are unknown, and the gap between them is preserved.

sections.heading: Small villages beside the larger centers

paragraphs.text: Painted Hand and Saddlehorn make the inhabited landscape more varied than a sequence of large pueblos alone. Their public descriptions identify homes and shared spaces at different scales. The buildings should be compared in their actual settings rather than represented by one monument-wide point.

rows.name: Painted Hand Pueblo
rows.architecture: A small village with a prominent tower and approximately twenty rooms.
rows.limits: This public pueblo is not the separately named Painted Hand/Strawman Petroglyph Panel; rock imagery elsewhere cannot supply its chronology.

rows.name: Saddlehorn Pueblo
rows.architecture: Rooms occupy an alcove and a higher pinnacle; an excavated kiva was subsequently reburied.
rows.limits: Older roof beams, mostly dated 1228–1232, may have been reused. They should not silently move the occupation onset back to the 1220s.

sections.heading: Sand Canyon and Castle Rock have separate histories

paragraphs.text: Crow Canyon’s excavation synthesis dates Sand Canyon’s main construction from the late 1240s or early 1250s into the late 1270s. Castle Rock’s project summary places residence from the 1260s into the 1280s, although BLM uses a broader 1250s–1280s window. These differences belong in the evidence notes; one universal founding date would hide them.

rows.name: Sand Canyon Pueblo
rows.dates: Main construction: late 1240s/early 1250s to late 1270s CE.
rows.architecture: Accreting household blocks accompanied planned community buildings and an enclosing masonry wall.
rows.limits: Early timber may have been salvaged. Only part of this large settlement was excavated; whole-village totals remain estimates.

rows.name: Castle Rock Pueblo
rows.dates: Primary-project residence:1260s to approximately mid-1280s CE.
rows.architecture: Buildings surround a sandstone butte and extend onto its summit.
rows.limits: Its setting was probably defensible, but the evidence does not name an enemy or establish all residents’ motives.

rows.name: Different local endings
rows.dates: Sand Canyon approximately 1280; Castle Rock approximately mid-1280s in the project summary.
rows.architecture: Excavation evidence supports violence at these two places.
rows.limits: Do not impose this ending on Lowry, Painted Hand, every small dwelling, or the entire region. No attacker identity is inferred.

sections.heading: Living relationships extend beyond residential windows

paragraphs.text: The BLM and CyArk interpretation at Painted Hand includes Tiana Cachini of Zuni Pueblo. It treats the village as an ancestral home and attributes a possible rain-priest relationship to the tower within Zuni interpretation. The monument’s broader public interpretation likewise describes enduring ties among descendant communities, ancestral places, plants, and water. Those relationships are not cut off at a map record’s final residential date.

The Hovenweep guide is the home for Goodman Point’s existing record. Its nearby large village can be compared with Sand Canyon without duplicating its identity here. Chaco and Mesa Verde provide further architectural and migration context within the regional Four Corners story.

pages.title: Inca civilization: the Tawantinsuyu and its connected landscapes
pages.intro: The Inca state linked communities, production zones, sacred places, and administrative centres across the Andes. Its roads and monumental architecture drew on earlier Andean histories and the work of many communities. Machu Picchu is one estate within this wider history.

sections.heading: Capital, state, and varied communities

paragraphs.text: Cusco was the imperial capital, with religious, governmental, and royal spaces forming a planned urban ensemble. The fifteenth-century Inca remodeling continued a much longer local settlement history. Surviving streets and walls now form part of a living city shaped again during colonial and later periods.

Imperial chronology remains a research question rather than a reliable date stamp for every site. Ogburn's 2012 analysis questions how colonial writers converted accounts of conquest into a linear sequence and argues for independent radiocarbon frameworks. Regional expansion, a ruler's life, construction, and a sample's age are different events.

Diversity within the state is visible at a small scale in Machu Picchu's burial sample. The 2023 genomic study supports a varied attendant community rather than a population drawn solely from the immediate Cusco region. Its authors combine ancestry results with archaeology and history; their sampled individuals should not stand for every imperial population.

sections.heading: Roads and the institutions along them

paragraphs.text: UNESCO describes four main routes originating at Cusco and linking with smaller roads. The wider network incorporated pre-Inca infrastructure and supported communication, movement, supplies, and state administration. Bridges, steps, paving, and drainage adapted to different terrains. The World Heritage property selects representative sections and associated places; it is not the full surviving network.

Peru's road-registration guide identifies a major highland longitudinal axis between Quito and Mendoza through Cusco. Huánuco Pampa's official inventory places that administrative centre on the Cusco–Quito corridor. The diagram below reduces this long system to four named reference places and three corridor connections; many intermediate settlements and branches are omitted.

rows.name: Road engineering
rows.dates: Built and adapted over centuries; major imperial expansion in the fifteenth century.
rows.architecture: Variable surfaces, retaining walls, stairs, bridges, and drains negotiated sharply different environments.
rows.limits: Do not assign one construction date or identical design to the whole network.

rows.name: Longitudinal and connecting roads
rows.architecture: The highland spine was complemented by coastal routes, transverse connections, and links between drainage basins.
rows.limits: The small diagram shows a selected corridor, not all four imperial quarters or a complete road inventory.

rows.name: Huánuco Pampa: administration and storage
rows.dates: Inca administrative centre; no precise foundation year established here.
rows.architecture: A planned highland centre on the Cusco–Quito road, with large storage facilities. Colcas included circular and rectangular buildings.
rows.limits: Storehouse totals are archaeological inventories, not counts of resident households.

rows.name: A living cultural network
rows.dates: Ancient routes with continuing community relationships.
rows.architecture: Selected road sections remain associated with local knowledge, maintenance practices, exchange, and cultural traditions.
rows.limits: The end of the Inca state did not end Andean peoples or all uses of its roads.

sections.heading: Religion and ritual

paragraphs.text: State ceremony linked the ruler and Inti, the Sun, with offerings and sacred places. Smithsonian interpretation also emphasizes Pachamama and roads as connections with a spiritual universe. Imperial worship and local sacred relationships should not be flattened into one identical practice everywhere. Inca-period religion is reconstructed through material remains, historical testimony, and living Andean traditions, each with a different relationship to the past.

sections.heading: Languages: Quechua and a debated court language

paragraphs.text: Quechua was important in the Inca world, but the empire incorporated speakers of many languages. Aymara and Puquina also belong to debates over its linguistic history. Cerrón-Palomino proposes Puquina connections for sparse names and reports of a special court language; this is a historical-linguistic hypothesis, not a demonstrated language for every ruler or resident. Language affiliation, political allegiance, and biological ancestry are separate questions.

sections.heading: Rise, conquest, and continuing peoples

paragraphs.text: A kingdom centred on Cusco expanded into Tawantinsuyu through military campaigns and state integration, especially during the fifteenth century. Conventional royal dates are being revised against radiocarbon evidence. Spanish invasion, Indigenous alliances, and the capture of Atahualpa in 1532 disrupted imperial rule; conquest and colonial transformation were processes rather than the disappearance of Andean peoples. Languages, communities, and traditions continued beyond the empire.

pages.title: Machu Picchu and the Inca heartland: architecture, water, and changing chronologies
pages.intro: Machu Picchu is a planned mountain settlement within a larger landscape of roads, terraces, sacred places, and royal estates. Its architecture and engineering can be described more securely than an exact construction year for every building.

sections.heading: A ridge settlement within a larger landscape

paragraphs.text: The archaeological settlement stands on a steep ridge about 2,430 metres above sea level, within the much larger mixed cultural and natural World Heritage sanctuary. UNESCO describes roughly 200 structures, organized into upper and lower parts and agricultural and residential areas. That approximate structural inventory is neither a count of houses nor an estimate of permanent residents.

The royal-estate interpretation connects the site with Pachacuti and an attendant community. A 2023 study generated genome-wide data for 34 people buried at Machu Picchu and compared them with 34 individuals from the Cusco area. The authors found considerable ancestry diversity extending across the empire and Amazonia. These sampled burials are not a census, and genetic affinities do not identify a person's language, named ethnic group, or precise place of birth.

rows.name: Main settlement and central open spaces
rows.dates: Fifteenth-century construction in the UNESCO overview; occupation chronology is discussed separately below.
rows.architecture: Stone-built compounds, open spaces, ramps, stairs, and terraces fit a narrow ridge. Upper and lower areas and agricultural and residential zones form an integrated plan.
rows.limits: The World Heritage property includes surrounding mountains and ecosystems; its boundary is much larger than the built settlement. Broad functional labels do not establish the exact use of every room.

rows.name: Temple of the Sun
rows.dates: Inca-period monument; no independently verified room-specific construction year in the cited description.
rows.architecture: A curved masonry building fitted over a large natural granite outcrop, with trapezoidal windows and a finely worked doorway.
rows.limits: Architectural integration with bedrock is observable. The modern building name and proposed astronomical roles require interpretation.

rows.name: Temple of the Three Windows
rows.dates: Inca-period construction; exact building dates remain unspecified here.
rows.architecture: A rectangular building beside a principal ceremonial open space, distinguished by three openings and finely fitted large stone blocks.
rows.limits: Describe the windows and masonry separately from claims about their symbolic meaning. A name does not establish a complete original ritual programme.

rows.name: Intiwatana hill and carved rock
rows.dates: Inca-period reshaping of the hill; exact carving date is not established by the cited study.
rows.architecture: A worked bedrock feature crowns a terraced eminence associated with nearby ceremonial open spaces and buildings. The hill, terraces, paths, and outcrop form one designed ensemble.
rows.limits: Astronomical interpretations should distinguish measured alignments from a fully demonstrated calendar or single exclusive function. 'Intiwatana' is also used for other places; this row concerns the hill within the llaqta.

sections.heading: Terraces, drinking water, and drainage worked together

paragraphs.text: Water supply and storm drainage solved different problems. Field research documented spring collection and gravity delivery to fountains, while engineering analysis examined how heavy rainfall moved through and away from the steep built site. A fountain's capacity should not be converted into an observed resident population, and a successful drainage design does not mean that every wall or slope was immune to movement.

rows.name: Agricultural terraces
rows.dates: Inca construction; the selected engineering study does not assign one building year to all terraces.
rows.architecture: Retaining walls contain planting soil above progressively coarser, permeable fills. The terraces support cultivation while controlling runoff and erosion.
rows.limits: The published field investigation found no branches from the main supply canal irrigating the upper agricultural terraces. Do not assume every terrace was irrigated simply because water channels exist nearby.

rows.name: Spring, supply canal, and fountains
rows.dates: Inca water system documented by fieldwork begun under a 1994 archaeological permit.
rows.architecture: A spring on the north slope of Machu Picchu mountain fed a gravity canal measured at 749 metres, supplying sixteen fountains in the settlement.
rows.limits: Measured spring yields varied seasonally. The engineering paper's proposed occupation dates and population figures are older interpretations; neither hydraulic capacity nor those dates overrides newer archaeological dating.

rows.name: Surface and subsurface drainage
rows.dates: Inca infrastructure; analyzed in a 1999 engineering study.
rows.architecture: An extensive drainage system addressed steep slopes and rainfall approaching two metres annually. It forms essential infrastructure beneath and between the visible buildings and terraces.
rows.limits: Rainfall values describe an engineering context, not a fixed annual climate for every year of occupation. Drainage performance and later conservation condition are separate questions.

sections.heading: Why the dates differ

paragraphs.text: A traditional historical model links Pachacuti's accession to 1438 and places Machu Picchu's beginnings around 1450–1460. That model depends heavily on colonial accounts. Ogburn's 2012 study challenged the wider imperial sequence using dates from Chamical in Ecuador and argued that conquest narratives may combine geographic and chronological order. Its results concern imperial expansion; they do not directly date Machu Picchu's individual buildings.

Burger and colleagues' 2021 AMS study dated bone and teeth from burials in four cemetery areas and inferred occupation around 1420–1532. A separate Bayesian study of Machu Picchu, Chachabamba, and Choqesuysuy modeled a small set of archaeological samples. Its Machu Picchu first-event estimate was 1422–1448 at 68.2% probability in one model, widening to 1421–1476 when allowing for wood's inbuilt age. These are different datasets and model outputs, not interchangeable exact foundation years. Calibration assumptions, residual charcoal, and the event actually sampled matter.

sections.heading: Related places in the heartland

paragraphs.text: Cusco, Ollantaytambo, Pisaq, and Choquequirao provide different comparisons: an imperial capital reshaped by later occupation, a planned valley town, dispersed estate architecture, and a mountain complex with extensive terraces. Similar masonry or landscape design does not make them simultaneous foundations or establish identical purposes. Each site's building history needs its own archaeological evidence.

rows.name: Cusco: imperial centre and later city
rows.dates: Major Inca remodeling in the fifteenth century over a much older settlement; colonial construction followed the sixteenth-century conquest.
rows.architecture: Religious and administrative buildings, royal compounds, finely cut walls, streets, and canchas survive within a continuously occupied city. Qoricancha is a key surviving component of the Inca ensemble.
rows.limits: The capital's long occupation cannot be assigned the short chronology of the empire. Later buildings often incorporate or overlie earlier fabric; an Inca wall and the building above it may have different dates.

rows.name: Ollantaytambo
rows.dates: Imperial and late Inca phases; chroniclers differ about its royal builder.
rows.architecture: A planned settlement beside the Patakancha near its Urubamba confluence. Qosqo Ayllu and Araccama Ayllu include plazas, palaces, enclosures, and shrines, complemented by terraces, storehouses, and walls.
rows.limits: The culture authority reports Sarmiento's attribution to Pachacuti and Garcilaso's to Wiracocha. These are historical attributions, not a resolved construction date for the entire complex.

rows.name: Pisaq / Pisac
rows.dates: Inca estate traditionally associated with Pachacuti; no precise foundation year established here.
rows.architecture: Dispersed terraces, agricultural platforms, domestic compounds, and ceremonial buildings occupy ridges above the Sacred Valley, near the approach from Cusco and routes toward Paucartambo.
rows.limits: The royal-estate interpretation is explicitly linked by the culture authority to Sarmiento de Gamboa. Its extent and varied sectors should not be collapsed into a single temple or fortress.

rows.name: Choquequirao
rows.dates: Inca complex; colonial-source interpretations associate an estate with Tupac Inca Yupanqui or Pachacuti rather than securely dating every sector.
rows.architecture: A mountain settlement above the right bank of the Apurimac, with plazas, terraces, and built compounds. Western terraces include pale-stone figurative designs, notably camelids, set into terrace walls.
rows.limits: It is a separate place from Machu Picchu. Differing official inventories count terrace motifs differently, so no combined figure total is asserted here; symbolic interpretations also remain proposals.

sections.heading: Named buildings share a city chronology, not an exact birthday

paragraphs.text: Machu Picchu’s gateways, residences, temples, and terraces formed parts of a connected settlement. Radiocarbon studies of people and deposits provide two existing occupation models, while individual walls generally lack separate construction dates. The models therefore remain alternatives for the settlement’s chronology rather than exact dates for every building.

rows.name: Temple of the Sun / Torreón
rows.dates: Inka architectural phase; site-context window 1420–1532 CE
rows.architecture: Curved fine masonry rises around a natural granite outcrop. Its windows and the worked rock form a deliberately integrated architectural ensemble.
rows.limits: The solar name and proposed ritual or astronomical functions do not establish a unique original use. No separate construction date is assigned.

rows.name: Casa del Inka / royal residence
rows.dates: Inka architectural phase; site-context window 1420–1532 CE
rows.architecture: The compound lies next to the first fountains and the Temple of the Sun. Its carefully finished masonry distinguishes it within the surrounding urban fabric.
rows.limits: The conventional royal-residence attribution does not identify a particular named occupant or date a visit. No separate construction date is assigned.

sections.heading: A plaza and its neighboring temples

paragraphs.text: The Sacred Plaza is a compact architectural ensemble. It should be distinguished from the long Plaza Principal between the western and eastern urban sectors. On the map, the Main Temple, Three Windows building and open Sacred Plaza each have a separate public locator so that their spatial relationships can be explored without treating them as one anonymous monument.

rows.name: Main Temple beside the Sacred Plaza
rows.architecture: The Main Temple forms part of the Sacred Plaza ensemble, alongside the Three Windows building and another enclosure. These are adjoining but distinct structures.
rows.limits: Architectural association does not prove simultaneous construction or one exclusive ceremonial function.

rows.name: Temple of the Three Windows
rows.architecture: Three large openings distinguish a fine masonry building beside the Sacred Plaza. Its relationship to neighboring buildings is documented in official plans.
rows.limits: The openings are physical evidence; proposed origin myths or symbolic meanings require additional interpretation.

rows.name: Sacred Plaza / Plaza de los Templos
rows.architecture: An open ceremonial space links the Main Temple, Three Windows building and neighboring enclosure; its architecture differs from the long central Plaza Principal.
rows.limits: This is the Sacred Plaza, not the central Plaza Principal investigated by geophysical studies. Its construction is not separately dated.

sections.heading: Worked rock, water and proposed ceremonial meanings

paragraphs.text: Machu Picchu’s buildings repeatedly incorporate natural stone. The Intiwatana ensemble, Temple of the Sun and Condor complex show different ways of reshaping or enclosing bedrock. Conventional names help visitors identify places, but a name can preserve a later interpretation rather than the original category used by residents. The physical evidence and the proposed function remain separate.

rows.name: Intiwatana hill and carved rock
rows.architecture: A terraced rocky eminence supports a worked stone feature and associated architecture above the ceremonial sector. The ensemble reshapes natural bedrock rather than simply placing a freestanding object on a flat site.
rows.limits: The exact carving date and every proposed astronomical function remain unestablished here.

rows.name: Temple of the Condor
rows.architecture: A worked rock, natural outcrops and built enclosures form the complex conventionally called the Temple of the Condor, in the eastern urban sector.
rows.limits: Its conventional name is interpretive. Neither a prison nor a sacrifice chamber is asserted.

rows.name: Conjunto Espejos de Agua / Water Mirrors
rows.architecture: Two circular stone features sit at floor level within an enclosure. Official publications use both water-mirror and mortar terminology for this place.
rows.limits: Astronomical observation is an interpretation, not proof that this was its only use. No independently dated installation phase is available.

sections.heading: Preparing terrain before raising buildings

paragraphs.text: Research beneath Plaza Principal proposes a sequence involving quarry use, drainage works and successive remodeling of the open area. This is a relative construction history. It is valuable even without a calendar date for every stage: buried features show that the present surface is the outcome of choices and alterations. The authors combine excavation with indirect subsurface imaging, so inferred continuations must be distinguished from excavated sections.

rows.name: Plaza Principal subsurface sequence
rows.dates: Relative phases within the Inka building history
rows.architecture: Quarrying, engineered drainage and reshaping precede the finished open-space ensemble.
rows.limits: No additional independently dated plaza record is proposed here; this is contextual explanation, and the Sacred Plaza map point must not be relabeled as Plaza Principal.

rows.name: Main Gateway
rows.architecture: A controlled opening marks an entrance into the built settlement from the agricultural side. It connects the city to paths through the wider mountain landscape.
rows.limits: Access control does not identify every visitor, route or ceremonial act, and this is not an independently dated gate.

sections.heading: From royal estate to continuing Andean heritage

paragraphs.text: The existing retainer-community record makes the city’s inhabitants more visible: people with diverse geographic ancestries lived in the estate context. Those results do not identify everyone’s spoken language or the route by which each person arrived. The site’s later history also cannot be reduced to “lost” and “discovered”: the heritage authority’s brochure describes intermittent later visitation and habitation, and its planning documents recognize neighboring Quechua communities.

Continue to the Inca civilization guide for Cusco, imperial formation and the wider political setting. The comparison connects a particular built estate to a larger history; it does not make every Inka place contemporary or give all residents the same role.

pages.title: Maya centres: different cities, histories, and monumental plans
pages.intro: These four public archaeological centres belong to a much larger Maya world. Their temples, palaces, inscriptions, reservoirs, and open spaces record distinct dynasties and changing regional relationships, rather than one capital governing an unchanging empire.

sections.heading: Four centres to compare

paragraphs.text: A site's broad occupation span is not the date of every surviving monument. Buildings could cover earlier structures, and carved texts could commemorate events long before their own dedication. Compare the material sequence, named rulers, and dated inscriptions at each centre before assigning a single founding or ending year to the whole Maya world.

rows.name: Tikal, Guatemala
rows.dates: Occupation extends from the Preclassic into the early tenth century; the principal monumental ensembles accumulated across many episodes.
rows.architecture: The Great Plaza, Lost World complex, twin-pyramid groups, palaces, ball courts, causeways, and reservoirs form parts of a much wider settlement.
rows.limits: The park boundary, monumental core, and residential landscape have different extents. Reservoirs and peripheral settlements are essential context; visible pyramids are only part of the city.

rows.name: Palenque, Chiapas, Mexico
rows.dates: A major Classic-period capital, especially prominent during the sixth through eighth centuries.
rows.architecture: The Palace, Temple of the Inscriptions, and Cross Group combine masonry buildings, modeled decoration, and extensive dynastic and mythological texts. Pakal's seventh-century reign is central to its monumental history.
rows.limits: A ruler's reign does not date every wall. Tombs, temple superstructures, texts, and later additions need separate archaeological histories.

rows.name: Copán, Honduras
rows.dates: A Classic dynasty began in the fifth century; the centre's political and monumental history changed substantially before early tenth-century abandonment.
rows.architecture: The Acropolis, plazas, sculpted stelae, and Hieroglyphic Stairway connect public space, royal monuments, and written accounts of dynastic authority.
rows.limits: The inscribed stairway is a historical monument as well as architecture. Interpretations must consider displaced blocks and reconstruction, rather than assuming the visible stair text survives entirely in original order.

rows.name: Chichén Itzá, Yucatán, Mexico
rows.dates: Monumental building spans different phases, including important northern ensembles around the Terminal Classic and Early Postclassic transition.
rows.architecture: El Castillo, the Temple of the Warriors, columned spaces, the Great Ball Court, and El Caracol occupy a landscape with cenotes and earlier building groups.
rows.limits: Architectural connections with central Mexico do not by themselves prove a single invasion date or the ethnicity of every builder. Later written traditions and archaeological construction sequences should remain distinguishable.

pages.title: Maya cultures: writing, ritual, and continuing communities
pages.intro: Maya history includes many languages, regional traditions, and political centres. Ancient monumental cities and contemporary Maya communities are connected histories, while particular practices and institutions changed over time.

sections.heading: Religion and ritual

paragraphs.text: Ceremony linked calendars, farming, sacred places, and political authority, with substantial local variation. Smithsonian accounts describe living Yucatec offerings connected with rain and harvests and highland Guatemalan ceremonies marking sacred-calendar cycles. These contemporary practices illuminate continuing relationships with time and land; they should not be projected unchanged onto every ancient temple or dynasty. Archaeological images and inscriptions add different kinds of evidence.

sections.heading: Languages and writing

paragraphs.text: Maya is not the name of one uniform spoken language. Smithsonian describes more than thirty living Mayan languages. Ancient writing combined signs for whole words with syllabic signs; decipherment relates signs to the languages encoded in particular texts. A carved inscription can preserve royal names, events, and calendrical statements, but script affiliation does not establish the everyday speech of every resident of a city.

sections.heading: Growth, political transformation, and survival

paragraphs.text: Maya centres developed through long Preclassic and Classic histories. During the late first millennium, many southern lowland dynasties and cities lost population or political power, while other regions followed different trajectories. Archaeologist Jeremy Sabloff emphasizes political fragmentation and population movement rather than the disappearance of Maya people. Northern centres and highland communities continued, followed by profound colonial disruptions and continuing Maya histories into the present.
