pages.title: Cahokia: earthworks and open spaces of a major Mississippian centre
pages.intro: Cahokia stands in the American Bottom near present-day Collinsville, Illinois. Its monumental core belonged to a wider agricultural and settlement landscape. Earthwork dimensions and mound totals are architectural evidence, not direct resident counts.

sections.heading: Reading three parts of the centre

paragraphs.text: UNESCO places Cahokia's greatest prominence around 1050–1150 CE within a longer Mississippian history. Mounds served different purposes: some supported buildings, others contained burials or marked important places. The present protected property, surviving mounds, and the original metropolitan landscape are different inventories. Modern reconstruction, erosion, and excavation also affect what a visitor sees today.

rows.name: Monks Mound and the Grand Plaza
rows.dates: Built and enlarged during Cahokia's Mississippian occupation; not a single construction event.
rows.architecture: A large, multiterraced earthen platform dominates the central open-space ensemble. Its summit supported a substantial building, while the plaza created space for gathering and public activity.
rows.limits: Reconstructing leadership roles requires interpretation of architecture and associated evidence. The modern name refers to much later monks and is not the original Indigenous name.

rows.name: Woodhenge
rows.dates: Mississippian-period post-circle constructions, known through excavated post settings; the standing display is reconstructed.
rows.architecture: Timber circles west of the monumental centre are interpreted in relation to seasonal solar observations. The reconstructed posts help explain a vanished wooden structure.
rows.limits: The modern timber is not original surviving wood. A seasonal alignment supports observation and timekeeping interpretations, but does not independently recover every associated ritual.

rows.name: Mound 72
rows.dates: A sequence of mortuary deposits and mound-building episodes within Cahokia's earlier monumental history.
rows.architecture: A comparatively small ridge-topped mound covered complex burial deposits and associated objects, providing evidence of mortuary ceremony and social distinctions.
rows.limits: Later reanalysis revised influential interpretations of the beaded burial. Avoid repeating the older male-warrior-and-retainers narrative as settled fact; biological assessments and social identities are distinct questions.

sections.heading: A village beneath the monumental plaza

paragraphs.text: The Grand Plaza was built over an inhabited landscape. Excavated domestic deposits and ceramics precede fills that reshaped the terrain into a much larger open space. These are two observations at the same place: earlier habitation and later earthmoving. Their overlapping rounded windows reflect archaeological resolution, not a contradiction that must be removed by inventing a precise turnover year.

rows.name: Pre-plaza habitation
rows.dates: Merrell and Edelhardt contexts, approximately 950–1050 CE
rows.architecture: Village deposits and ceramics survive beneath later plaza fill.
rows.limits: A sampled occupation context, not every household or an annual residence record.

rows.name: Grand Plaza construction
rows.architecture: Filling and leveling created an extensive engineered open space.
rows.limits: The display range is an editorial expression of “middle 11 th century,” not a probability interval.

sections.heading: Monks Mound: separate modeled boundaries

paragraphs.text: A statistical reassessment proposes rapid major construction at Monks Mound. It estimates separate ranges for the beginning of the main mound, its completion, and completion of the first terrace. The ranges express uncertainty about when each event happened, rather than the duration of continuous work.

rows.name: Main mound start
rows.architecture: Modeled boundary before the principal mound-building effort.
rows.limits: Contextual dates constrain the event; this is not a directly dated basket-load of earth.

rows.name: Main mound completion
rows.architecture: Modeled completion of the main body before the separate first-terrace boundary.
rows.limits: Overlapping boundary distributions do not reverse the stratigraphic order.

rows.name: First-terrace completion
rows.architecture: Completion boundary for the modeled terrace phase.
rows.limits: The geographic anchor is mound-wide, not a mapped construction front.

sections.heading: Different mounds preserve different histories

paragraphs.text: The smaller mounds cannot all be assigned Monks Mound’s model. Mound 48 has a tentative single-episode interpretation, while Mound 51 preserves at least two stages above a filled borrow pit. Fox Mound is visible in the paired southern group but lacks the excavation history needed for comparable phase dating. The map therefore shows different degrees of chronological confidence.

rows.name: Mound 48
rows.architecture: Coring suggests one main construction episode.
rows.limits: “Probably” is retained; the phase window is not a measured construction duration.

rows.name: Mound 51 / Persimmon Mound
rows.architecture: Two or more stages, fire features and an underlying filled borrow pit.
rows.limits: The individual stages remain undated in the inspected source.

rows.name: Mound 60 / Fox Mound
rows.architecture: Rectangular platform paired with conical Round Top at the southern plaza edge.
rows.limits: Form and pairing are better established than exact date or function.

sections.heading: Timber monuments and an enclosure rebuilt

paragraphs.text: Woodhenge and the stockade make vanished wooden architecture visible through post settings and reconstruction. The official brochure assigns the timber-circle sequence to 1100–1200 and the four enclosures to 1175–1275. Both are broad sequences. They show repeated work, but they do not supply an exact construction year for every post or prove an annual threat of attack.

rows.name: Woodhenge circles
rows.architecture: Partly excavated post circles; the standing display reconstructs the third circle.
rows.limits: Older institutional date ranges differ. The map labels the public area, not original surviving posts.

rows.name: Stockade / palisade
rows.architecture: Successive log enclosures defined the central precinct.
rows.limits: The point is a southern public reconstruction; no battle or named attacker is inferred.

sections.heading: Mound 34: activity before and after a platform

paragraphs.text: East of Monks Mound, the Ramey Plaza group adds a different local sequence. Mound 34 covers earlier structures, some placed around 1200, and evidence of copper working. The research account then distinguishes an initial platform, a larger mound and adjoining terraces. Burning at a summit building is an observation; its cause cannot be read directly from the burned material.

rows.name: Premound buildings and working area
rows.architecture: Wall-trench structures and copper-working evidence precede the mound.
rows.limits: The rounded window is not an excavator’s confidence interval or a lifetime for every building.

rows.name: Platform and terrace construction
rows.dates: Broad post 1200 urban context, not a direct date
rows.architecture: Successive platform work, terrace additions and a summit building.
rows.limits: The outer 1400 limit is contextual; individual stages remain unresolved.

sections.heading: After the medieval city, Indigenous histories continue

paragraphs.text: The River L’Abbe mission was established on Monks Mound’s first terrace in 1735 and operated until 1752. It belongs to Cahokia people of the Illinois Confederation and French mission history, centuries after the main urban phase. Regional evidence also rejects an equation between urban decline and an empty landscape. The Peoria Tribe continues Illinois community histories; the Osage Nation’s account connects ancestral heritage and continuing responsibilities to the mound landscapes around St. Louis.

Mound building linked diverse Mississippian communities across different towns and centuries. These archaeological traditions belong within longer Indigenous histories. Living tribal connections to ancestral landscapes continue beyond the periods when particular monumental centers flourished.

rows.name: River L’Abbe mission
rows.architecture: A later mission on the first terrace of Monks Mound.
rows.limits: Reuse the existing mission record with a refined mound location; do not duplicate it as an ancient construction phase.

pages.title: Mississippian cultures: connected societies, not one nation
pages.intro: Mississippian is an archaeological label for diverse communities sharing aspects of agriculture, settlement, material culture, and ceremony across much of the eastern and southeastern United States. Cahokia was an important centre within this varied world.

sections.heading: Religion and ritual

paragraphs.text: Mounds, public gathering places, mortuary deposits, and images on shell, copper, ceramics, and stone provide evidence of ceremonial life. Illinois State Museum stresses that religious ideas are reconstructed by combining archaeology with historical accounts, not read directly from objects. Shared symbols across regions suggest connections, while local differences and changing practices caution against assuming one uniform religion or an identical role for every mound.

sections.heading: Language and identity

paragraphs.text: The archaeological category does not identify a single language or tribe. At Cahokia, researchers infer a population drawn from different regions, likely speaking multiple languages or dialects. No securely deciphered local writing provides a citywide linguistic census. Connections with later Indigenous nations are essential historical evidence, but should not be converted into a simple one-to-one language assignment for every earlier town or ceremonial centre.

sections.heading: Rise, changing centres, and continuing communities

paragraphs.text: Maize farming, exchange, migration, and new forms of political organization contributed to the growth of mound-centred communities, with different regional chronologies. At Ocmulgee, the Macon Plateau centre diminished by about 1200 while other Mississippian places continued; Lamar developed later nearby. Warfare, population movement, and colonial violence and disease reshaped communities at different times. The decline of a centre is not the disappearance of its descendants.

pages.title: Pacific monumental places: four distinct island histories
pages.intro: This collection compares monuments across a vast ocean without treating them as one culture. Pohnpei, Tonga, Rapa Nui, and Hawaiʻi have distinct languages, political histories, ceremonial traditions, and relationships with their ancestral places.

sections.heading: Nan Madol and Pohnpei

paragraphs.text: Nan Madol combined chiefly residences, ceremonial places, and mortuary structures within Pohnpei's political history. UNESCO relates it to the Saudeleur era and continuing Nahnmwarki institutions, rather than a vanished people. Pohnpeian is a living language associated with the island; this contemporary linguistic connection is not a decoded record of every ancient resident's speech. Architecture and oral traditions provide complementary kinds of historical evidence.

rows.name: Nan Madol, Pohnpei
rows.dates: UNESCO broadly dates the surviving stone palaces, temples, tombs, and residential domains to about 1200–1500 CE.
rows.architecture: More than one hundred constructed islets, basalt walls, coral fill, and waterways form a monumental complex off southeastern Pohnpei.
rows.limits: Islet counts are not house or population totals. Separate individual construction dates from the broad Saudeleur-era range; customary ownership and spiritual significance continue.

sections.heading: Tonga: capitals, tombs, and continuing chiefly histories

paragraphs.text: Heketā and Lapaha belong to the history of Tuʻi Tonga authority. Tonga's national submission associates royal tombs and ongoing burial traditions with both spiritual and political power. Tongan is a distinct living language; neither its relationship to other Polynesian languages nor similar stonework makes these monuments part of a single Pacific state. Genealogical traditions, recorded histories, and archaeological dates should be identified separately.

rows.name: Heketā and Lapaha, Tongatapu
rows.dates: The trilithon is traditionally attributed to Tuʻitātui around 1200; royal tomb development at Lapaha has a longer, varied history.
rows.architecture: Haʻamonga ʻa Maui uses two upright coral-limestone slabs and a lintel. Lapaha's langi are stepped earthen funerary platforms faced with stone.
rows.limits: These places are on Tonga's UNESCO Tentative List. The submission explicitly questions the origins of later sundial claims; oral attributions are not precise laboratory dates.

sections.heading: Rapa Nui: ancestors, platforms, and later ceremonial changes

paragraphs.text: Moai represented ancestors within Rapa Nui's own ceremonial landscape. Ahu platforms, quarries, rock art, houses, and the later Orongo ceremonial village record varied activities and changing practices. Rapa Nui is also a living Polynesian language supported by contemporary revitalization programmes. Political and ritual transformation and the severe effects of colonial intrusion should remain distinct from unsupported claims that monument building ended in one simple ecological collapse.

rows.name: Rapa Nui: Rano Raraku, ahu, and Orongo
rows.dates: Monumental and ceremonial traditions changed over centuries; the UNESCO synthesis places major works broadly within the eleventh–seventeenth centuries.
rows.architecture: Rano Raraku preserves carving stages; ahu carried ancestral statues, including the fifteen-moai ensemble at Ahu Tongariki. Orongo has a different ceremonial and architectural character.
rows.limits: The broad span is not a secure first-settlement date. Standing displays and re-erected statues require separate conservation histories; no island-wide resident count is inferred.

sections.heading: Hawaiʻi: a historically dated temple and political unification

paragraphs.text: Puʻukoholā links a particular Hawaiian heiau with Kamehameha's rise, prophecy, and worship associated with Kū. NPS places it within a hierarchical chiefly society and the kapu system, which was overturned in 1819. ʻŌlelo Hawaiʻi is the Indigenous Hawaiian language and remains central to cultural continuity. These events have their own historical chronology, distinct from the earlier monuments of Pohnpei, Tonga, or Rapa Nui.

rows.name: Puʻukoholā Heiau, Kawaihae, Hawaiʻi Island
rows.dates: Built under Kamehameha in 1790–1791, a specifically documented late-eighteenth-century project.
rows.architecture: A substantial dry-stone temple platform occupies a coastal hill. Its construction and dedication formed part of Kamehameha's struggle for power.
rows.limits: The heiau's completion is distinct from the later unification of the Hawaiian Islands. It is a continuing culturally significant place, not a generic example of all Polynesian religion.

pages.title: Caral and the Supe Valley: buildings, food and changing centres
pages.intro: Caral was one settlement in an inhabited Supe Valley linked to the Pacific coast. Monumental platforms, gathering spaces, and residential architecture connected neighboring communities with farming and marine resources.

sections.heading: A valley of places, not one enormous dot

paragraphs.text: Caral’s central zone includes monumental platforms, residential spaces and open gathering areas. Its published 2001 study describes six major platform mounds, with the Pirámide Mayor the largest. The settlement plan is evidence of organized construction; it is not a census of inhabitants or proof that every feature was contemporary.

Lurihuasi and Chupacigarro are separately mapped here because they have named localities and explicit dated contexts. Áspero provides coastal context. Miraya, Alpacoto and other substantial neighbours appear in the research, but their individual building chronologies require further work before every structure can be animated.

rows.name: Caral: central zone
rows.dates: Published construction and occupation references mainly 2627–2020 calibrated BCE
rows.architecture: Major platform mounds, residential architecture and sunken circular plazas.
rows.limits: The 2001 abstract gives a different younger endpoint, 1977 BCE. The atlas preserves the main-text/Table 1 interpretation and notes the discrepancy.

rows.name: Caral: two platform/plaza contexts
rows.dates: Reference dates around 2470 and 2290 calibrated BCE
rows.architecture: Two construction-associated observations, not a date for the entire city.
rows.limits: Mapped at the public Caral site anchor. Exact sample positions and annual construction progress are not reconstructed.

rows.name: Chupacigarro
rows.architecture: Platform and sunken circular plaza complex.
rows.limits: A single reference date has uncertainty and does not establish a one-year construction campaign.

rows.name: Lurihuasi
rows.architecture: Large communal and residential complex near Caral.
rows.limits: The older radiocarbon determination has substantial error. One dated context does not establish the duration of the whole settlement.

rows.name: Áspero
rows.dates: Earlier excavation series summarized as 3000–2400 calibrated BCE
rows.architecture: Coastal settlement and artificial platform mounds.
rows.limits: This sample window is narrower than the site’s full known history.

sections.heading: People, work and connections

paragraphs.text: Plant remains and marine foods at Caral connect inland cultivation with coastal resources. Cotton, foods from cultivated plots, shellfish and fish place daily work alongside monumental building. Moving food and material inland is evidence of connection; it does not by itself identify a trader, the frequency of exchange or an exact road.

Gathering plazas and residential sectors provided different settings for activity within Supe settlements. The contrast brings communal building and household life into the same landscape. Construction samples help date particular episodes within the longer histories of these places.

sections.heading: Transformation, uncertainty and later communities

paragraphs.text: Sand deposits cover late Preceramic occupation at Caral; ceramic-bearing deposits above them record later activity. Sandweiss and colleagues proposed interactions among earthquakes, El Niño, coastal change and blown sand. They presented a testable explanation, not a precisely dated single disaster that automatically explains every local departure.

At Vichama, the early monumental sequence is dated to 1800–1500 BCE and includes six architectural periods. Later contexts dated to 1000–1300 CE belong to a separate occupation. These observations extend the local story without claiming that all Caral residents moved to Vichama or that the intervening centuries were continuously occupied.

rows.name: Vichama: early sequence
rows.architecture: Public and residential architecture through six building periods.
rows.limits: The broad sequence is not a foundation date for each building.

rows.name: Vichama: later contexts
rows.architecture: Later occupation at an older place.
rows.limits: The long gap remains visible; late occupation does not establish continuous use since the early monumental phase.

sections.heading: What the map can and cannot yet show

paragraphs.text: Caral’s dated construction deposits belong to a wider Supe landscape of neighboring centers and coastal connections. The sequence of every building and the timing of exchanges remain incompletely known. Individual samples provide reference points within those longer histories.

pages.title: Kuk: a working landscape through time
pages.intro: Kuk preserves separate episodes of cultivation and water management in the New Guinea highlands. It is an agricultural landscape with changing practices, not a single town founded once and occupied unchanged for ten thousand years.

sections.heading: Reading the phases

paragraphs.text: Early plant-use evidence and the later engineering of mounds and ditches answer different questions. The Phase 1 authors disagree about whether channel 101 was substantially artificial. The safer interpretation keeps early activity visible while explaining why a fully developed drainage system is less certain.

The two older atlas entries now use the scientific calibrated onset windows: 6950–6440 cal BP for mounding and 4350–3980 cal BP for ditching, referenced to 1950. An onset window is not a claim that every structure stayed in use throughout that range.

rows.name: Phase 1: wetland margin
rows.architecture: Plant use and modified surfaces; interpretation of channel 101 disputed.
rows.limits: Plant exploitation is better established than the strongest drainage/agriculture claim.

rows.name: Phase 2: mounds
rows.architecture: Mounded cultivation changes growing conditions at the wetland edge.
rows.limits: Agricultural practice, not first settlement of New Guinea.

rows.name: Phase 3: ditching
rows.architecture: Ditched cultivation begins.
rows.limits: Not a continuous link between every earlier and later field system.

rows.name: Phase 4: gridded fields
rows.dates: Approximately 2000–1100 years before 1950; late ash boundary 720–980 CE
rows.architecture: Major disposal channels and narrow ditches divide fields.
rows.limits: Rounded phase and uncertain ending; not every plot cultivated every year.

rows.name: Phase 5: renewed drainage
rows.dates: Charcoal 1310–1620 CE; ditch wood and spade association 1430–1650 CE
rows.architecture: Flat-bottomed ditches and raised fields.
rows.limits: These dated materials do not fix the exact onset of the whole phase.

rows.name: Phase 6: sweet-potato era
rows.dates: Approximately 1700 into the early twentieth century
rows.architecture: Renewed gardens, reuse of some ditches, changes in pig husbandry.
rows.limits: The first local sweet potato is not directly dated to 1700.

sections.heading: Gardens, fallows and tools

paragraphs.text: Channels moved water, while field surfaces and raised ground affected the conditions around roots. The authors discuss soil fertility, crop pests, drought and the practical costs of maintaining ditches. These are explanations for changing land use, not measurements of annual crop yields.

A wooden spade associated with dated ditch wood makes labour tangible: people dug, recut and maintained drainage. The evidence also allows disuse and renewal. Some older alignments were reused in later gardening, while others survived as abandoned features.

Wetland gardening and cultivation on surrounding dry land had different histories at Kuk. Ditches could fall out of use and later be reused while farming continued elsewhere in the valley. Gaps in one agricultural system therefore need not mean that people left the wider landscape.

sections.heading: Kawelka history, warfare and the twentieth-century observation

paragraphs.text: Kawelka oral histories connect departure from Kuk with defeat in warfare. Published reconstructions suggest dates around 1914 or 1920. This is represented as an approximate local episode; the record does not invent battle participants, casualties or a precisely surveyed relocation route.

European visitors found Kuk’s wetland overgrown and uninhabited in 1933, following Kawelka departure from the locality. Customary ownership continued, and the observation did not describe the whole Wahgi Valley. Later return, research, and land use added further chapters to this history.

rows.name: Kawelka departure
rows.architecture: Oral histories connect departure to warfare.
rows.limits: Chronology and circumstances remain qualified; no count of deaths is asserted.

rows.name: 1933 observation
rows.architecture: Wetland described as swamp grassland after departure.
rows.limits: A local observation, not the end of Kawelka identity or ownership.

sections.heading: Connections to the larger atlas

paragraphs.text: The independent sweet-potato movie follows the crop. This place movie instead follows Kuk in the shared world, including its earlier cultivation and later community history. Every dated observation is also available on the master map. Field geometry, local dryland settlements and more detailed exchange histories remain research priorities.

pages.title: Upano: individual centres in a connected landscape
pages.intro: People built settlements, roads, and engineered fields in the Upano Valley. Excavation reveals local construction and occupation, while nearby lake sediments preserve cultivation and forest use. The proposed regional chronology remains disputed.

sections.heading: Sangay and Kilamope are different places

paragraphs.text: At Sangay, also called Huapula, the excavated Complex XI lies beside the Huapula stream. Platforms surround low plazas, and a path links the complex to the stream. This local arrangement sits within a much larger settlement of platform groups and streets.

At Kilamope, the excavated western complex has two sunken plazas and a central platform bounded by elongated mounds. Excavation on the southern platform revealed a housing structure. This is evidence of domestic activity at a particular centre, not merely a diffuse zone of cultural influence.

rows.name: Sangay / Huapula, Complex XI
rows.dates: Contextualized within the proposed 500 BCE–300/600 CE Kilamope/Upano horizon
rows.architecture: Platform group, plazas, path to stream and domestic evidence.
rows.limits: The public coordinate locates Complex XI. Regional phase dates do not directly date each platform.

rows.name: Kilamope, western complex
rows.dates: Contextualized within the same proposed early horizon
rows.architecture: Two plazas, peripheral platforms and excavated house evidence.
rows.limits: A separate settlement down the valley; the reference point does not outline every building.

rows.name: Later Huapula occupation
rows.architecture: Reuse of earlier mounds, with a different settlement pattern.
rows.limits: Not proof of violent replacement or a secure language assignment.

sections.heading: How strong is the timeline?

paragraphs.text: Rostain and colleagues proposed a sequence based on stratigraphy, pottery and radiocarbon work. A 2024 scholarly e-letter challenges consistency between the narrative and supporting chronology. The atlas retains the mapped earthworks while explicitly qualifying the dates and cultural assignments; it does not replace one uncertain sequence with another invented one.

LiDAR describes surviving landforms. It cannot tell us by itself when each structure was built, how many people occupied every platform, what language they spoke, or whether a mapped road was active throughout a regional phase. The current movie shows named excavated centres; detailed surveyed road geometry and building-specific chronology remain expansion work.

sections.heading: A lake record adds a different kind of continuity

paragraphs.text: A 2025 study of Lake Cormorán identifies crop microfossils and changes in vegetation. It places local cultivation from about 570 BCE and a decline ending around 550 CE. Because the evidence comes from a lake catchment, it cannot establish that all settlements across the Upano Valley were simultaneously abandoned.

The same study identifies a later wave of land use beginning around 1500 CE. This provides evidence of activity after the famous mound-building period. It does not identify the farmers’ language, ancestry or relationship to colonial government, and its environmental signal is not an excavated town.

rows.name: Lake Cormorán: early cultivation
rows.architecture: Maize indicators and vegetation changes within the catchment.
rows.limits: Age-model and catchment limits; not a universal urban chronology.

rows.name: Lake Cormorán: later land use
rows.architecture: Renewed cultivation and disturbance after a long local interval.
rows.limits: No ethnic label or colonial consent inferred from pollen.

sections.heading: Keeping the wider world present

paragraphs.text: Upano’s named centers formed part of a wider Amazonian history of settlement and landscape engineering. Roads and fields connected built places, while environmental evidence records changing land use. The sequence of individual centers and the periods when particular roads were used remain incompletely dated.

sources.title: Stéphen Rostain et al. — Two thousand years of garden urbanism in the Upper Amazon
Alden Mauro Yépez et al. — E-letter concerning the consistency of the cultural sequence in the Upano supplement
Mark B. Bush et al. — Ecological legacies and recent footprints of the Amazon’s Lost City
CNRS News — Ancient Cities in the Amazon: interview with Stéphen Rostain

pages.title: Chavín de Huántar
pages.intro: Follow successive building projects and specific deposited objects at Chavín, with the disagreements between architectural and ceramic sequences kept visible.

sections.heading: Building a monument through successive projects

paragraphs.text: People assembled and repeatedly altered a stone ceremonial complex at the meeting of highland valleys. Construction joins, enclosed passages, stairways, drains and ventilation systems reveal successive decisions. Kembel and Haas place the principal growth of the monumental architecture between 1200 and 800 calibrated BCE. Their dates concern building materials and construction sequences, rather than a complete census of settlement. New masonry could enclose earlier spaces, change circulation and create restricted interiors. Buildings A–D, the Circular Plaza and the Black-and-White Portal belong to this changing architectural setting, but each component cannot simply inherit the starting date of the entire sequence.
Scene anchor at the earlier end of a construction-model interval, not a precise foundation year.

sections.heading: An intense period of architectural transformation

paragraphs.text: The architectural chronology places thirteen of fifteen construction phases across roughly 1200–800 calibrated BCE, with especially intensive building during 1000–800. That concentration points to repeated projects within the monument rather than an unchanged temple lasting for centuries. Passages, stairs and courts shaped access and movement, while construction seams preserve traces of transformations that are no longer obvious from the exterior. The relative architectural sequence is better resolved than an independent absolute date for every room. Rebuilding required labor, but the inspected chronology does not count workers or establish their political obligations. The material story is one of enlargement and reorganization, with older architecture repeatedly incorporated into new arrangements.
Contextual anchor for the modeled 1000–800 cal BCE pulse; phase medians are not available in inspected abstract.

sections.heading: Urabarriu and a competing starting point

paragraphs.text: Urabarriu pottery belongs to the early history of Chavín as an inhabited ceremonial place. Burger dates the phase to 950–800 calibrated BCE, later than the beginning proposed by the architectural study. The disagreement concerns how pottery, charred remains, and building materials fit into the site's sequence. These materials can date different activities, so the competing chronologies remain distinct rather than yielding a single agreed foundation year.
950 BCE anchors Burger’s Urabarriu model; competing construction model begins earlier.

sections.heading: Activity during architectural stasis

paragraphs.text: Around 800 BCE, the architectural model shifts from intensive growth to stasis, while Burger’s ceramic model begins Chakinani. Limited monumental enlargement does not establish that people stopped gathering, depositing objects or maintaining spaces. Gallery 3 provides a concrete setting for those practices: it is embedded in the South Atrium platform near the Circular Plaza, within the architectural group that contains the Ofrendas and Caracolas galleries. Its deposits contain carefully contextualized artifacts, although their broad modeled envelope cannot date every visit. Ceramic phases, building sequences and deposits reveal related histories, with the date of gallery construction remaining distinct from the dates of objects placed inside it.
800 BCE is a phase-boundary anchor in competing models, not a single dated transition.

sections.heading: Inhalers, plants and restricted interiors

paragraphs.text: Objects excavated from Gallery 3 reveal what participants handled in a restricted interior. Residue studies identified vilca and tobacco through complementary chemical and microbotanical methods on bone inhalers and related equipment. These findings support psychoactive-plant use in the small gallery, while the identities, experiences and motivations of individual participants remain unknown. Vilca does not demonstrate an Amazonian caravan: the authors identify suitable lower Mosna environments roughly a day’s walk away. The published contextual envelope is approximately 800–350 BCE. A date within that range provides orientation, but the tested artifacts need not have been used together or deposited during a single ceremony.
700 BCE is an illustrative anchor inside the contextual envelope; no specific use event dated to that year.

sections.heading: Different endings for buildings and ceramic phases

paragraphs.text: The later history has several different chronological endings. The existing Rick-based record places janabarroid contexts around 800–500 calibrated BCE; Burger places Janabarriu at 700–400. Kembel and Haas describe architectural stasis followed by physical collapse. The 2025 Gallery 3 paper also pairs prose about closure around 500 BCE with a modeled contextual envelope extending toward 350 BCE. These observations concern different evidence and models. None alone establishes the disappearance of a people or language. Changing use, continued deposition and damaged architecture are better supported than a single day when an entire community supposedly abandoned its ceremonial landscape.
500 BCE is a contextual comparison point; competing endpoints and gallery envelope remain explicit.

sections.heading: Dated observations and named places

rows.name: Chavín: modeled monumental construction growth
rows.architecture: Architectural-mortar dating places thirteen of fifteen construction phases across 1200–800 cal BCE. Within that span, 1000–800 is an especially intensive period; built-in ages and renovations require separate treatment.
rows.limits: Abstract supports dates; no sample-level claims. Abstract-reported calibrated construction model. Not the occupation interval of the whole settlement; intensive nested phase 1000–800. Public place reference only; the named structure or excavated sample is not separately geolocated.

rows.name: Chavín: Urabarriu contexts in Burger’s model
rows.architecture: Burger’s revised sequence places Urabarriu at 950–800 cal BCE. This alternative chronology must be shown alongside the earlier architectural construction model.
rows.limits: Published ceramic/radiocarbon phase model, not a universally accepted foundation boundary. Public place reference only; the named structure or excavated sample is not separately geolocated.

rows.name: Chavín: Chakinani phase in Burger’s model
rows.architecture: The revised ceramic sequence places Chakinani at 800–700 cal BCE while the architectural chronology describes 800–500 as a period of stasis. Activities and material sequences need not have identical boundaries.
rows.limits: Alternative phase estimate; not a direct date on a named plaza or gallery. Public place reference only; the named structure or excavated sample is not separately geolocated.

rows.name: Chavín Gallery 3: psychoactive-plant residues on inhalers
rows.architecture: Bone inhalers and related artifacts from Gallery 3 preserve microbotanical and chemical evidence of vilca and tobacco. The small internal gallery gives a specific setting for controlled ritual practice; residue evidence does not establish participants’ identities or an Amazonian trade route.
rows.limits: Public site proxy only; Gallery 3 has no invented individual coordinate. Published modeled floor/suprafloor context envelope; residue use is associated with these contexts. Not a direct date of each inhalation or a secure exact sealing date. Public place reference only; the named structure or excavated sample is not separately geolocated.

rows.name: Chavín: later Janabarriu range in an alternative model
rows.architecture: Burger’s Janabarriu range of 700–400 cal BCE differs from the existing Rick-based 800–500 chronology. Both are attributable scholarly models, not duplicate measurements of an uncontested boundary.
rows.limits: Explicit competing chronology; do not merge with existing 800–500 calibrated BCE observation. Public place reference only; the named structure or excavated sample is not separately geolocated.

sections.heading: Interpretations and remaining questions

paragraphs.text: Do not harmonize Kembel/Haas 1200–800 construction, Burger 950–400 ceramic/settlement model and existing Rick-based 800–500 janabarroid contexts into an invented consensus.
Gallery 3 prose around 500 BCE and contextual model through approximately 350 BCE require a caveat; supplementary chronological table was not checked.
Psychoactive residue does not establish specific subjective experiences, participant identities, an Amazonian origin or a fixed exchange route.
Language, ethnic identity, exact worker numbers and precise coordinates of restricted interiors are unsupported by these sources.

pages.title: Tiwanaku
pages.intro: A changing urban community, major monuments and later activity: follow what separate kinds of evidence say about the city’s growth and transformation.

sections.heading: A settlement before the monumental capital

paragraphs.text: People established a settlement at Tiwanaku before its best-known stone monuments were built. Later construction and immigration transformed it into a planned center in the Titicaca basin. A statistical model combining radiocarbon dates estimates foundation around AD 180; the broad 400–900 urban phase describes the later city. The earlier estimate does not identify a first house or a founding ethnic group. Settlement, monument building, and the growth of a political center unfolded through related stages of the place’s history.
Approximate modeled boundary; no exact founding event or invented confidence range.

sections.heading: Making Pumapunku

paragraphs.text: Stoneworkers at Pumapunku shaped blocks into carefully worked forms and assembled a major monument within Tiwanaku. Marsh and colleagues estimate the start of construction near AD 580. Later damage and displacement separated many blocks from their original positions. Vranich uses the surviving pieces to explore how the building may once have fitted together. The blocks themselves preserve the builders’ work; the reconstructed arrangement remains a hypothesis where the original masonry no longer survives in place.
580 is a boundary median, not a precise construction ceremony.

sections.heading: Reworking stone in a growing ceremonial city

paragraphs.text: A surface within Pumapunku’s sequence around modeled median AD 630 separates the last phase using newly quarried and carved stone from subsequent reuse. Builders continued to work with an inherited stock of masonry. Nearby monuments, including Akapana, Kalasasaya, the Semi-subterranean Temple and Putuni, have their own architectural histories rather than one shared foundation date. The model places Pumapunku’s main construction end around 710 and the citywide major construction boundary around 720. Those endpoints concern a particular scale and category of work. Later people still altered spaces and reused stone, so an end to major new monument building does not mean an end to all communal construction.
630, 710 and 720 are approximate modeled medians; scene anchor only.

sections.heading: Later communities remake older places

paragraphs.text: The ninth and tenth centuries included new communal work in an already old city. The current synthesis identifies later projects around AD 920–970 that reused inherited stone and spaces. At Putuni, earlier kitchens, stone-lined drains and mortuary activities were followed by razing, filling and construction of a large courtyard. Dated burials and a burned beam constrain parts of that sequence, but neither dates every wall or proves one destructive fire. People were selectively rebuilding and changing uses after the main period of new monument construction. A wood sample may predate the action associated with it, making context as important as the laboratory measurement.
940 is an orientation point within the contextual 920–970 range, not a directly dated project.

sections.heading: Permanent neighborhoods come to an end

paragraphs.text: The combined residential model places a major change near AD 1010: permanent residential activity in the sampled central neighborhoods ends within a main-text 95 percent interval of 970–1060. The abstract instead prints 970–1050. This is a bounded claim about permanent residence, not evidence that every person left on the same day. Individual neighborhoods have wider uncertainty ranges, and later small camps and burials represent different forms of presence. Long-lived house floors and rebuilt walls preserve evidence of continuing households; a short-lived hearth in an older ruin records another kind of activity. The end of the capital’s permanent neighborhoods was therefore not the end of all human connection to the place.
1010 is the combined modeled median; main text 970–1060 at 95%, abstract 970–1050.

sections.heading: Different practices end at different times

paragraphs.text: The last permanent houses and the last sampled redware discard have different modeled endings. Redware discard has a median around AD 1040 and a 1010–1080 95 percent interval. A vessel could remain in use, survive as an heirloom or enter later deposits, so this is not a universal last manufacturing date. The center’s contraction also differed from the wider basin’s history. Ceramic practices and raised-field activity continued at Lukurmata and Tiraska, while genomic work finds continuity among a small set of sampled Lukurmata individuals. Continued farming and sampled ancestry do not establish continued imperial government, and neither identifies a community’s language.
1040 is a modeled last-discard median; regional continuity is discussed without inventing new local dates.

sections.heading: Monuments become an inherited and recorded landscape

paragraphs.text: An early Spanish description in 1549 belongs to the later history of Tiwanaku’s monumental landscape. By then, its buildings already carried histories of reuse, damage and interpretation. Vranich’s architectural study draws on documentary evidence to explain why displaced and incomplete masonry requires careful reconstruction. The account is evidence of people encountering the remains, rather than an unfiltered picture of the original city. Subsequent looting and movement of blocks further changed what survives, although the study does not date every disturbance. Standing and fallen monuments continued to matter long after the ending of permanent residence in the ancient capital.
Documentary year, not an ancient architectural phase.

sections.heading: Dated observations and named places

rows.name: Tiwanaku: modeled early settlement boundary
rows.architecture: The corrected current article places the start of Tiwanaku around AD 180, preceding the familiar 400–900 monumental-city overview. This is a model-based approximate foundation, not a dated ceremony.
rows.limits: Current article abstract’s approximate modeled foundation; confidence range not reproduced in inspected abstract, so retain approximate singleton rather than invent one. Public place reference only; the named structure or excavated sample is not separately geolocated.

rows.name: Pumapunku: construction and reuse sequence
rows.architecture: Pumapunku’s construction sequence includes a change from newly quarried/carved stone to reuse, with major construction ending around modeled median AD 710. Its surviving displaced blocks do not justify a fully certain reconstruction.
rows.limits: Boundary medians, not full confidence limits or exact start/end years; newly carved stone ceases near median 630, followed by reuse. Public place reference only; the named structure or excavated sample is not separately geolocated.

rows.name: Tiwanaku: late communal projects using existing stone
rows.architecture: Later projects around 920–970 demonstrate renewed communal work after the main period of new monument construction. At Putuni, rebuilding involved razed/fill deposits, a large courtyard and reused stone; dated wood and burials constrain contexts rather than every wall.
rows.limits: Authors’ contextual range for later communal projects; not the complete construction span of Putuni or every named building. Public place reference only; the named structure or excavated sample is not separately geolocated.

rows.name: Tiwanaku: modeled end of permanent residence
rows.architecture: The combined model places the end of permanent residential activity near AD 1010, with the main-text 95% interval 970–1060. Small later camps, burials and practices in neighboring communities must remain distinct from the ending of the capital’s permanent neighborhoods.
rows.limits: Modeled ending boundary for sampled permanent residence; abstract instead prints 970–1050. It is not an interval of continued occupation everywhere, nor the end of later visits. Public place reference only; the named structure or excavated sample is not separately geolocated.

rows.name: Tiwanaku: modeled last redware discard
rows.architecture: Redware discard at central Tiwanaku ends near modeled median AD 1040. Later ceramics can be heirlooms or redeposited, and redware practices continue at other Titicaca settlements. This is an activity-specific boundary, not the extinction of a population or tradition.
rows.limits: Modeled last discard of sampled local redwares, not a universal last manufacture date; heirloom/redeposition questions remain. Public place reference only; the named structure or excavated sample is not separately geolocated.

rows.name: Tiwanaku: an early Spanish description of the monuments
rows.architecture: An early Spanish description in 1549 belongs to the later history of how Tiwanaku’s ruins were seen and recorded. Subsequent displacement and looting complicate reconstruction of ancient building arrangements.
rows.limits: Historical documentary date reported in the original architectural study; not a construction date. Public place reference only; the named structure or excavated sample is not separately geolocated.

sections.heading: Interpretations and remaining questions

paragraphs.text: Use corrected current 2023 article, read with 2024 correction; original figures and supplements were replaced.
Residential boundary discrepancy: body 970–1060 95%, abstract 970–1050. Keep it explicit; do not invent a corrected confidence bound.
Model medians 180, 580, 630, 710, 720, 1010 and 1040 are not exact dated events. Bayesian priors, calibration mixture and sample context matter.
Major-monument construction ending near 720 does not contradict later projects using reused stone around 920–970.
Do not infer whole-population disappearance, language or migration motives from seventeen genomes or end of central residence.
The sources do not establish a single conquest or drought as a complete explanation; local violent deaths and climate correlations are not a demonstrated empire-wide mechanism.

pages.title: Chan Chan and Chimor
pages.intro: Follow the growth and reorganization of adobe compounds, working communities and changing political authority without treating every wall as contemporary.

sections.heading: The first compounds in an expanding city

paragraphs.text: Chan Chan’s adobe walls belong to successive urban projects. Kolata’s brick-seriation model places the primary occupation of Chayhuac and Uhle around AD 900–1100. Their modern names, Chayhuac An and Xllangchic An, connect older scholarship with the named archaeological compounds. Walls, entrances and water-related features could be altered within and after these broad phases. Courts, storage and ceremonial spaces formed settings in which access and activities were organized. The estimated primary-occupancy phases are not radiocarbon foundation dates. Neither compound has a securely identified first ruler in the evidence considered here, and the royal-palace interpretation does not supply written biographies of its occupants.
900 anchors the start of an estimated 900–1100 primary-occupancy phase.

sections.heading: New walled compounds and controlled movement

paragraphs.text: Tello and Laberinto, now Tsuts An and Fechech An, belong to the next estimated primary-occupancy phase, approximately AD 1100–1200. Their architecture organized movement through courts, approaches to U-shaped structures and access to storage spaces. These arrangements support questions about administration, but do not identify the exact function of every room or status of every occupant. Topic interprets U-shaped buildings through information flow and a changing relationship between stewards and bureaucrats. That remains an attributed architectural interpretation, distinct from the estimated compound chronology. The physical organization of entrances and spaces provides stronger direct evidence than an assumed administrative title for each person who worked there.
1100 is the opening anchor of the estimated 1100–1200 compound phase.

sections.heading: A city of differently organized complexes

paragraphs.text: Gran Chimú and Squier occupy the Middle Chimú phase, approximately AD 1200–1300, in Kolata’s reconstruction. Their modern names are Utzh An and Fochic An. Different internal layouts and interpretations of unfinished features complicate any image of identical palaces repeated across the city. Those differences can reveal changing projects, access and priorities without proving that each compound belonged to one named king. Beyond the large compounds, small irregular agglutinated rooms contain evidence for crafts. The great walled complexes and these smaller working spaces formed a heterogeneous urban setting; neither every artisan’s administrative affiliation nor identical simultaneous use of every compound can be established.
Estimated primary-occupancy phase 1200–1300; no precise reform or ruler succession.

sections.heading: Storage, craft and the organization of labor

paragraphs.text: Velarde and Bandelier, now Ñing An and Ñain An, are assigned an estimated primary-occupancy phase around AD 1300–1400. They belong to a city whose built spaces supported different kinds of work. Courts, audiencias, storerooms, wells and funerary platforms formed distinct settings, while craft evidence also comes from densely arranged smaller rooms outside the major compounds. Metalworking is specifically documented in the urban discussion. This does not make every resident a specialized metalworker or establish uniform control over production. Scholars interpret administration through the spatial pattern, but the organization of labor remains less directly observed than the surviving walls, tools and production debris.
1300 anchors the estimated 1300–1400 primary-occupancy phase.

sections.heading: Nik An and Chol An in the late capital

paragraphs.text: Tschudi and Rivero, known today as Nik An and Chol An, belong to Kolata’s latest primary-occupancy phase, approximately AD 1400–1470. They give architectural detail to the broader description of Chan Chan’s fifteenth-century apogee. Later projects also replaced and reworked older parts of the city, so earlier buildings did not all survive unchanged. Nearby Huanchaquito-Las Llamas provides separate evidence for a mass killing during cal AD 1400–1450. It is a different locality, not an event inside either compound. Heavy-rain mud is associated with that deposit, while the specific motive and an ENSO-disaster explanation remain interpretations rather than established facts.
1400 anchors a compound phase; nearby sacrifice has its own 1400–1450 calibrated range and is not mapped at this point.

sections.heading: Political conquest without an invented empty city

paragraphs.text: The official conservation history places the Inca conquest of Chimor around AD 1470. That convention marks a political transition, rather than proving that every household vanished or every compound was destroyed in the same year. Kolata’s final primary-occupancy phase also ends at 1470, but a scheme organized around a political boundary does not directly date the last activity in each building. Incorporation into a new political order and the later survival of architecture are different historical processes. The evidence considered here does not establish a precise battle, a route taken by invading forces or a citywide destruction layer at the conventional conquest date.
Approximate historical convention, not exact archaeological abandonment.

sections.heading: Dated observations and named places

rows.name: Chan Chan: Chayhuac and Uhle primary-occupancy phase
rows.architecture: Chayhuac (Chayhuac An) and Uhle (Xllangchic An) occupy the earliest primary-occupancy phase in Kolata’s urban model. Later architectural modifications must be distinguished from this broad estimated phase.
rows.limits: Kolata 1990 brick-seriation primary-occupancy estimate; not direct radiocarbon dates of compound foundations. Public place reference only; the named structure or excavated sample is not separately geolocated.

rows.name: Chan Chan: Tello and Laberinto phase
rows.architecture: Tello (Tsuts An) and Laberinto (Fechech An) represent a later early-Chimú phase in the proposed sequence, extending the story from an undifferentiated adobe city to named walled compounds.
rows.limits: Primary-occupancy estimate from brick seriation; no exact ruler or foundation event is established. Public place reference only; the named structure or excavated sample is not separately geolocated.

rows.name: Chan Chan: Gran Chimú and Squier phase
rows.architecture: Gran Chimú (Utzh An) and Squier (Fochic An) are placed in the Middle Chimú primary-occupancy phase. Architectural differences and unfinished features cannot be converted automatically into ruler biographies.
rows.limits: Published estimated primary-occupancy phase, not a precise construction or administrative reform date. Public place reference only; the named structure or excavated sample is not separately geolocated.

rows.name: Chan Chan: Velarde and Bandelier phase
rows.architecture: Velarde (Ñing An) and Bandelier (Ñain An) belong to the earlier Late Chimú phase in Kolata’s sequence. Their contexts can anchor discussion of courts, storage and administrative spaces without assigning all city craft production to these specific compounds.
rows.limits: Published primary-occupancy phase estimate. Public place reference only; the named structure or excavated sample is not separately geolocated.

rows.name: Chan Chan: Nik An and Chol An late phase
rows.architecture: Tschudi (Nik An) and Rivero (Chol An) are placed in the latest primary-occupancy phase. This adds named architectural context to the existing broad fifteenth-century apogee observation.
rows.limits: Primary-occupancy phase estimate ending at the conventional conquest boundary; not proof of total abandonment. Public place reference only; the named structure or excavated sample is not separately geolocated.

rows.name: Chan Chan: approximate Inca political transition
rows.dates: Inca conquest conventionally placed around AD 1470
rows.architecture: The official conservation history places Inca conquest around AD 1470. Political incorporation should be distinguished from later use, survival and modification of Chan Chan’s architecture.
rows.limits: Approximate historical chronology; not a radiocarbon year, destruction layer or universal residential endpoint. Public place reference only; the named structure or excavated sample is not separately geolocated.

sections.heading: Interpretations and remaining questions

paragraphs.text: Brick-seriation dates are estimated primary-occupancy phases, not laboratory dates for every wall. Preserve the model’s attribution and do not invent precise compound coordinates.
The palace-per-ruler interpretation and information-control reading are scholarly models. Topic’s full paper was not inspected.
Modern compound names differ from older literature; official master-plan overview has a spelling variation for Gran Chimú, while its entry uses Utzh An.

Huanchaquito-Las Llamas is a separate place. Its mass killing, rain-related mud and calibrated range are supported, but a specific ENSO-sacrifice motive remains conjectural. No new observation is proposed until its public coordinate is independently verified.
Inca conquest around 1470 is not proof of immediate total abandonment.

pages.title: Wari: cities, households and the Moquegua enclave
pages.intro: Compare planned places and local observations in the Moquegua enclave. Separate building phases, household histories, exchange and evidence that remains unplaced.

sections.heading: Making an irrigated colonial landscape

paragraphs.text: People in the Wari-associated Moquegua enclave built and maintained an agricultural landscape around their hilltop complexes. Nash describes a canal longer than 20 kilometers that brought at least 700 hectares into cultivation, with part operating by around AD 650. Cerro Baúl and nearby Cerro Mejía were settled before 700. Water management, farming, and household work sustained these neighboring settlements. The canal and buildings developed through their own sequences, and their broad dates do not establish a single founding campaign.
650 is an approximate by-then operating statement for part of the irrigation system.

sections.heading: Households with different ways of living

paragraphs.text: Households in the Moquegua enclave differed in their architecture, diets, and ways of preparing food. Cooking, storage, work, and access to water were central to everyday life at Cerro Baúl and Cerro Mejía. Nash interprets this variety as evidence of a polyethnic colonial community: people with different backgrounds living within the enclave. The household comparison concerns a broad archaeological phase around the period of irrigation development. It does not identify the birthplace, language, or reasons for moving of each resident.
Shares the approximately 650 irrigation orientation. Household diversity summarizes the wider enclave phase; it is not a census or a claim that each household existed in 650.

sections.heading: Rebuilding Cerro Baúl’s summit

paragraphs.text: Moseley and colleagues describe major reorganization around AD 800, when earlier Cerro Baúl summit structures were leveled or replaced. The later complex brought ceremonial buildings, residences and productive areas into a changed arrangement. D-shaped temples and a pottery workshop with raw materials and tools document different activities. A Nazca-style drum in a ceremonial context provides an object connection, without establishing the language or ethnicity of everyone present. This was rebuilding of an existing colony, rather than evidence of a single master plan completed in one year. The approximate phase does not directly date every wall or demonstrate that nearby settlements followed the same schedule.
Approximate contextual rebuilding phase; no precise common foundation for every component.

sections.heading: Work in the brewery and later hillside homes

paragraphs.text: Milling, boiling and fermentation took place in distinct areas of Cerro Baúl’s brewery. Seven boiling firepits and molle remains support a specific account of preparation, while serving vessels and feasting evidence connect that work to gatherings. Nearby Cerro Mejía has later household evidence than the older early-only model allowed. A burnt-seed sample from a late Unit 17 context has a reported calibrated component at AD 882–995, representing 90.2 percent probability. These are different observations: the summit brewery’s contextual phase is not the same measurement as the hillside household’s seed sample. Together they reveal varied productive and domestic activity across the enclave.
900 is a shared orientation point; brewery phase and Mejía calibrated seed range have distinct semantics.

sections.heading: Closing a brewery, not erasing a region

paragraphs.text: Burning in the brewery and the breaking of serving vessels underpin an interpretation of ceremonial closure around AD 1000. The sequence does not establish a battle, identify an attacking army or show that every Wari-associated household left Moquegua simultaneously. The approximate date also comes from an older chronological synthesis. Later research emphasizes varied local histories, including later Cerro Mejía household samples and an unfinished project at Cerro Petroglifo. The brewery’s termination is therefore one building’s history within a wider changing region. Other communities and activities cannot be assigned the same ending simply because they participated in the Wari-associated enclave.
Approximate closure interpretation in older synthesis, not an exact radiocarbon year.

sections.heading: Dated observations and named places

rows.name: Wari Moquegua enclave: irrigated fields and colonization
rows.dates: Part of the irrigation system operating by around AD 650
rows.architecture: A canal longer than 20 km brought at least 700 hectares into the enclave’s irrigated landscape, with part operating by around 650. Cerro Baúl and Cerro Mejía were settled before 700; neither the complete route nor each household’s arrival is dated by that statement.
rows.limits: Broad colony-area point; no invented canal route or terrace endpoint. Approximate terminus statement in Nash 2022, not the date of the whole canal. Buried terrace carbon is a different sampled context and is not substituted for construction. Public place reference only; the named structure or excavated sample is not separately geolocated.

rows.name: Cerro Baúl: major reorganization of the summit
rows.architecture: Major rebuilding around AD 800 leveled or replaced earlier summit structures. The visible later complex included ceremonial, residential and productive spaces; separate components should not all inherit an exact construction year.
rows.limits: Approximate contextual phase of rebuilding, not a year-precise architectural event. Public place reference only; the named structure or excavated sample is not separately geolocated.

rows.name: Cerro Baúl: brewing and provisioning in the later complex
rows.dates: Later summit phase, broadly around AD 800–1000 in the older synthesis
rows.architecture: Separate milling, boiling and fermentation spaces, including seven boiling firepits and molle remains, document brewing work at Cerro Baúl. Associated feasting and serving vessels support ceremonial provisioning, without fixing the identities or political obligations of all participants.
rows.limits: Site-area reference only; exact brewery coordinate deliberately not invented. Contextual architectural-use range, not direct dates of every batch, firepit or vessel; later regional chronology differs. Public place reference only; the named structure or excavated sample is not separately geolocated.

rows.name: Cerro Baúl: interpreted ceremonial brewery closure
rows.dates: Around AD 1000 in Moseley et al. 2005
rows.architecture: Burned brewery architecture and broken serving vessels are interpreted as a ceremonial termination around AD 1000 in the older study. This does not demonstrate an enemy attack or the simultaneous ending of all Wari-associated activity in Moquegua.
rows.limits: Approximate contextual closure interpretation. Burning and smashing support a sequence; no exact calibrated calendar day/year is established. Public place reference only; the named structure or excavated sample is not separately geolocated.

rows.name: Cerro Mejía: late household-context radiocarbon evidence
rows.dates: AD 882–995, reported 90.2% probability component for AA 90356
rows.architecture: A late Cerro Mejía household-context burnt-seed sample calibrates primarily to AD 882–995. It challenges the older claim that all Mejía occupation ended before 800 and records activity later than the original early-colony model allowed.
rows.limits: Named public settlement but no canonical precise point recovered. Keep unplaced or at clearly labeled regional extent; do not assign this to the Cerro Baúl summit coordinate. SHCal 20/OxCal 4.4 calibration of burnt seeds from a late Unit 17 context. Not the full 95.4% distribution and not the complete occupation of the household. No verified public site coordinate has been recovered. Retained as geographically unplaced evidence; no substitute point is drawn.

rows.name: Cerro Petroglifo: offering for an unfinished project
rows.architecture: A construction-related offering at Cerro Petroglifo dates an unfinished project in the later enclave sequence. The locality was not occupied; the offering cannot be converted into a settlement founding date or continuous occupation lasting to 1223.
rows.limits: Discontinuous reported calibrated components; outer envelope is indexing convenience, not continuous probability or occupation. Author interprets unfinished construction after 1050. No verified public site coordinate has been recovered. Retained as geographically unplaced evidence; no substitute point is drawn.

sections.heading: Interpretations and remaining questions

paragraphs.text: Cerro Baúl and Cerro Mejía preserve a local Moquegua sequence within the wider Wari-associated world. Huari and Pikillacta offer other settings whose histories should be compared without assuming that every center developed simultaneously.

Nash’s later household dates extend Cerro Mejía’s history beyond the earlier interpretation that occupation ended before 800. Old wood and reused beams can be older than the buildings in which they were placed.
The published ranges 882–995 and 887–995 contain 90.2% and 88.5% of their samples’ dating probability. They are parts of broader date distributions, rather than complete 95.4% ranges.
An offering at Cerro Petroglifo dates activity at an unfinished project rather than occupation of completed houses. Its possible dates fall in separated intervals within the broad 1045–1223 span.

Precise locations for particular houses, brewery spaces, and canal segments are not established here. Cerro Mejía and Cerro Petroglifo have archaeological evidence but lack verified public coordinates in this study.
Polyethnic is an archaeological interpretation; forced versus voluntary migration, languages and exact origins remain unresolved.
The earthquake chronology proposed for Pikillacta remains unverified in the sources used here.

pages.title: Moche: Huacas de Moche and a long-lived urban landscape
pages.intro: Follow particular north-coast communities and construction contexts, rather than assigning every place to one uniform Moche state or one shared ending.

sections.heading: Settlement before the monumental city

paragraphs.text: Huacas de Moche has a history longer than the monumental Moche phases that make the place famous. Rengifo and colleagues identify early settlement evidence on Cerro Blanco, including components designated PCB 1 and PCB 2 and stone-built rectilinear spaces. Their synthesis places Salinar within a broad regional phase of about 400 BCE to AD 50. That range describes an archaeological tradition and context, not the continuous life of one excavated house. The same study distinguishes the absence of diagnostic Gallinazo negative-painted pottery at Huacas proper from Gallinazo evidence at nearby Huaca Las Estrellas. Early inhabitants therefore belong in the story, with differences between neighboring places preserved rather than folded into an uninterrupted generic occupation.
400 BCE is a broad phase anchor; integer -399 uses astronomical numbering.

sections.heading: Marine foods in an urban household compound

paragraphs.text: Architectural Compound 9 connects the city to daily preparation, storage and eating. The studied complex covered about 656 square meters and contained 48 spaces with residential, kitchen, storage and burial functions. Roselló and colleagues assigned its sampled contexts to AD 470–600 using the chronology available in 2001. Donax clams and hake dominate the marine assemblage, alongside many less common taxa. Those remains show that coastal resources reached an urban community, while the authors’ proposals about selection and redistribution remain interpretations of the pattern. The dates here are the study’s contextual chronology, not newly calibrated measurements; the original radiocarbon BP ages must not be converted to calendar years by simple subtraction.
470 anchors the 2001 study’s 470–600 contextual interval; no new calibration was performed.

sections.heading: A new temple and a changing urban sequence

paragraphs.text: The site synthesis distinguishes the Old Temple from a New Temple phase placed around AD 700–850. This was a landscape repeatedly transformed: superposed urban floors and contexts of craft and food preparation record changes beyond the monumental façades. A recent textile study summarizes the Old Temple’s cessation closer to 650, illustrating why one exact rebuilding date would be misleading. Both sources point to architectural change, but their broad summaries and chronological purposes differ. Later residential contraction around 850 also does not mean every activity stopped. The synthesis identifies subsequent funerary and ritual reuse, including architectural compounds 45 and 47 and parts of Huaca del Sol, preserving the distinction between a changed city and an empty site.
700 anchors the synthesis’s 700–850 phase; alternative transition around 650 remains explicit.

sections.heading: Textiles extend the history of Moche practice

paragraphs.text: Textiles from Huaca del Sol’s Section 4 reveal a later history than older narratives of abrupt Moche disappearance allowed. Twenty AMS measurements on selected pieces from an assemblage of more than 200 fragments concentrate in the tenth century, with some distributions extending across AD 1000. Techniques and imagery include locally S-spun cotton Moche forms, Highland Moche combinations, Moche-Wari forms and Wari material. These are useful categories for practices and objects, not direct labels for each person’s ethnicity or language. Dates measure fibre growth rather than death or burial; reopened tombs and possible heirlooms complicate deposition. The evidence nevertheless supports continued, changing traditions in a place whose major urban and temple phases had already shifted.
950 anchors the tenth-century concentration; individual calibrated ranges and burial histories differ.

sections.heading: Chimú families use the older sacred landscape

paragraphs.text: Later cemetery evidence shows that the significance of Huacas de Moche did not end with the contraction of its Moche-period city. Rengifo and colleagues assign an Early Chimú group of 25 individuals to approximately AD 1100–1250, supported by two radiocarbon determinations. This does not date every person to the same moment, but it establishes another phase of funerary use in the inherited landscape. The authors distinguish a subsequent Middle Chimú group of eighteen burials, dated relatively rather than by radiocarbon. Keeping those methods separate matters: an archaeological phase can organize the narrative without creating laboratory precision that the evidence does not have. The continuity is one of place and practice, not proof that political institutions or personal identities remained unchanged.
1150 is a contextual anchor within the 1100–1250 phase supported by two dates.

sections.heading: Late Chimú activity in an enduring place

paragraphs.text: A hearth in Architectural Compound 43 supplies a specific late Chimú observation within this long-lived landscape. The published charcoal determination has a calibrated component of AD 1390–1451 representing 90.2 percent probability; it is not the complete 95.4 percent distribution, nor a direct date for every activity in the compound. The broader site synthesis also describes late offerings involving miniature objects, Spondylus and feathered garments, followed by evidence associated with the Chimú-Inca period. These different contexts show continued use but must not be merged into one ceremony. Nearby Huanchaquito-Las Llamas is a separate archaeological locality, and no evidence here makes its mass killing an event inside Compound 43 or identifies the hearth’s particular users.
1420 anchors a reported 1390–1451 calibrated component; probability and charcoal-context caveats remain explicit.

sections.heading: Dated observations and named places

rows.architecture: Early settlement evidence at Cerro Blanco includes PCB 1 and PCB 2, with stone-built rectilinear spaces and Salinar associations. This precedes the monumental Moche city; nearby Gallinazo evidence must not be generalized automatically to Huacas proper.
rows.limits: Published complex-area satellite-frame proxy, approximately 2 km radius; not the location of the specific excavated context. Broad archaeological phase assigned to early settlement components; not a single house’s occupation interval or a directly measured 450-year sequence. rows.name: Huacas de Moche CA 9: marine foods in an urban compound

rows.architecture: Architectural Compound 9 combined domestic, storage, kitchen and burial spaces. Its marine assemblage is dominated by Donax clams and hake, with a wider range of secondary taxa; selection and distribution models address access to coastal foods without establishing a specific route.
rows.limits: Published complex-area satellite-frame proxy, approximately 2 km radius; not the location of the specific excavated context. Authors’ contextual calendar chronology, not newly calibrated ranges. Raw radiocarbon ages were not converted by subtraction. Public place reference only; the named structure or excavated sample is not separately geolocated.

Broad published architectural phase; Quilter et al. 2024 summarize transition around 650. Both estimates should be attributed rather than averaged. Public place reference only; the named structure or excavated sample is not separately geolocated.

rows.dates: Broad tenth-century concentration; some individual distributions extend beyond AD 1000
rows.architecture: Twenty AMS textile dates from Huaca del Sol Section 4 support substantial tenth-century activity, with some material extending into the early eleventh century. Moche, Highland Moche, Moche-Wari and Wari textile forms coexist in the studied assemblage; fibre dates, reopened tombs and possible heirlooms prevent exact burial dates or fixed ethnic assignments.

Descriptive century-scale concentration, not a combined calibrated 95% interval, complete burial interval or ending boundary. Individual SHCal 20/OxCal 4.4 distributions differ. Prefer individual Table 1 dates for precise event ingestion. Public place reference only; the named structure or excavated sample is not separately geolocated.

rows.name: Huacas de Moche: Early Chimú cemetery activity
rows.architecture: An Early Chimú cemetery group of 25 individuals is assigned approximately to 1100–1250. Later burial at the same archaeological landscape demonstrates that the end of Moche temple-centered phases did not end its funerary significance.
rows.limits: Published complex-area satellite-frame proxy, approximately 2 km radius; not the location of the specific excavated context. Site synthesis phase supported by two radiocarbon determinations; not an identical date for all 25 people. Public place reference only; the named structure or excavated sample is not separately geolocated.

rows.name: Huacas de Moche CA 43: late Chimú hearth context
rows.dates: Cal AD 1390–1451, 90.2% reported probability component, Beta-250412
rows.architecture: A hearth in Architectural Compound 43 provides radiocarbon evidence for late Chimú activity at Huacas de Moche. This sampled burning context should be distinguished from broad cultural periods and from the separate Huanchaquito-Las Llamas mass-killing site.
rows.limits: Published complex-area satellite-frame proxy, approximately 2 km radius; not the location of the specific excavated context. Published calibrated component for charcoal 560±40 BP; not the complete 95.4% distribution, not independently recalibrated, and subject to wood-age/context limits. Public place reference only; the named structure or excavated sample is not separately geolocated.

sections.heading: Interpretations and remaining questions

paragraphs.text: Valley-specific Moche chronologies remain beyond what can be established from the available abstract of Koons’s 2024 study.

Rengifo places the Old Temple in 50–700 and the New Temple in 700–850. Quilter instead summarizes major building in the third and fourth centuries and a transition around 650. These accounts do not establish one agreed rebuilding year.
The dated textiles concentrate in the tenth century, with some possible sample dates extending beyond 1000. Their distributions do not establish a single ending year for textile use or deposition.
Fibre-growth dates, reopened tombs and possible heirlooms do not give exact deaths or a single simultaneous cemetery event. Textile categories are not direct ethnic/language assignments.
CA 43 and CA 42 reported calibrated components carry 90.2% and 84%, not complete 95.4% distributions.
Some official visitor descriptions differ from the primary studies on dimensions, temple names, and the extent of Gallinazo occupation. Those differences remain unresolved.
A wooden-model burial has a broad date range of 1449–1648, spanning periods before and after Spanish arrival. Elsewhere at the site, later activity continued after residential contraction around 850.
The location represents the area containing both huacas, with an approximate two-kilometer radius. It does not pinpoint an excavated room or deposit.
