pages.title: Teotihuacan
pages.intro: Look inside the city’s building sequence, changing apartment compounds and later tunnel occupations. Different neighbourhoods did not share one simple ending.

sections.heading: Creating a monumental mountain

paragraphs.text: The Sun Pyramid presents a long building history behind its apparently unified mass. Excavators distinguish the earlier landscape, construction of the main pyramid, and the adjoining adosada platform. An artificial tunnel adds another architectural layer below the monument. Sugiyama and colleagues proposed a main-building date of 170–310 CE and a tunnel date of 140–240 CE; Sload argues for an earlier chronology. The scene therefore introduces a growing monumental center while showing how excavated sequences can support competing construction histories.
Viewing year within disputed construction model, not completion year.

sections.heading: Neighbourhood households and work

paragraphs.text: La Ventilla was a neighborhood of compounds within Teotihuacan. Archaeologists identify LV 2 with elite and administrative activity and LV 3 with lapidary workers, craftspeople who shaped stone. These neighboring spaces reveal households, specialized production, and unequal access to space within the city. Their later archaeological histories also preserve changes in how the compounds were used.
Contextual Classic-period view anchored by existing urban record.

sections.heading: Burned surfaces, competing clocks

paragraphs.text: Burned architectural surfaces provide a different clock from pottery or inscriptions. At the Superimposed Buildings, archaeomagnetic measurements estimate the last strong heating experienced by sampled materials. Two models place it in the fifth century, while another yields an earlier range. Other sampled places produce still different or multiple possible dates. The city consequently should not change from flourishing to empty in one synchronized frame. This scene follows one measured burning context and keeps its chronological disagreement visible alongside the continuing urban landscape.
Last-heating estimates, not one proved city-wide destruction.

sections.heading: A neighbourhood reused

paragraphs.text: At La Ventilla, later burials cut through earlier walls and floors after buildings had fallen into disrepair. Burial 27 in LV 2 supplies a calibrated probability component of 540–610 CE, placing activity within a compound whose earlier organization had changed. The deposits show people engaging with an existing built environment rather than occupying a newly cleared blank space. LV 3 has a separate, later burial window. These observations support a local reuse sequence without making one neighborhood's history the timetable for the entire city.
Calibrated burial evidence; reoccupation inference.

sections.heading: Lives inside the old quarry landscape

paragraphs.text: The old quarry tunnels of Pirul and Varillas, behind the Sun Pyramid, became places of domestic, craft, burial and ritual activity. Their later occupants used spaces created by earlier extraction, adding another inhabited setting to the transformed city. The modeled Coyotlatelco phase spans approximately 640–820 CE. At this viewing year, the separately dated LV 3 burials also provide neighborhood evidence. Together the records reveal multiple places of activity after major political change, although they do not establish one unbroken citywide population or a single new community.
Modeled local occupation phase.

sections.heading: Mazapa occupations

paragraphs.text: The tunnel sequence includes a Mazapa occupation phase modeled to 940–1230 CE. This takes the story well beyond the conventional endpoint of Teotihuacan's principal urban-development phase. The studied underground spaces preserve working and living activities, including evidence of bifacial tool production in Pirul. The workshop's precise position in every chronological phase is not independently established in this introductory report. The useful comparison is between a place's changing uses over centuries and the much shorter history of the government that built its great monuments.
Modeled local phase 940–1230 CE.

sections.heading: Aztec-period return and ritual

paragraphs.text: Aztec III occupation evidence returns the studied tunnel landscape to view in approximately 1390–1460 CE. The intervening local hiatus matters: later use is a new episode in an old place, not proof that every earlier neighborhood remained continuously occupied. Teotihuacan's monumental remains and excavated spaces continued to offer settings for activity long after the Classic city's political system had ended. This final scene closes with a layered landscape, allowing the later record to remain visible without extending the original urban government's lifetime.
Modeled evidence window after a local hiatus.

pages.title: Monte Albán
pages.intro: Explore a hilltop city’s household works, inscriptions, ballcourt and tomb reuse, with competing interpretations of government and conquest.

sections.heading: A new hilltop city

paragraphs.text: Around 500 BCE, Monte Albán's founders established a hilltop city whose residential terraces transformed a demanding setting. Households shared retaining walls and drainage arrangements, while farming and small-scale irrigation tied the settlement to surrounding land. Nicholas and Feinman use these material relationships to argue that coordinated production and comparatively collective institutions helped the city grow. Their argument redirects attention from a single ruler to the work needed to sustain neighborhoods. The approximate foundation date introduces this process rather than dating every terrace or irrigation feature.
Approximate foundation 500 BCE, encoded 1−500=-499.

sections.heading: Images made and remade

paragraphs.text: Monte Albán’s Danzantes carvings were moved and reused in later buildings. Winter argues that their original wall was dismantled after a relatively short period, giving the earlier images new settings for remembrance. The figures’ meanings remain disputed: Winter’s interpretation as remembered founding participants differs from readings that emphasize captives and violence. The sequence of dismantling and reuse is better established than an exact demolition year.
Early urban era; relative sequence, not a dated demolition. The viewing year anchors the existing city phase, not the relative wall-reuse event.

sections.heading: Structure J and uncertain place names

paragraphs.text: Structure J incorporates carved monuments whose texts and images have often been read as a register of conquered places. Carter reassesses the proposed readings and the certainty of those identifications. The carvings are attributed to the Pe phase, approximately 300–100 BCE, but that estimate is not automatically the construction date of the entire building. Visitors can examine a specific material source for political claims while seeing why uncertain place names cannot safely become an imperial territory drawn on the map.
Pe-phase carving estimate 300–100 BCE; not automatically Structure J construction.

sections.heading: A ballcourt and public space

paragraphs.text: Builders added a ballcourt beside Monte Albán’s North Platform around 100 BCE, according to INAH. The court joined the city’s expanding landscape of public structures, residential terraces, and plaza buildings. Its construction records one particular addition to a city that had already been inhabited for centuries.
Approximate construction 100 BCE.

sections.heading: Homes, ancestors and intercity contacts

paragraphs.text: The residence associated with Tomb 105 connected elite domestic life with the commemoration of ancestors at Monte Albán. Its construction is broadly dated to 500–800 CE. Residence, burial space, and the surrounding terrace landscape formed parts of the same urban community, sustained by household work and food production. INAH also describes earlier connections with Teotihuacan, although those relationships do not establish that outside powers directed every local political change.
Residence construction window 500–800; earlier contacts 200–500 are retrospective context.

sections.heading: Political decentralization

paragraphs.text: Between roughly 800 and 900 CE, Monte Albán lost population and much of its monumental prominence as people and institutions became concentrated elsewhere in the Oaxaca Valley. Feinman and Nicholas challenge the older explanation of a simple Mixtec invasion replacing Zapotec society. They instead emphasize changes in regional settlement and political organization. The city’s decline formed part of this wider reorganization of inhabited communities.
Approximate demographic/monumental change 800–900.

sections.heading: Reusing an ancestral tomb

paragraphs.text: Tomb 7 combines an older burial structure with later Postclassic objects and activity. The broad 900–1520 CE interval describes that later assemblage and reuse, not the original construction of the tomb or a precisely dated single burial. This layered setting gives the final scene a different purpose from the earlier story of city growth. Localized Mixtec presence, particularly in later centuries, must be considered alongside continuing Zapotec communities. The site's ancestral significance could persist even as its former urban and political role changed.
Viewing year within broad Postclassic assemblage 900–1520; not precise burial date.

pages.title: Calakmul
pages.intro: Follow a Maya centre through construction, murals, royal inscriptions and later use, separating political titles from the lives of the people around them.

sections.heading: An older monumental and hydraulic landscape

paragraphs.text: Structure II preserves sealed Preclassic deposits beneath the later monumental building. That sequence places Calakmul's history before the famous seventh-century Snake court. The surrounding landscape also includes seasonal bajos, reservoirs and canals, connecting urban life with the collection and management of water. Folan and colleagues describe these features at the scale of the settlement and its setting. They do not provide a construction year for every reservoir. The opening scene therefore introduces an established place and its environmental infrastructure without animating all components as one building campaign.
Illustrative view in existing Late Preclassic phase; no exact building construction year.

sections.heading: Chiik Nahb begins to grow

paragraphs.text: Chiik Nahb's Structure 1 was repeatedly rebuilt, preserving earlier versions inside later work. Carrasco Vargas and colleagues place the start of the construction sequence within approximately 420–620 CE. This building history makes a northern complex visible alongside the central monumental group. Its later murals and final remodeling belong to subsequent chapters, rather than being compressed into the date of its first construction. Following one structure through successive transformations gives the guide a concrete architectural thread that continues across changes in the city's court and political fortunes.
Ceramic-based start window 420–620 CE.

sections.heading: Monuments around Structure V

paragraphs.text: The monuments around Structure V establish a sequence of publicly displayed dates. Folan and colleagues identify northern stelae dated to 623 CE, while others around the structure belong to later seventh-century activity. Their positions connect political and ritual statements with movement through the central plaza. This is a narrower observation than saying the whole building was constructed in 623. The scene uses the dedication evidence to show monuments being added to an existing architectural setting, making the plaza a changing record of public memory.
Epigraphically dated dedication.

sections.heading: The Snake court moves

paragraphs.text: Stela 33, erected in 657, looks back to an accession in 579. That retrospective statement must not be mistaken for proof that the earlier king ruled from Calakmul. Martin distinguishes the Kaanu'l, or Snake, polity from the city itself and argues for its earlier seat at Dzibanche before a seventh-century transfer. The scene places the dated monument in Calakmul while allowing its text to refer elsewhere and earlier. Political identity, the location of a court and the age of a settlement consequently remain separate questions.
Stela 33 dedication in 657 anchors discussion of the broader seventh-century court transfer.

sections.heading: Food, work and circulation

paragraphs.text: The murals of Structure 1, Sub 1–4, bring women, men, prepared foods and circulated goods into view. Their painted and written details include maize foods, salt and tobacco. A stylistic date of approximately 620–700 CE anchors this particular remodeling, rather than all activity in Chiik Nahb. The scenes broaden a history often dominated by kings and warfare by showing exchange and consumption. A market interpretation is plausible but debated; the paintings themselves do not establish a permanent market institution or the exact routes by which every commodity arrived.
Stylistic mural date 620–700 CE.

sections.heading: A defeat within continuing city life

paragraphs.text: Calakmul suffered defeat by Tikal in 695 CE, according to INAH’s historical account. The setback occurred while the city remained a place of urban activity and mural painting. Later rebuilding at Chiik Nahb shows that this defeat did not immediately end construction. The history of the royal court therefore unfolded alongside longer histories of people using and changing the city’s buildings.
Military event in institutional synthesis; not a destruction date. Existing urban-phase record provides current city context; no independently added military-event record.

sections.heading: Late rebuilding and unfinished work

paragraphs.text: The final remodeling of Chiik Nahb's Structure 1 began within the broad 820–1020 CE interval and was left unfinished. This material sequence extends well beyond the old record's selected major-urban-phase endpoint of 700. INAH also reports a last dated stela in 909, a different category of evidence from construction stratigraphy. The two observations help keep late activity visible while resisting a false exact ending. An unfinished project can reveal disrupted work, but it does not identify the last inhabitant or by itself explain why the project stopped.
Final-remodeling initiation window 820–1020 CE.

sections.heading: Visits to an older sacred city

paragraphs.text: INAH recounts that Alonso de Ávila encountered Calakmul’s old city in the early sixteenth century and observed occasional Indigenous ritual visits. The account describes people returning to a sacred place long after its Classic court had ended. Its date is broadly assigned to the first half of the century. This remains an account attributed through INAH; the underlying colonial text has not been independently checked here.
Early 16th-century report;1530 is an orientation year only.

pages.title: Copán
pages.intro: Explore buried architectural phases, Oropéndola and the Hieroglyphic Stairway, then the evidence for activity after royal monumental production changed.

sections.heading: Before the royal Acropolis

paragraphs.text: Excavation beneath the Northern Court Complex reaches constructions assigned to approximately 350–400 CE, before the royal Acropolis took its later form. Investigators reached these levels below the later buildings around Court 4 B, including Loro, Tucán and Pato. Their names locate the excavated context but do not give those later buildings the dates of the deposits beneath them. The opening scene establishes a place already being built and used, allowing the subsequent appearance of royal architecture to be understood as a transformation of an earlier landscape.
Viewing year within report's approximate Division VI, 350–400 CE.

sections.heading: A new architectural center

paragraphs.text: Within the early Acropolis sequence, Hunal stands out for its red-painted talud-tablero façade and north-facing stair. Nearby Tartan marked a boundary between an early ballcourt complex and the Acropolis, while other buildings and drains expanded the constructed setting. These features belong to the report's broad 400–450 CE division. Hunal's architectural form invites comparison with central Mexico, but resemblance alone cannot demonstrate conquest or a person's ethnicity. The building and associated tomb support investigation of dynastic beginnings while leaving their more specific identifications open to additional evidence.
Viewing frame within Division V, 400–450 CE; not exact Hunal construction or founder accession.

sections.heading: Oropéndola inside the later pyramid

paragraphs.text: Builders enclosed Oropéndola within the later Structure 10 L-16 at Copán. Its carved stone mosaic façade differs from the modeled stucco of other early buildings, and its arrangement can be compared with nearby Rosalila. The sequence of buried structures suggests construction around 550–600 CE, supported by lintel samples and pottery. The earlier temple survived because later building projects incorporated it within the growing Acropolis.
Viewing year within suggested construction window 550–600 CE.

sections.heading: A stairway remembers a ruler

paragraphs.text: In 710 CE, according to Fash's research account, Ruler 13 dedicated the first Hieroglyphic Stairway to commemorate Ruler 12, who had died in 695. The inscription and architectural sequence connect a public stairway with a royal burial and remembered reign. Archaeological investigation beneath the structure supports the distinction between this first version and its later extension. The stairs thus record an act of making history visible in stone, while the current date belongs to the dedication rather than to every event recalled in its text.
Epigraphic dedication year in Fash's 2017 research account.

sections.heading: Rewriting dynastic continuity

paragraphs.text: The expanded Hieroglyphic Stairway received another dedication under Ruler 15, dated to 755 CE in Fash's account. Different carving styles help distinguish the earlier and later inscriptions, even though fallen and rearranged blocks complicate their reconstruction. References to Ruler 13's death at the hands of Quiriguá place conflict within the monument's political story. The renewed building effort also demonstrates that defeat did not simply stop dynastic representation. A one-year difference in some institutional summaries is retained as a chronological discrepancy rather than silently resolved.
Later dedication year in Fash's 2017 account; one-year variants occur in institutional summaries.

sections.heading: Households, rainwater and a changing court

paragraphs.text: Copán's residents relied on water collection and distribution as well as the royal monuments that dominate surviving views. Research interprets the East, West and Hieroglyphic Stairway courts as parts of a rainwater-collection system, and investigation near Las Sepulturas supports an ancient pond. Índigo and Temple 22 connect drainage and water imagery; Structure 9 N-82 brings maize and water symbolism into a residential setting. These features link subsistence, community organization and authority, although their exact operating dates and the proposed social relationships are not all independently established.
Illustrative late Classic viewing year, supported by existing broad phase and the later-activity model; water features lack independent narrow dates here.

sections.heading: After royal monument building

paragraphs.text: An influential 1990 settlement model separates the decline of royal authority around 800 CE from continuing nonroyal elite activity over roughly two more centuries. Its evidence came from a large program of survey, excavation and obsidian-hydration dating. This makes the wider settlement landscape central to the question of what followed the royal court. The result remains an older, method-dependent model, accessed here through its abstracts. It supports a carefully labeled later-activity scene rather than a claim that a particular palace was still occupied in 950.
Viewing year within an older model of subroyal activity, approximately 800–1000 CE; confidence explicitly limited.

pages.title: Paquimé
pages.intro: Follow earlier houses, the multistorey town, animal husbandry and a directly dated interment. Wider connections did not make this place a copy of another city.

sections.heading: Settlements beside water

paragraphs.text: INAH's account begins with pit-house settlements near streams and springs around 600 CE, well before the surviving multistory town. Their setting puts access to water and everyday settlement choices at the beginning of the story. Around 900, the institutional sequence describes a change toward earthen courtyard houses. The early interval is a broad place-area phase, not a direct date for the later public buildings. Keeping it separate makes Paquimé's development visible without projecting its eventual monumental form backward over several centuries.
Illustrative frame within official early-settlement account, approximately 600–900 CE.

sections.heading: Courtyards and earthen walls

paragraphs.text: Around 900 CE, the official sequence describes a transition from pit houses to earthen-walled houses arranged around courtyards. Household and workshop spaces provide a view of architecture organized around recurring activities rather than isolated monuments. The approximate date marks a change in the settlement account; it is not evidence that every household rebuilt at once. Later mitochondrial research also challenges a simple population-replacement explanation for Paquimé's growth, although those maternal-line results cannot assign identities or origins to the occupants of any particular courtyard.
Approximate change around 900 CE; not an exactly dated citywide rebuilding.

sections.heading: The Medio town

paragraphs.text: During the Medio period, large residential units, plazas, specialized buildings and public works transformed Paquimé's scale. Casa Amurallada is a named component that INAH assigns to this phase, while the existing town record supplies the conventional 1200–1450 CE frame. Some regional chronologies begin the phase closer to 1150, so the starting boundary remains approximate. Recent mitochondrial results suggest substantial maternal-line continuity across the town's rise. Architectural elaboration and increasing connections therefore need not be narrated as a new population simply replacing an older one.
Viewing year near conventional Medio onset; regional chronology can start around 1150 or 1200.

sections.heading: Water through the town

paragraphs.text: The water system connected collection, filtering, storage and distribution with life inside the town. INAH describes the Depósito de Agua, a principal reservoir and channels supplying residential spaces. These components help explain the maintenance and coordination needed to sustain dense earthen architecture. Irrigation also belongs to the wider agricultural account, but it should not be confused with a fully reconstructed street-by-street supply network. The viewing year falls within the town's broad phase; no independent narrow construction date was verified for each tank, filter or channel.
Illustrative view within the broad town phase; no independently dated construction year for each channel.

sections.heading: Raising macaws and moving knowledge

paragraphs.text: Scarlet macaws connect Paquimé's architecture with animal care, specialized labor and wider circulation. Casa de las Guacamayas provides a named setting for bird keeping, while isotope research on 29 specimens indicates that most were probably raised locally, with some possible nonlocal origins. The checked abstract does not establish that every sampled bird came from that house. Nor do strontium values trace a unique trade route. The scene therefore brings local husbandry into the exchange story rather than treating every exotic bird as a newly imported object.
Illustrative Medio-phase frame; isotope specimens are not independently assigned to 1320.

sections.heading: A dated act at the House of the Well

paragraphs.text: The House of the Well contains an activity dated more directly than many of the town's architectural phases: an interment associated with its central roof-support post. The radiocarbon result calibrates to 1301–1397 CE at 95.4% probability. Tree-ring measurements from the building are older and lack outer rings, preventing their simple use as exact construction dates. The source interprets the interment in relation to ritual and the building's erection. Those interpretations remain distinct from the measured dating result and from claims about the entire community.
Viewing frame within calibrated 1301–1397 CE, 95.4% probability.

sections.heading: Decline without an invented disappearance

paragraphs.text: Paquimé’s large-scale occupation declined during the fifteenth century, bringing its main town phase to an end around the conventional date of 1450. Its households, water systems, bird keeping, and ritual spaces had developed through different histories. The changing use of this built landscape transformed the regional center, although the available evidence does not establish one final departure date or a single cause of decline.
Late-phase viewing frame; approximately fifteenth-century decline, not a last-person date.

sections.heading: Dated observations and named places

Approximate official historical phase in CE; site-area narrative, not a direct sample or date for surviving multistory units. sections.heading: Interpretations and remaining questions

paragraphs.text: Scholars place the beginning of the Medio phase around either 1150 or 1200. Its chronology therefore remains broader than a single agreed starting year.
Timbers from the House of the Well lack their outer rings, so their tree-ring dates do not identify the exact year of construction.
One individual's close parental relatedness cannot establish all Paquimé residents' marriage practices, status or identity.
Macaw isotope values constrain possible origins, not a unique source locality or drawn trade route.
Maternal mitochondrial continuity does not demonstrate absence of all migration, language continuity, or an ethnic identification.
No verified source here establishes one citywide massacre or the disappearance of everyone at 1450.
The construction dates of individual water-management features and their precise locations remain unresolved in the available documentation.
Verified descendant perspectives remain an important gap in the sources presented here.
Isotope measurements help investigate origins and diets. Their implications for elite ritual and political organization require additional interpretation.

pages.title: Poverty Point
pages.intro: Explore individually dated earthworks and habitation, and the materials connecting Poverty Point with a wider world.

sections.heading: Earthworks and changing spaces

paragraphs.text: Six concentric ridge segments and an open central area organized a complex that also included substantial mounds. Mound A has a western cone, an eastern platform and a ramp, with different sediments and construction treatments. Its form should not be reduced to the popular but unproven claim that it was deliberately a bird effigy. Timber-circle traces reveal another architectural medium: wood could mark gathering spaces even when no standing posts survive.

The 2024 chronology argues for relatively concentrated building. Dates below a mound are older than its construction; they do not directly date its completed surface. That distinction matters when comparing mound construction, plaza filling and use of the ridges.

rows.name: Mound A
rows.dates: Main building placed in the approximate 3300–3200 cal BP synthesis
rows.architecture: Cone, platform and ramp; approximately 22 m high.
rows.limits: A site-wide construction synthesis is not an independently dated history of each component.

rows.name: Plaza and timber circles
rows.dates: Late Archaic contexts; some structures precede later plaza filling
rows.architecture: Post circles and deliberately placed fill.
rows.limits: Relative order is clearer than dates for every gathering or reconstruction.

sections.heading: Food, heat and imported stone

paragraphs.text: Wetland foods and upland resources supported a substantial settled community. Archaeological syntheses identify fish and other aquatic animals, aquatic plants, nuts, fruits and seeds. Heated clay objects substituted for scarce local cooking stones and could be used in earth ovens. Their abundance reflects repeated food preparation rather than evidence that farming was required to organize monument building.

Imported material was not reserved for one narrow category of prestige object. Tool making, cooking vessels and ornament drew on varied rocks and minerals. Copper provenance is a question about compositional similarity to sampled geological sources, with uncertainty remaining over precise sources and the mechanisms of movement. Neither a chemical group nor a distant source establishes the path taken by an artifact.

sections.heading: Three clocks that should stay distinct

paragraphs.text: The existing institutional settlement interval, 1700–1100 BCE, is a broad synthesis. Kidder and Grooms instead model a selected sequence, with start-boundary uncertainty at 3535–3430 cal BP and end-boundary uncertainty at 3250–3135 cal BP, both at 95.4% probability. Their approximate 3300–3200 cal BP construction pulse is a third kind of claim. None of these is a dated census of continuous occupation.

Calibrated BP uses 1950 as its reference year. The numbers in the model can therefore be placed on a calendar after calibration; a raw radiocarbon measurement cannot be converted by simply subtracting it from 1950. Earlier dates from residual or naturally burned material need not mark cultural activity or the founding of a mound.

sections.heading: Connections and unresolved social questions

paragraphs.text: Poverty Point belongs in comparisons of community organization and monument building, but similarity to another earthwork landscape does not establish ancestry or direct transmission. Its relationship with earlier Lower Mississippi Valley sites is a chronological research question, not proof that one center invented an entire regional culture.

Labor arrangements, the social obligations behind imported materials and the meaning of repeated timber structures remain open. The evidence supports skill, planning and sustained connections while leaving considerable uncertainty about leadership and ritual. Those limits are more informative than assigning an undocumented king, migration or catastrophic ending.

pages.title: Hopewell earthworks
pages.intro: Visit distinct earthwork complexes and compare their chronologies, ceremonial spaces and material connections without making them one city.

sections.heading: A landscape of named centers

paragraphs.text: Mound City, Hopewell Mound Group and Seip occupy different places and preserve different combinations of buildings, earthworks and deposits. Mound City has a compact enclosure with numerous mounds; Hopewell Mound Group joins a D-shaped enclosure and square; Seip combines circles, a square and substantial submound architecture. The public locators identify each complex, not individual graves or households.

rows.name: Mound City
rows.architecture: Enclosure, mounds, buildings and prepared ceremonial facilities.
rows.limits: Reconstructed surfaces and broad phase dates do not date every structure.

rows.name: Hopewell Mound Group
rows.architecture: D-shaped and square enclosures, submound buildings and activity areas.
rows.limits: Separate probability ranges, not one occupation interval.

rows.name: Seip
rows.architecture: Circular/square geometry, Seip-Pricer and additional buildings.
rows.limits: Seven selected dates; present central mound is reconstructed.

sections.heading: Craft, offerings and ceremonial interiors

paragraphs.text: Ohio Hopewell contexts include shaped copper, stone tools and ornaments, effigy pipes and other carefully worked materials. Their placement in buildings, basins or offerings matters as much as their appearance. A center could be a place of production and gathering without resembling a densely occupied urban neighborhood. The distribution of activities around monuments complicates simple images of empty ritual sites or ordinary residential towns.

At Seip, connected building remains, fire features and the burned offering provide specific settings for interpreting objects. Deliberate burning should first be understood in those settings; it cannot be treated as evidence of a shared regional calamity merely because other centers also contain burned materials.

sections.heading: What the chronology actually measures

paragraphs.text: The 2023 study evaluated a large radiocarbon corpus and compared increasingly selective sets. Its main regional onset is not simply 90–120 CE: that interval holds only 36.2% of probability, with another 32.1% at 130–170 CE. The broader 95.4% onset range is 70–185 CE. Reporting just the first interval would conceal the second probability peak.

Individual-center models give different boundaries. Charcoal, annual plant material and artifacts can have different relationships to the activities being dated. Long-lived wood, residual deposits and mixed contexts are among the reasons that chronological selection matters. A model boundary is a statistical estimate for a chosen sequence, not an observed year when all ceremonies began or ended.

sections.heading: Indigenous interpretation and continuing relationships

paragraphs.text: Barnes and Lepper’s drum proposal is a concrete example of interpretation shaped by Indigenous knowledge. Comparison with Shawnee drum construction gives the Seip spheres a possible functional context that earlier labels missed. The proposal remains testable and uncertain; acknowledging that uncertainty does not diminish the contribution of the knowledge that generated it.

Hopewell is an archaeological term covering related practices, materials and ceremonial landscapes. It is not a demonstrated single language, tribe or centralized state. Archaeology can trace changes in those practices without claiming that Indigenous peoples vanished when a material style changed. The named complexes invite comparison with other earthwork traditions while retaining their separate local histories.

pages.title: San Agustín
pages.intro: Follow local settlements, burial architecture and sculpture through their separate histories in the upper Magdalena.

sections.heading: Three mesitas, distinct histories

paragraphs.text: Mesita A, B and C are neighboring archaeological groups rather than interchangeable names for one monument. A has two principal funerary mounds; B combines three large mounds with a long residential and ceremonial history; C has a smaller funerary arrangement and a reported seventh-century context. Their relationships are best understood through buildings, deposits and household distributions together.

rows.name: Mesita A
rows.architecture: Principal mounds with corridors, chambers and statues; simpler surrounding tombs.
rows.limits: A broad cultural attribution does not date each burial.

rows.name: Mesita B and Household 68
rows.dates: Formative residential history; Regional Classic monuments
rows.architecture: Mounds, statues and differentiated household/craft evidence.
rows.limits: Public Mesitas locator is not a household coordinate; social rank is interpreted.

rows.name: Mesita C
rows.architecture: Former mound, statues and numerous simpler tombs.
rows.limits: Assays and calibration probabilities absent from the checked guide; earlier disturbance matters.

rows.name: La Estación
rows.architecture: Approximately 9 m structure, interpreted as ceremonial.
rows.limits: Function and exact building position remain less secure than the phase-associated structure itself.

sections.heading: Households, craft and agricultural work

paragraphs.text: The Mesitas research combines extensive shovel probing with artifact distributions to identify household clusters. Its ceramic phases provide broad comparisons through time, not year-by-year population totals. Household 68’s unusual pottery density is evidence of a distinctive activity area, but identifying feasts, collective storage or other specific activities requires more than a dense scatter alone.

During the Regional Classic, different parts of the core show contrasting relationships with gold ornament production, pottery making, obsidian exchange and ritual. González interprets this as several sources of influence and possible competition among prominent groups. The material distinctions are firmer than a reconstruction of tribute obligations, kinship factions or named offices.

sections.heading: Stone figures and the treatment of the dead

paragraphs.text: The best-known sculptures were parts of funerary architecture and inhabited landscapes. Monumental chambers and simpler surrounding tombs expressed differences in treatment after death. Rich sculpture does not necessarily imply abundant grave goods, and variation between neighboring groups should not be flattened into one standard ceremony.

A and B preserve stronger archaeological context for reconstructing some arrangements than areas disturbed before systematic study. The carved streambed at Fuente de Lavapatas has a broad stylistic attribution, but the checked sources do not provide a sufficiently secure construction date for a separate timed movie chapter. Its channels and figures can be discussed without manufacturing an exact building year.

sections.heading: Changing traditions without invented continuity

paragraphs.text: The park guide uses Formative 1 at 1000–600 BCE, Formative 2 at 600–300 BCE, Formative 3 at 300 BCE–1 CE, Regional Classic at 1–900 CE, and Recent at 900–1350 CE. These are archaeological conventions, with other regional works extending Recent to 1530. They should not be stitched into exact occupation endpoints or a single uninterrupted political history.

After the principal statuary-and-tomb tradition, ceramic change, agricultural intensification and the La Estación building suggest altered ways of organizing work and ceremony. The evidence does not securely assign all phases to one named language or a modern ethnic identity. Comparison with Tierradentro is useful for architecture and settlement, provided local chronologies and social histories remain distinct.

pages.title: Tierradentro
pages.intro: Explore named tomb groups alongside settlement evidence, distinguishing uncertain tomb dates from better-resolved local occupation phases.

sections.heading: Named groups and architectural differences

paragraphs.text: The public archaeological groups preserve different choices in chamber size, roof treatment, supports and decoration. Segovia includes elaborate carved pillars and painted interiors; El Duende D4 has a rectangular room and distinctive roof form; El Aguacate generally has smaller chambers without central columns. These differences deserve comparison without automatically turning them into separate peoples or a precise developmental sequence.

rows.name: Alto de Segovia
rows.dates: Conventional hypogeum window approximately 600–900 CE, contested
rows.architecture: Named chambers S1, S4 and S9; pillars, niches and painting.
rows.limits: Direct chamber construction dates are not established by the guide.

rows.name: El Duende
rows.architecture: D4 rectangular chamber, roof treatment and geometric painting.
rows.limits: Architectural variation is not itself an absolute date.

rows.name: El Aguacate
rows.architecture: Small ridge-top chambers; A0 with distinctive painted motifs.
rows.limits: Domestic layer near A60 has no precise date in this source check.

rows.name: El Tablón
rows.architecture: Anthropomorphic statuary, often with pectorals.
rows.limits: Settlement phase does not directly date carving of individual stones.

sections.heading: Burial practices and the houses of the living

paragraphs.text: Hypogea could receive human remains after initial burial elsewhere, so a bone’s biological age and its later deposition are different events. Carved architectural forms and painted interiors made the chambers more than storage spaces, but the sources do not preserve a complete account of ceremonies or the identities of participants.

Regional survey places the monuments among changing settlements. Early 3 concentrations at Segovia, Middle-period occupation around El Tablón and later residence near San Andrés prevent the funerary landscape from being treated as isolated from daily life. The domestic layer at El Aguacate is especially useful as a warning against assuming that all tomb groups stood apart from habitation.

sections.heading: Two chronological systems and a translation error

paragraphs.text: The regional study uses Early 3 at 300 BCE–100 CE, Middle at 100–1300 CE and Late at 1300–1650 CE. These local ceramic phases differ from the generalized Alto Magdalena sequence. Their boundaries should not be exchanged merely because period names appear similar.

The English park guide prints 600–900 BC for the hypogea where the Spanish version reads 600–900 d.C. The CE reading is used here, with the uncertainty emphasized in the sources. The regional study also reports contamination problems with extremely early apparent bone dates. Neither the mistranslation nor contaminated samples justify a new early tomb-building episode.

sections.heading: Living territory and unresolved affiliations

paragraphs.text: The archaeological park lies within the Nasa resguardo of San Andrés. That present relationship is essential context for understanding the place, while the checked archaeological sources do not establish a single language or an unbroken named identity for every ancient monument builder. Historical accounts themselves describe several peoples and uncertain territorial limits.

Tierradentro and San Agustín share useful points of comparison in statuary, mortuary architecture and the relationship between monuments and settlement. Their local sequences should nevertheless remain separate. More secure dating, contextual research and Indigenous knowledge can refine those relationships without requiring the current gaps to be filled by an invented migration or common political state.

pages.title: Casarabe urban landscapes
pages.intro: Look at individual centers and engineered landscapes, separating dated construction, regional models and later agricultural evidence.

sections.heading: Five centers with different evidence

paragraphs.text: Cotoca and Landívar are major centers, while Cerrito, Santa María and Salvatierra show other scales and configurations of the same broad architectural tradition. Lidar identifies elevated platforms, enclosures and connections; excavation at Salvatierra supplies stratigraphy and dated samples. Combining these approaches reveals a connected landscape without making every mapped structure contemporary.

rows.name: Cotoca
rows.architecture: Large raised core, U-shaped and other platforms, multiple enclosures and causeways.
rows.limits: No directly dated sequence for every enclosure; approximately 147 ha is enclosed area.

rows.name: Landívar
rows.architecture: Platforms beside a former channel, three enclosing circuits and raised approaches.
rows.limits: 315 ha outer enclosure does not measure dense housing or population.

rows.name: Cerrito
rows.architecture: Raised platform core, substantial structures, enclosure and connected causeways.
rows.limits: Individual construction phases remain undated in this source.

rows.name: Santa María
rows.architecture: Platforms, dams, reservoirs and enclosing earthwork.
rows.limits: Do not confuse its reservoirs with Pond 690 in the separate farming study.

rows.name: Salvatierra
rows.dates: Selected Phase 1 sample 495–591; Phase 5 sample 1081–1158 CE, modeled 95.4%
rows.architecture: Excavated deposits within an architectural complex with platforms and water storage.
rows.limits: Sample dates do not individually date all buildings or demonstrate uninterrupted occupation.

sections.heading: Seasonal water and agricultural work

paragraphs.text: Water could be both an excess and a scarce resource. Canals could drain savannah soils in wet months, while reservoirs and farm ponds retained water through drier periods. Santa María’s arrangements provide a named architectural example of water management; the separately sampled agricultural ponds address a different scale of evidence. The purposes of every canal and basin should not be treated as identical.

The 2025 study examined 178 phytolith samples from eighteen profiles. Maize dominates the sampled agricultural evidence, but the body of the paper also reports Cucurbita in two adjacent pond samples and a Manihot pollen grain. The proposed seasonal farming system and possibility of multiple harvests do not establish that all regional food consumption was maize, nor that every household followed one uniform strategy.

sections.heading: Networks, enclosures and political uncertainty

paragraphs.text: Causeways connect some known centers and branch through an engineered landscape. Gaps and platforms near enclosure crossings have been interpreted as restricted access, while some enclosure forms may have had defensive roles. These are functional hypotheses from architecture, not documentation of named wars, armies or boundaries. Other causeways have no identified destination, leaving their daily or ceremonial uses unresolved.

The study proposes a settlement hierarchy with several tiers and describes low-density urbanism: monumental centers embedded within a broad modified landscape. That interpretation does not supply a precise population or prove one centralized state. Smaller unmounded settlements may be less visible in lidar, so the mapped hierarchy is also shaped by what the method can detect.

sections.heading: Radiocarbon, landforms and later activity

paragraphs.text: The regional 500–1400 CE horizon comes from dated excavations and archaeological comparisons. At Salvatierra, the selected Phase 1 and Phase 5 contexts are modeled charcoal likelihoods within a stratigraphic sequence. A charcoal age is not automatically the date when a platform was raised, and early samples beneath buildings can represent natural activity or earlier use rather than the Casarabe construction itself.

Pond 690’s approximately 1250–1550 calendar CE sequence was modeled from sediment dates. It extends later than the broad urban-system horizon and is retained as its own observation. The result cannot extend the occupation of every town to 1550 or establish the cultural identity of every later pond user. Sampled forest profiles likewise leave other woodland uses possible even where cultivation and fire were not detected.

pages.title: Nan Madol: building, water and chiefly life
pages.intro: Follow separate construction projects in Nan Madol and the evidence for changing use; an early tomb date is not the beginning of every islet.

sections.heading: Basalt, coral and architectural context

paragraphs.text: Nan Madol combines monumental basalt architecture with coral deposits used in construction. Dates from an enclosing wall and central-vault fill at Nandowas should remain separate observations, even when both contribute to one tomb complex’s history.

sections.heading: A changing shoreline

paragraphs.text: Relative sea-level reconstruction indicates that the site’s construction-era water setting differed from its modern appearance. Present canals and shorelines cannot simply be projected backward unchanged. This environmental result does not erase human engineering.

sections.heading: Building phases and unresolved causes

paragraphs.text: The 2024 coral chronology distinguishes an early phase, a concentrated early cluster and a larger later phase. Climatic or political explanations are interpretations of those patterns; the ages do not by themselves prove a universal crisis, forced-labor system or exact date of political replacement.

sections.heading: Pohnpeian institutions and continuing meaning

paragraphs.text: The nomination’s historical discussion and the World Heritage description connect Nan Madol to continuing chiefly authority and social practice. The archaeological study concerns a living cultural inheritance, rather than an unnamed vanished population.

The nomination is internally uneven: its summary ends residential use by the 1820s, while its detailed history retains chiefly occupation on a few islets into the early 1900s. Its 1826–1885 phase supplies a context window, not a dated assembly or continuous occupation of every islet. Ceremonial significance and household residence are separate.

pages.title: Budj Bim: an engineered water landscape
pages.intro: Explore engineering and settlement in the Budj Bim cultural landscape with distinct dates for landforms, construction and continued use.

sections.heading: Country provides the setting; engineering has its own chronology

paragraphs.text: Budj Bim’s lava landscape gave later communities a particular terrain of rock and water. The eruption, the earliest dated channel infill and later wall building are different events. None should be used as a substitute date for the others.

sections.heading: Reading a system rather than an isolated wall

paragraphs.text: Channels, weirs and dams worked together with wetlands to manage and harvest aquatic resources, including kooyang, short-finned eels. Excavation at Muldoons identifies successive local construction episodes; the whole landscape cannot be assigned one uniform building year.

sections.heading: Three components, broad public references

paragraphs.text: The World Heritage property comprises a northern component around Tae Rak, central Kurtonitj and southern Tyrendarra. The public component coordinates orient the reader within a large cultural landscape. They do not identify individual channels, private places or excavation grids.

sections.heading: Residence, access and the companion community history

paragraphs.text: The Kurtonitj house and Lake Condah Mission add nineteenth-century histories to the engineering record. They have their own dates and meanings. Gunditjmara histories follows the people and colonial institutions; this place study follows how evidence is situated in the landscape.

pages.title: Gunditjmara histories: Country, work and persistence
pages.intro: Connect engineered Country with Gunditjmara community histories, colonial intrusion, coercive institutions and continuing agency.

sections.heading: A living people, not an extinct archaeological category

paragraphs.text: Gunditjmara institutions describe continuing responsibilities to Country. Dated channels, barriers, houses, and objects record particular activities within that living history, whose duration extends beyond the archaeological sequence.

sections.heading: Work, knowledge and material evidence

paragraphs.text: The Muldoons sequence documents local engineering changes, while Kurtonitj documents a household context centuries later. Neither assemblage stands for every Gunditjmara person. Their different dates and methods are preserved so that community history is not compressed into one material style.

sections.heading: Mission life, coercion and choices

paragraphs.text: Lake Condah Mission followed resistance to removal from Country. Colonial supervision and the 1886 exclusionary policy then constrained residence. Describing those constraints also requires retaining community choices, family connections and the continuing importance of the site.

sections.heading: How this study connects to Budj Bim

paragraphs.text: The Budj Bim study follows aquaculture engineering and the changing water landscape. This Gunditjmara study follows household life, resistance and mission history. Links between them connect these perspectives on Country and community life.

pages.title: Lapita communities and successors
pages.intro: Follow particular settlements and connections across islands, then ask what changed after the archaeological label Lapita ceased to describe pottery.

sections.heading: What the name Lapita can and cannot do

paragraphs.text: Lapita is an archaeological category built around material patterns, especially decorated pottery. It is useful for comparing sites, but it is not a single ethnic identity, a biological ancestry or a language automatically readable from a potsherd.

sections.heading: Settlement and everyday food

paragraphs.text: Kamgot’s shoreline reconstruction and plant and marine remains bring local work into a history often dominated by voyaging. Uripiv’s isotope study adds evidence about diet and childhood residence. These methods answer different questions and must retain their own limits.

sections.heading: Seafaring without invented routes

paragraphs.text: Fishing assemblages, exchanged materials and related material practices demonstrate maritime connections at different scales. They do not authorize drawing a particular family’s voyage between every sampled site. Chronological models can compare island sequences while leaving uncertain routes uncertain.

sections.heading: After decorated pottery, and among living communities

paragraphs.text: Later occupation at Uripiv shows why the end of a pottery category is not an automatic departure. Vanuatu Cultural Centre authors also describe the contemporary significance of Lapita research. That living engagement is acknowledged here without adding post-1934 events to the historical map.

pages.title: Aztec: building and remaking an Animas community
pages.intro: A local chronology of construction, alteration, communal use, and living Pueblo connections at Aztec Ruins.

sections.heading: An Animas River community, not an Aztec city

paragraphs.text: Aztec Ruins is an ancestral Pueblo place in the Animas River valley. Its modern name came from an incorrect association with Mexico’s Aztec Empire. Several great houses, smaller dwellings, roads, and communal structures formed a planned community whose history connects to Chaco Canyon while developing its own local pattern.

West Ruin’s hundreds of rooms did not all serve the same purpose. The National Park Service describes gathering, ceremony, work, exchange, and storage; its interpretation places much early domestic life in nearby smaller buildings. Later room alterations make the functions of a particular chamber more informative than treating the entire great house as a single apartment block.

sections.heading: West Ruin was built in stages

paragraphs.text: Builders assembled West Ruin in stages: Kiva L, the north and east wings, and the west wing preserve distinct construction observations. Later alterations changed the great house after this initial building sequence.

Tree-ring dates are especially informative here, but their relationship to construction still requires architectural evidence. Walls can abut older work, and a roof timber can be stored or reused. The surviving plan also contains centuries of changes, so it cannot be read as a picture of one founding moment.

rows.name: Kiva L
rows.architecture: Early circular structure in the main core.
rows.limits: An early construction phase, not completion of West Ruin.

rows.name: North and east wings
rows.architecture: Large multistory room blocks.
rows.limits: The wings belong to West Ruin; they are not Aztec East.

rows.name: West wing
rows.architecture: Further multistory construction westward.
rows.limits: NPS rounds this phase to 1120–1130.

sections.heading: A changing plan and a longer-lived neighbor

paragraphs.text: Renovation changed circulation and room use at West Ruin. New plaza-facing rooms and inserted kivas could close off earlier spaces; later partitions produced smaller chambers. A style name such as McElmo or Mesa Verde describes an archaeological pattern and does not by itself demonstrate that one population replaced another.

Aztec East followed a different tempo. Its masonry and timber sequence extends from an early core through repeated later additions. Much remains unexcavated, so a broad sequence is more defensible than a precise date for its whole footprint. The chronology of old beams must be considered together with the walls that hold them.

rows.name: West Ruin renovation
rows.dates: After 1130; substantial work in the late 1100s
rows.architecture: Added rooms and kivas within an older great house.
rows.limits: The broad phase combines several operations.

rows.name: West Ruin later changes
rows.architecture: Partitions, kivas, roof renewal and changing domestic use.
rows.limits: 1250 on the map is a representative mid-century date.

rows.name: Aztec East
rows.architecture: A great house enlarged and remodeled over generations.
rows.limits: Published summaries differ in the last construction decade; the broad envelope is explicit.

sections.heading: Communal architecture beyond ordinary rooms

paragraphs.text: Hubbard’s concentric walls and central kiva make it a distinct feature rather than another wing of West Ruin. Earlier adobe architecture lies underneath. The Great Kiva stands separately in West Ruin’s plaza and continued to serve gatherings while other parts of the complex changed.

The Great Kiva seen today includes a 1934 reconstruction supervised by Earl Morris. Excavated features informed that work, but the modern roof and upper walls should not be confused with intact twelfth-century fabric. Its architecture helps visitors understand scale while also requiring interpretation of what is original, rebuilt, or uncertain.

rows.name: Hubbard Tri-wall
rows.architecture: Concentric-walled structure above earlier adobe buildings.
rows.limits: A broad architectural date, with a conflicting earlier estimate on a general NPS travel page.

rows.name: West Great Kiva
rows.dates: Later twelfth and thirteenth centuries of communal use
rows.architecture: Large plaza chamber with surrounding surface rooms and substantial roof supports.
rows.limits: The purpose of individual surrounding rooms is unresolved; reconstruction dates to 1934.

sections.heading: Departure and relationships that continue

paragraphs.text: The end of settlement in the late thirteenth century did not end Pueblo history. NPS connects regional migration with existing communities along the Rio Grande, in the Zuni region, and at Hopi villages. These are broad historical connections, not individually documented routes from each room at Aztec.

Many Southwestern Native peoples maintain spiritual relationships with this ancestral place through oral traditions, prayer, and ceremony. Archaeological dates explain episodes of building and use; they do not place an expiration date on those relationships. Read this local study alongside the Four Corners parent guide and the separate Chaco and Salmon studies.

pages.title: Salmon: a great house through changing generations
pages.intro: A local chronology distinguishing Salmon Pueblo’s first construction, continued occupation, later rebuilding, and final-use evidence.

sections.heading: A great house beside the San Juan River

paragraphs.text: Salmon Pueblo occupies a river-valley setting north of Chaco Canyon. Around 1090, builders created an E-shaped great house with multistory rooms and two prominent communal structures: the elevated Tower Kiva in the central block and the Great Kiva in the plaza. The present name comes from a later landholding family; descendant communities know the place through other names and histories.

Its two broad archaeological phases organize the evidence: Chacoan, about 1090–1125, and San Juan, about 1125–1280. These labels help compare deposits and alterations. They should not be read as a vacant interval or as proof that all residents changed at one moment.

rows.name: Great House
rows.architecture: E-shaped, multistory room blocks.
rows.limits: The construction point does not date every wall.

rows.name: Chacoan occupation
rows.architecture: Residential use as well as communal activity.
rows.limits: The phase boundary is approximate.

rows.name: San Juan occupation
rows.architecture: Continued use with extensive architectural changes.
rows.limits: Rounded phase limits differ from the final-fire decade.

sections.heading: Two kivas with different histories

paragraphs.text: The Tower Kiva and Great Kiva are not interchangeable names. Unit 64W stood on a raised central platform; Unit 130W occupied the open plaza to its south. Their different forms, deposits, and rebuilding histories let the guide connect the visible plan with specific archaeological observations.

A date is only as direct as its evidence. The archive reports tree-ring support for the Tower Kiva’s first building episode. For the Great Kiva, the early date is inferred from context because no tree-ring date marks its initial construction. Both appear around 1090 on the clock, but their confidence explanations differ.

rows.name: Tower Kiva, 64W
rows.architecture: Raised central kiva within the main room block.
rows.limits: Mapped to the central-core polygon with about 35 m uncertainty.

rows.name: Great Kiva, 130W
rows.architecture: Detached communal chamber in the plaza.
rows.limits: Initial date is contextual, not a measured first-construction timber date.

sections.heading: Room 96W shows change within an existing place

paragraphs.text: Room 96W began as a square Chacoan chamber and was converted into a round kiva toward the end of that phase. Later additions included more of the features associated with San Juan kivas. The circular insertion created small spaces between its walls and those of the original square room.

This is a useful local example because it makes change tangible without inventing a migration event. A published synthesis places the conversion in the 1120s, while the archive explicitly reports that no tree-ring dates came from the room. Its mapped location therefore remains the great-house complex anchor, and the chronology retains its interpretive status.

rows.name: Room 96W conversion
rows.architecture: Square chamber adapted into a kiva.
rows.limits: No tree-ring dates from the room; the map does not claim a room-center coordinate.

rows.name: Distributed room and kiva changes
rows.architecture: Smaller rooms and numerous inserted kivas.
rows.limits: A sequence of local changes, not one rebuilding day.

sections.heading: A new Great Kiva roof in 1263

paragraphs.text: The Great Kiva supplies a particularly clear late construction observation: its roof was replaced in spring or summer 1263. The archive describes hundreds of beams cut over nearly twenty years. Timber age therefore records procurement as well as the moment those materials entered the rebuilt roof.

Later work also included refacing interior masonry and constructing a surrounding cobble berm. A broader research synthesis discusses flooding in the river-side settlement and interprets the berm as flood protection; the unit summary emphasizes structural support. These functions can be discussed together, but the precise date of every part of the berm is not established by the roof date.

rows.name: Great Kiva roof
rows.architecture: Replacement roof assembled from older and newly available timber.
rows.limits: Dates the roof episode, not all other alterations or final use.

sections.heading: Fire, migration, and a living ancestral place

paragraphs.text: An intentional fire ended the Tower Kiva’s final use in the late thirteenth century, according to SPARC. The burning belongs to the end of the San Juan occupation, but it does not establish warfare.

Many Tribes and Nations maintain ancestral connections to Salmon Pueblo. SPARC itself acknowledges that its present archaeological archive does not supply those communities’ interpretations and histories. It is a valuable record of excavation and research, not a substitute for descendant voices or a basis for assigning one uniform migration route to every household.

Use the Four Corners guide for the regional story, and compare Salmon with Aztec and Chaco as separate local studies. Their connections matter, but their different building tempos and patterns of reuse remain visible when each place keeps its own chronology.

pages.title: Canyon de Chelly / Tséyi’: a living homeland
pages.intro: Tséyi’, or Canyon de Chelly, holds Pueblo villages, Diné farms and art, and histories of military violence, forced removal, and return. Its 1931 designation as a national monument took place within Navajo land and a continuing Diné homeland.

sections.heading: Tséyi’: a lived landscape

paragraphs.text: Canyon de Chelly, or Tséyi’, brings together the main canyon, Canyon del Muerto, tributary canyons and surrounding uplands within the Navajo Nation. Water, cultivable ground, alcoves and pathways supported many forms of dwelling and farming. The surviving Pueblo buildings are one part of that history. Diné families continue to live and cultivate here, while Pueblo descendants maintain connections to ancestral places.

Dates in this study describe particular buildings, rebuilding episodes and historical events. Antelope House, White House and Mummy Cave did not all begin or cease use together. The current NPS history places a broader Puebloan departure in the mid-1300s; an older institutional account uses about 1300. Those broad summaries remain distinct from the excavator’s proposed earlier end to Antelope House’s main village around 1270. Neither account dates the disappearance of a people.

sections.heading: Antelope House: successive communities at one place

paragraphs.text: Excavation revealed earlier buildings beneath the masonry visible today. Structure 67 has a cluster of structural cutting dates in 691–693. A much larger Pueblo I village, with wood-and-adobe walls, was built around 825–850. Evidence becomes sparse during much of approximately 950–1100, although structures remained in the south. The later village therefore should not be displayed as seven centuries of unchanged, continuous occupation.

The later masonry settlement grew through rooms added around kivas, increased building heights, new floors and changes in storage space. The circular Central Plaza was a late addition above Kiva C, followed by further remodeling. Morris’s excavation report places this construction after 1200; the 2013 visitor brochure’s 1300s date is incompatible with that sequence. The report’s late dates are less secure than its early structural dates, but its reasoning can be examined directly.

rows.name: Antelope House, Structure 67
rows.architecture: Burned structural members below the later village provide a tightly bounded construction observation.
rows.limits: Later burning is separately dated; the complex point does not survey this buried structure.

rows.name: Antelope House, later masonry village
rows.architecture: South and north room blocks, kivas, storage rooms and successive floors record rebuilding.
rows.limits: The dates bracket one phase. Earlier use, possible later visits and Diné reuse are separate.

rows.name: Antelope House, circular Central Plaza
rows.dates: After 1200, within the later village phase
rows.architecture: An initially open plaza was changed through new floors and rooms partly replacing its wall.
rows.limits: No precise wall-construction year is known; a visitor brochure instead says 1300s.

sections.heading: White House and Mummy Cave: reading different kinds of dates

paragraphs.text: White House combines a lower multistory pueblo with an upper alcove dwelling, whose white plaster gave the complex its familiar name. NPS summarizes roof-timber evidence as building activity beginning around 1060 with additions as late as 1275. Breternitz’s analysis also records an earlier timber, a cluster in the 1070s and a late occupation associated with Mesa Verde pottery. A timber’s last ring, a building addition and a village’s final use are different observations.

At Mummy Cave, a more specific claim is possible: Breternitz dates the tower’s second and third floors to 1284. This does not date every room in its east and west alcoves. NPS connects the central tower complex with movement from Mesa Verde in the 1280s, an interpretation that belongs beside the architecture and tree-ring evidence. It cannot establish the birthplace of every builder or a traced migration route.

rows.name: White House
rows.architecture: Lower pueblo and upper cliff rooms form one complex.
rows.limits: The early timber outlier is not automatically a founding date; 1275 is not a universal abandonment date.

rows.name: Mummy Cave tower
rows.dates: 1284 CE for second and third floors
rows.architecture: Upper floors of the central tower have contextual tree-ring evidence.
rows.limits: The map point identifies the whole Mummy Cave complex, not a surveyed tower footprint.

sections.heading: Diné art, farming and memory

paragraphs.text: Antelope House’s familiar name also points to a later history. The NPS North Rim guide records local Navajo attribution of antelope paintings beside the village to Dibe Yazhi, or Little Sheep, who lived here in the 1830s. The later brochure uses the broader early 1800s. The map preserves this attribution without turning it into a scientifically measured pigment date or assigning all nearby images to one artist.

In her contribution to the NPS brochure, Diné writer Ailema Benally explains relationships among landscape, language, families and responsibility passed between generations. This perspective helps readers understand why Tséyi’ is more than a collection of old buildings. Morris’s excavation report also records Dan Anagal’s account of family use of remodeled Antelope House rooms before the Second World War. These are attributed statements, rather than a claim to speak for all Diné people.

rows.name: Paintings beside Antelope House
rows.architecture: Antelope images attributed locally to Dibe Yazhi.
rows.limits: The 1800–1850 display range is an editorial broad bracket, not an exact art date.

sections.heading: Military violence, captivity and return

paragraphs.text: In January 1805, a Spanish force commanded by Antonio Narbona attacked a Navajo refuge at the place now called Massacre Cave. Bradley’s handbook reproduces part of the commander’s letter and separately describes a Navajo account centered on people taking shelter. Narbona reported 115 killed and 33 captives; those figures and his classification of the dead remain attributed to him. They are not treated as an independent count, and the story of the refuge is not reduced to the commander’s categories.

U.S. troops entered Canyon de Chelly in 1864 and destroyed homes, orchards, and livestock to force Diné surrender. The campaign formed part of the Long Walk and confinement at Bosque Redondo. Families experienced different departures and routes, while some people remained in the homeland. Return followed in 1868.

The 1868 treaty enabled Diné people to return to a limited reservation within their homeland. Rebuilding followed severe losses, and return did not restore every earlier land right. Living communities continued the history of residence, work, and responsibility in the canyon.

rows.name: Massacre Cave vicinity, Canyon del Muerto
rows.architecture: A refuge became the site of a Spanish military attack, killing and capture.
rows.limits: Broad vicinity anchor only; the overlook is not the event site and no firing positions are mapped.

rows.name: Canyon system: U.S. destruction campaign
rows.architecture: Homes, orchards and livestock were targeted to drive surrender.
rows.limits: Landscape-scale observation, separate from the existing Long Walk and internment records.

rows.name: Long Walk, Bosque Redondo, and return — existing atlas evidence
rows.architecture: Reused records connect local destruction to forced marches, captivity and negotiated return.
rows.limits: No duplicate route or invented common assembly point is added.

sections.heading: 1931: protecting archaeology on Navajo land

paragraphs.text: The national monument’s creation involved negotiations and local concern about land use. Navajo council approval did not eliminate questions from canyon residents: a 1930 petition objected to boundaries that might restrict grazing and collecting wood. A later petition accepted assurances that existing rights would remain. These discussions show residents as participants with specific concerns, rather than an empty landscape being set aside for visitors.

Congress authorized the monument on 14 February 1931, and President Hoover proclaimed it on 1 April. The enabling act reserved Navajo land interests and agricultural and grazing uses while assigning preservation and related infrastructure responsibilities to NPS. The monument’s creation did not begin Diné residence or transfer away all Navajo interests. Contemporary NPS history continues to describe a living community and a partnership with the Navajo Nation.

rows.name: Canyon de Chelly National Monument
rows.architecture: Legal protection for archaeological resources with Navajo land interests and uses expressly reserved.
rows.limits: The broad map anchor is not a boundary polygon or the location where officials signed the documents.

sections.heading: How to read this local map

paragraphs.text: White House, Antelope House and Mummy Cave use the public NPS archaeological feature points, checked against the official visitor map. Overlooks have different coordinates. Buried Structure 67, the Central Plaza and the Mummy Cave tower are described at their parent complex because this study has not surveyed their individual footprints. The 1805 episode uses a broad northern Canyon del Muerto anchor, and the 1864 and 1931 observations use a broad canyon-system anchor.

Read this study with the Four Corners regional guide for wider settlement change, and with Mesa Verde and Chaco for comparisons in architecture and movement. A stylistic resemblance, a dated beam and a claim about migration are related kinds of evidence, but they do not have identical precision. In particular, Tséyi’ does not supply one uniform departure date for all Pueblo communities or one fixed arrival date for all Diné histories.
