pages.title: Atlantic Canada: coastal communities, fisheries and displacement
pages.intro: Deep coastal evidence, sea-going work and living Indigenous communities connect with colonial fisheries, Acadian displacement, treaty diplomacy and imposed schooling through 1934.

sections.heading: Long coastal histories

paragraphs.text: Debert in Nova Scotia preserves an early landscape of stone-tool use. A modern calibrated synthesis places its pooled age around 12,630 calendar years before 1950, roughly 10,680 BCE. The excavations did not recover animal bones, so the familiar image of a caribou-hunting camp is an interpretation rather than a direct faunal observation there. Farther north, the Atlantic coast supported very different communities through time. At Phillip’s Garden on Newfoundland, dwellings, middens and abundant seal remains document Dorset settlement and hunting during a later sequence extending approximately from 40 BCE to 770 CE.

Metepenagiag in New Brunswick brings community knowledge into the history of archaeological recognition. Elder Joe Augustine remembered what earlier generations had told him about a sacred place; this helped identify the mound now bearing his name. Textiles, basketry, copper ornaments and distinctive pipes preserve ceremonial practices and distant material connections. The community’s history places the cemetery before 600 BCE, while heritage accounts also use a rounded age of 2,500 years. Neither estimate dates the beginning of Mi’kmaq presence. The nearby Oxbow settlement and the living community give the mound a broader human setting.

sections.heading: Voyages, fisheries and lived settlements

paragraphs.text: Norse woodcutting at L’Anse aux Meadows is securely fixed to 1021 CE by tree-ring evidence. That precise year dates an activity, not the full lifespan of the settlement or an unlimited European presence. Later Basque crews at Red Bay built a seasonal whaling industry in Labrador: ovens rendered blubber, coopers assembled barrels, and vessels carried oil to European markets. The surviving shore structures and wrecks make this work unusually tangible. Both places belong within a longer Atlantic world, whose Indigenous histories are not suspended when a European ship appears.

French colonists established the Port-Royal habitation in Mi’kma’ki in 1605, with Mi’kmaq relationships and Membertou central to its circumstances. At Ferryland, Calvert’s plantation began in 1621 and continued as a fishing and commercial place after he left. These colonial ventures did not exhaust the island’s settlement history. Boyd’s Cove preserves Beothuk housepits attributed to roughly 1650–1720, showing an Indigenous community living through the age of expanding fisheries. Buildings, seasonal work and local knowledge followed different rhythms at each place; a colonial foundation date should not stand for the beginning of human occupation.

sections.heading: Military ports, treaties and forced removal

paragraphs.text: Britain’s Halifax expedition entered Kjipuktuk in June 1749, bringing a fortified colonial settlement into a harbour already used by Mi’kmaq people. Diplomacy continued amid conflict. Jean-Baptiste Cope and Governor Hopson concluded the 1752 Peace and Friendship Treaty at Halifax; its written provisions addressed hunting, fishing, exchange and peace. This relationship differed from a blanket surrender of Mi’kma’ki. On Epekwitk, Skmaqn/Port-la-Joye was a meeting place where Mi’kmaq and French representatives renewed their alliance. Colonial administration and military competition grew around these existing relationships, rather than replacing Indigenous politics with an exclusively European story.

The fall of Fort Beauséjour on 16 June 1755 intensified British control at Chignecto. At Grand-Pré on 5 September, Acadian men and boys were confined and informed of deportation. They belonged to a society that had turned tidal marsh into farmland using dykes and wooden sluices. Removing households therefore also severed relationships to an engineered agricultural landscape. After Louisbourg fell in 1758, British authorities organized another mass removal from Île Saint-Jean, now Prince Edward Island. More than 3,000 French and Acadian inhabitants were deported; shipwreck and illness made the sea journey deadly.

sections.heading: Continuing communities under new pressures

paragraphs.text: The effects of conquest were different for different peoples. Mi’kmaq history on Epekwitk continued after the Acadian deportation, even as British surveys failed to reserve island land for Indigenous people. Acadian return, dispersal and renewed settlements also continued beyond the departures. In Labrador, Moravian missionaries established themselves at Nain in 1771, where Inuit were already living. Nunatsiavut’s own account keeps Inuit language, work and community at the centre of that history. A mission brought new trade and religious institutions to an existing place; it did not create Inuit society or erase the people living there.

By 1930, the colonial intervention into Indigenous family life included the opening of Shubenacadie residential school. Many Mi’kmaw and Wolastoqkew children were compelled to attend this federally funded, church-run institution. Constructed in 1928–1929, it enrolled students from 1930 and continued long after this atlas’s 1934 endpoint. The account developed with Survivors and descendants describes an assimilation project directed at cultures and identities, not simply a school building. Ending the map’s chronology in 1934 leaves that history ongoing, alongside communities whose fishing, language, kinship and cultural life persisted through profound disruption.

pages.title: Pacific Canada: shorelines, villages and colonial encounters
pages.intro: Footprints, clam gardens, houses, trade and Indigenous communities across the coast and Fraser interior.

sections.heading: Shorelines and homes before the trading posts

paragraphs.text: The Pacific coast opens with people’s footsteps. At Calvert Island, researchers identified 29 impressions made by at least three people, including a juvenile. Pine wood associated with the track surface places this episode between 13,317 and 12,633 calibrated years before 1950. The impressions preserve a brief encounter between feet and wet ground; they cannot tell us how long those people stayed. The setting lies within Heiltsuk and Wuikinuxv homelands, where changing shorelines have shaped which early traces survive and where archaeologists can find them.

Farther south, people remade intertidal beaches. On northern Quadra Island, rock walls retained sediment and created flatter terraces suitable for clams. Research in Kanish and Waiatt bays places some gardens at least 3,500 years ago, with subsequent work extending the construction history to at least 3,800 years. These structures belong to Laich-Kwil-Tach and northern Coast Salish homelands. They show food production through close knowledge of tides, shellfish and sediment, rather than a simple division between farming societies and people who merely collected wild foods.

sections.heading: Villages, households and ocean connections

paragraphs.text: In the interior, Keatley Creek’s housepits preserve another form of settled life near the Fraser River. A published radiocarbon model places the aggregated village approximately 250–1150 CE, with interruptions inside that span. Its large houses and household deposits have prompted debate about how people lived together and how inequalities developed. Brian Hayden’s reading of the dates differs from that model. The disagreement concerns particular structures and sequences: the evidence for substantial houses is firmer than a single, uncontested story of when the whole village grew or declined.

The coast also contained large wooden houses, public art and centres of authority. SG̱ang Gwaay preserves nineteenth-century Haida cedar-house remains and carved poles within a place of continuing cultural importance. At Yuquot, Mowachaht leaders dealt with ocean-going traders and competing European powers in the late eighteenth century. Yuquot was a centre of the sea-otter trade in 1785–1795 and the setting for the Vancouver–Quadra negotiations of 1792. These were encounters at established communities whose political and ceremonial lives cannot be reduced to the visiting ships.

sections.heading: Commerce becomes colonial government

paragraphs.text: Fort Langley, established by the Hudson’s Bay Company in 1827, brought a different commercial presence to the lower Fraser. Its business included salmon, agricultural produce and overseas shipments as well as furs. The fort’s later moves, rebuilding and changing economic role matter: a modern reconstructed enclosure is not the original 1827 post. Across the river and surrounding valley, Kwantlen and other Stó:lō communities remained essential to the region’s economy. The proclamation of the mainland colony at the fort in 1858 connected commercial infrastructure with a new form of colonial authority.

In Tŝilhqot’in country, expansion brought armed conflict. During the 1864 war, colonial officials invited leaders into discussions that were presented as peace negotiations. Five war chiefs were subsequently imprisoned, tried and executed at Quesnel on 26 October. Tŝilhqot’in histories remember their defence of land and people, and later provincial statements acknowledge the wrongful hangings. Ahan’s execution at New Westminster in 1865 was a separate event. Keeping the places and dates distinct makes responsibility clearer than treating the entire conflict as one undifferentiated frontier episode.

sections.heading: Children, ceremony and continuing communities

paragraphs.text: By 1894, St. Michael’s at Alert Bay appears in the National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation’s register as an operating Anglican residential school. A school is a different kind of historical place from a village or trading station: its institutional presence signals intervention in children’s lives and community relationships. The register supplies a local chronology for an institution whose effects reached across families and generations. Its operation continued far beyond this atlas’s 1934 endpoint, which is a limit of the historical view rather than a closing date.

At ʼMimkwa̱mlis on Village Island, Dan Cranmer hosted a major potlatch in 1921 despite Canada’s ban. Prosecution and the confiscation of regalia followed, sending treasured belongings away from their owners. U’mista’s account explains that songs, dances and masks carried histories and obligations; taking them was an intrusion into how communities transmitted knowledge and authority. The gathering therefore belongs beside houses and food-producing landscapes in this regional history. It also prevents a story ending with colonial institutions from obscuring the people who continued to hold and practise their traditions.

pages.title: Prairie Canada: foodways, Métis settlements and treaty encounters
pages.intro: Hunting, cultivation, river-lot communities, treaties and colonial institutions across the northern plains.

sections.heading: Hunting and processing in deep time

paragraphs.text: At Wally’s Beach in southern Alberta, cut marks on horse and camel bones accompany artifacts near an ancient river crossing. New treatment and radiocarbon measurement of the bones revised the hunting and butchering evidence to about 13,300 calibrated years before 1950. Several carcasses occur in a small area, but their proximity does not prove that they all belonged to one hunt. The findings show people dealing with animals no longer present on the plains, while leaving open the larger balance of causes behind their extinction.

The Atkinson site near Lauder, Manitoba, offers a different kind of evidence. A hearth, tools and bison remains belong to a published fifth-millennium BCE occupation envelope. The animal parts are interpreted as material brought to a processing place rather than proof that bison were killed exactly there. This distinction reveals the work between a hunt and a meal: selecting portions, carrying them, extracting useful food and using a campsite. Farther north, the Quarry of the Ancestors adds an Alberta stone-resource landscape to this wider picture.

sections.heading: Gardens beside rivers and prairie edges

paragraphs.text: Fishing and cultivation met at Lockport on the Red River. Excavators found charred maize kernels, substantial storage pits and hoes made from bison shoulder blades. A recent research synthesis places the farmers approximately 1250–1450 CE; an older government field guide highlights evidence around 1400. These materials demonstrate more than the presence of an imported food. Tools and storage facilities make cultivation part of the local economy. The rapids also offered productive fishing, so the site resists a simple story in which agriculture replaced every older food practice.

Southwestern Manitoba adds another farming landscape. At the Olson site south of Melita, bison scapula hoes helped researchers move beyond earlier hints of cultivation. Associated material dates to the late 1400s or early 1500s. Similarities with other farming tools and pottery invite comparisons across the northeastern plains and adjacent woodlands, but they do not establish a named people’s movement on their own. The tools make cultivation visible at a particular place, adding a practical history of planting and working soil to the prairie narrative alongside the better-known evidence for hunting.

sections.heading: Métis commerce, settlement and collective rights

paragraphs.text: The Red River Métis emerge in this selection as traders, political actors and makers of settlements. On 19 June 1816, Cuthbert Grant’s party clashed with Governor Robert Semple’s party at Frog Plain, also known as Seven Oaks, during escalating disputes over pemmican and the fur trade. The Manitoba Métis Federation remembers the victory as an assertion of rights to trade and travel in the homeland. This political significance need not turn the day into a literal beginning of Métis peoplehood; communities and relationships already made that assertion possible.

In 1872, Xavier Letendre established a ferry and commercial enterprise where the Winnipeg–Fort Carlton trail crossed the South Saskatchewan River. Batoche developed with stores, warehouses and family river lots. Its history therefore begins in this guide with work, transport and home-making rather than battle. The later 1885 confrontation between the Métis provisional government and Canadian forces grew amid disputes over land and authority. Canadian victory after four days of fighting did not erase the community: residents rebuilt lives there, even as subsequent economic changes and dispossession placed further pressures on them.

sections.heading: Treaties, schools and the expanding Canadian state

paragraphs.text: Treaty gatherings were local events within much larger political relationships. Treaty 1 was concluded at Lower Fort Garry on 3 August 1871 between Crown representatives and Anishinaabe and Swampy Cree signatories. Treaty 7 followed at Blackfoot Crossing on 22 September 1877, involving the Blackfoot nations, Tsuut’ina and Stoney Nakoda. Blackfoot Crossing was already a gathering place, selected by Crowfoot for these negotiations. Marking the meetings makes the participants and geography visible; a treaty point cannot by itself explain every promise, later breach or differing understanding of what had been agreed.

The residential school at Lebret, also known as Qu’Appelle, is documented by NCTR from 1884 under Catholic administration. Placing it beside treaties and Métis settlements shows how colonial power entered communities through multiple institutions. Land negotiation, military intervention and the schooling of children were connected historical pressures, but each requires its own evidence and chronology. The school’s operation continued long after 1934. Ending this regional view at that year leaves those later experiences to further study; it does not imply that colonial harms, prairie communities or Indigenous political life stopped then.

pages.title: Northwest Canada: tools, trade and changing authority
pages.intro: Ancient hunting technology, northern exchange, Klondike displacement and treaty encounters.

sections.heading: Northern technology and the limits of early evidence

paragraphs.text: The Yukon’s deep history begins here with two very different kinds of preserved evidence. Bluefish Cave II holds a dated horse mandible whose surface marks have been argued to show human butchering during the last glacial maximum. The human interpretation remains debated because natural processes can also mark bone and the archaeological context matters. Farther south, ice preserved a composite hunting dart with wooden shaft sections, sinew, a stone point and feathers. These objects belong to different times and questions; neither should become a claim that one camp remained occupied throughout the intervening millennia.

The southern Yukon dart has a published calibrated date of 6131–5995 years before 1950. Chemical work identified beaver castoreum on the artifact, adding a material that usually leaves little trace in stone-tool histories. Its construction brings together knowledge of wood, animals, attachment and flight. The location is deliberately shown only at a broad southern-Yukon scale, within Kwanlin Dün and Carcross/Tagish homelands. Protecting the findspot does not prevent telling the technological story, and identifying the residue does not establish a single purpose for its use.

sections.heading: Trade along rivers and across mountains

paragraphs.text: At Teetł’it zheh / Fort McPherson, a Hudson’s Bay Company post opened in 1840 to trade with Gwich’in and Inuvialuit. The post moved about six kilometres in 1848, so its founding and the later community’s position must be distinguished. The Peel River connected this enterprise to established northern movement and exchange. The Gwich’in Social & Cultural Institute places the town within Teetł’it Gwich’in history, rather than treating the company’s arrival as the beginning of local life. The company established a new institution within an older homeland.

Fort Selkirk illustrates conflict over those trading relationships. Northern Tutchone people used the Yukon–Pelly confluence for fishing, visiting and exchange, while Chilkat Tlingit traders connected the interior with the coast. The Hudson’s Bay Company established a post in 1848. In 1852, Chilkat Tlingit traders attacked it and expelled its occupants. Accounts differ over the exact day and details of the fort’s relocation, but the year and trading conflict are clear. The company’s departure did not mean the region became empty or that Indigenous commerce came to an end.

sections.heading: Cooperation, gold and displacement in the Klondike

paragraphs.text: Fort Reliance began in August 1874 after Tr’ondëk Hwëch’in leader Gàh Ts’yàt sought a trading station near his home. The World Heritage account describes an early period of mutually beneficial exchange with the Alaska Commercial Company. Archaeological remains include Indigenous housing forms and commercial cabins, giving physical expression to people living and working alongside one another. This matters for a history often dominated by the gold rush: local leaders made choices about trade before the much larger influx of newcomers transformed the region’s balance of power.

The gold rush brought a sharper rupture. Newcomers displaced Tr’ondëk Hwëch’in from their seasonal fishing place at Tr’ochëk in 1896. After an initial move near Dawson and negotiations involving leaders, government and church officials, families relocated to Moosehide in spring 1897. They continued travelling to fish camps, hunting areas and gathering places. Moosehide became a year-round village without reducing people’s lives to a single settlement dot. Moosehide remains a living community with a continuing relationship to the river, and access is governed by the people who care for the place.

sections.heading: Institutions, households and treaty promises

paragraphs.text: Carcross/Tagish First Nation dates the Chooutla residential school’s operation from 1911 under Anglican administration. The school belonged to a changing network of institutions that reached into Yukon family life, and its different buildings should not be collapsed into one timeless structure. In the Mackenzie Delta, the Greenland and Pokiak families established Aktlarvik / Aklavik, where the Hudson’s Bay Company opened a post in 1912. These neighbouring decades thus include both institutional intervention and Indigenous community-building, with different local actors and consequences rather than one uniform northern experience.

Treaty 11 was signed at Fort Providence on 27 June 1921, followed by meetings in other northern communities. Commissioner Henry Conroy recorded questions about hunting, fishing, trapping and freedom of movement, alongside requests for medical care and support. His report is valuable evidence of the negotiations but remains a colonial official’s account. It cannot substitute for Dene understandings of the relationship. The northern story through 1934 therefore closes with unresolved political obligations, while the Tuktut Nogait coastal sites keep Inuit seasonal settlement visible alongside the inland institutions.

pages.title: Arctic Canada: houses, hunting and encounters with the state
pages.intro: Local archaeological sequences, Inuit dwellings, whaling labour, trade and colonial institutions through 1934.

sections.heading: Different Arctic histories in particular places

paragraphs.text: Northern Ellesmere Island has a history of repeated, sometimes widely separated uses. At Rivendell near Lake Hazen, Parks Canada describes occupation about 1050–950 BCE associated with the transition between Independence I and Independence II assemblages. These are archaeological classifications, useful for comparing objects and structures rather than identifying a modern nation. Lake Hazen’s basin also mattered to later Inuit and Inughuit hunters and fishers. Keeping the local observations separate prevents the long regional sequence from becoming a fictional story of continuous settlement or one people simply replacing another everywhere at once.

Iqaluktuuq on Victoria Island brings the chronology forward to Late Dorset evidence after 1300 CE. That finding matters because the timing of Dorset and Thule Inuit histories varies by region, and possible encounters remain subjects of research. Somerset Island’s Thule whaling landscape offers a different form of evidence: houses incorporating bowhead bones and environmental effects around settlements. These places show how archaeology can identify local activities without turning the disappearance of a named material tradition into an unsupported claim about massacre or the fate of every individual.

sections.heading: Houses, hunting grounds and a violent encounter

paragraphs.text: Near present-day Iqaluit, Qaummaarviit preserves qarmait, tent rings, caches and many kinds of tools. Nunavut Parks describes whale-bone frameworks covered with skins, snow around winter dwellings and warmth from qulliit, the lamps that made indoor life possible. The field-project account places activity from around 1200 CE into the nineteenth century. The houses belonged to a useful hunting setting, near seals on the ice and caribou on the mainland. Some visible structures are restored, so their educational appearance must be distinguished from the archaeological evidence beneath and around them.

At Kugluk on the lower Coppermine River, Inuit people fished at the rapids long before the place acquired the English name Bloody Falls. In 1771, Dene companions of Samuel Hearne attacked an Inuit fishing camp there. Hearne’s account and later heritage interpretation document this violent encounter, but it should not stand for all relations between the peoples of the region. The community’s preference for the name Kugluk restores attention to the place itself: fishing, travel and continuing Inuit significance, alongside the remembered violence.

sections.heading: Whaling stations and religious encounters

paragraphs.text: Cumberland Sound became a meeting place between Inuit and commercial whalers. At Qikiqtan, called Kekerten by outsiders, visiting ships began wintering before buildings were added in 1857. Inuit knowledge of whales, waters, clothing and provisioning made the station’s work possible. Surviving foundations and equipment connect the global demand for whale products with labour carried out at this particular island. Commercial whaling brought new materials and relationships, but it neither invented Inuit whaling nor made Inuit expertise a minor addition to an otherwise self-sufficient foreign industry.

Across Cumberland Sound, Uumanarjuaq / Blacklead Island acquired an Anglican mission when Edmund James Peck and Joseph Parker arrived in 1894. A sealskin church brought a new religious institution into an existing whaling setting, using locally familiar materials. Missionary work, translation and Inuit responses unfolded over years; arrival does not date the conversion of a whole population. Read beside Qikiqtan, the mission shows how trade and religion could share the same maritime connections while posing different choices and pressures for people living around the sound.

sections.heading: Trading posts, trials and Canadian authority

paragraphs.text: Arviat’s permanent Hudson’s Bay Company post dates to 1921, following earlier seasonal exchange. The hamlet’s history emphasizes Paallirmiut skill as traders moving between inland and coastal worlds, obtaining goods and joining marine hunting with commerce. The post therefore represents a change in the location and permanence of an institution, rather than the founding of Inuit life in the region. Families’ movements cannot be inferred from the presence of a store alone. Later settlement policies and forced relocations require a separate history beyond this guide’s 1934 endpoint.

At Mittimatalik / Pond Inlet, a 1923 trial made Canadian law conspicuously present. Three Inuit were tried over trader Robert Janes’s death in 1920; Nuqallaq received a ten-year prison sentence. Qikiqtani’s history explains the threats attributed to Janes and interprets the trial as a display of state authority. On Devon Island, the opening of the Dundas Harbour RCMP detachment in 1924 added another institutional foothold. Posts, patrols and courts did not arrive in an empty Arctic: they entered places with existing Inuit law, knowledge, movement and relationships.

pages.title: Aleutian Islands: maritime communities, colonial pressures and continuity
pages.intro: The Aleutian and Pribilof islands hold histories of skilled maritime life, enduring villages and profound colonial disruption. Tools, houses, gardens, churches and working harbours reveal how Unangan communities lived and changed across the centuries before 1934.

sections.heading: Stone-working places at the eastern end of the chain

paragraphs.text: On Anangula, near Umnak Island, early craftworkers struck long blades from prepared stone cores and shaped their edges into cutting, scraping and gouging tools. Flakes preserve the labour of making tools around 9,000 years ago, far more clearly than the wood and bone that rarely survived there. The raw stone came from elsewhere, making the workshop part of a landscape of movement and material knowledge. This early blade site is separate from the younger village remains also visible on Anangula; the two should not become one settlement lasting unchanged for millennia.

The Quarry Site on Amaknak adds two distinct episodes to the eastern islands’ chronology. Charcoal associated with charred stones and a possible hearth dates to 7730–7580 calibrated years before 1950. Charcoal near the upper cultural limit gives a later range of 6950–6740 calibrated years before 1950. Blades and microblades connect these observations to stone-working traditions. The samples demonstrate activity at different times, not continuous residence through the centuries between them. They also fill part of what once looked like a poorly documented stretch of regional history.

sections.heading: Houses, boats and coastal food

paragraphs.text: At Chaluka beside present-day Nikolski, successive houses, discarded tools and food remains accumulated into a substantial village mound. Its roughly four-millennia history belongs to a living community landscape. On Amaknak, excavations at the Bridge site exposed portions of 30–40 partly sunken, stone-lined structures. Some had several rooms. Fireplaces, vents and channels beneath floors show builders organizing warmth and work indoors, while repair and rebuilding altered the houses. The dated charcoal samples come from different contexts, so the broad site chronology cannot be assigned wholesale to every room or wall.

Maritime skills joined these homes to their resources. Unangan hunters used covered skin boats, often called bidarkas, while larger open boats carried people and cargo. Sea-lion skins supplied boat covers, and other parts of the same animals became food, tools and clothing. Fishing could require cooperation: two paddlers could stabilize their boats while hauling a large halibut. Salmon, birds and marine mammals offered different seasonal opportunities. Sharing catches distributed food and the work of processing it, helping households manage the uncertainty of any individual hunting trip.

At the western end of the chain, the Near Islands synthesis places early settlements on Agattu and Shemya by roughly 3,000 years ago. At Aga Cove and Krugloi Point, coastal resources sustained households far from the eastern islands. Fishhooks, cutting tools, harpoon points and woodworking implements changed through the archaeological sequence. These were communities with their own histories, not simply the last stops on one known voyage. Much later, Attu residents still moved between a winter village and summer fishing places, showing how permanent homes and seasonal travel could coexist.

sections.heading: The fur trade enters through violence and coercion

paragraphs.text: Russian fur hunters encountered armed resistance at Agattu in 1745 and moved on to Attu. The historical account describes captive-taking and an attack that killed fifteen Unangan men in an effort to seize women. This was an intrusion into inhabited islands with established communities and political relationships. Farther east, Ivan Solov’ev’s expedition reached Sanak in 1771; the island’s history records renewed violence before the Russians departed in 1772. Sea-otter commerce expanded through these encounters, imposing demands on local skills and labour as well as taking animals from coastal waters.

The Pribilofs became a different kind of fur-trade workplace. Russian-associated settlements appeared at Garden Cove on St. George in 1786 and near Marunich on St. Paul in 1787. Hunting companies forced Unangan men from Aleutian and Alaska Peninsula communities to travel north for commercial sealing. These voyages served merchants’ demands rather than a freely chosen search for a new home. Sod houses, camps and later settlement consolidation gave the extraction economy a material geography. The forced movements also separated hunters from the households and subsistence work of their home communities.

sections.heading: Gardens and company-directed settlement changes

paragraphs.text: Korovinski on Atka Island preserves two different village histories. An ancestral settlement ended following a major volcanic disruption, centuries before Russians and Unangan reoccupied the locality around 1820. The later settlement included houses, warehouses and a church serving the Russian-American Company’s western administration. Extensive garden plots survive behind sod walls, with furrows still marking cultivation. Potatoes brought a new food-producing practice into this maritime economy. The excavator suggests the walls helped protect crops from domestic animals; their exact purpose and the productivity of the gardens remain interpretations rather than measured annual totals.

Companies also reorganized where people lived. In 1823, the Russian-American Company moved Sanak’s population and hunting group to Belkofski as sea-otter grounds declined; hunters continued returning to Sanak. On St. Paul in 1825, the company shifted the Polovina settlement toward Village Cove, where loading ships was easier. At Attu, a company settlement established at Chichagof Harbor in 1805 developed into the island’s sole permanent winter village by 1830. Later, families leaving Korovinski established present-day Atka around 1870. A move in permanent homes could transform daily life without ending travel or knowledge of older places.

sections.heading: Church craft, seasonal movement and industrial shores

paragraphs.text: At Unalaska, local builders working with Ioann Veniaminov erected the first Church of the Holy Ascension in 1826, after his arrival in 1824. A replacement followed in 1858. The church constructed in 1894–1896 incorporated timbers from both predecessors, connecting generations of labour in one building. Its nave, sanctuary, side chapels and bell tower form a cruciform plan; interior work, especially the Chapel of St. Innocent’s icon screen, preserves Unangan craftsmanship. Missionary teaching and translation belonged within an existing community whose people participated in making the institution’s material world.

Changing commerce continued after Russian rule. A trading post opened on Sanak in 1873, and Akutan’s 1878 post linked settlement growth with trade and cod processing. At Attu in 1909, Jochelson’s expedition accompanied residents from Chichagof Harbor to Sarana Bay for the summer, recording seasonal movement rather than abandonment. Akutan’s industrial whaling station opened in 1912, processing whales for a commercial industry quite different from household food gathering. It remained active at the atlas’s 1934 endpoint. Villages, coastal work and community knowledge continued alongside these new demands, rather than ending when imperial ownership changed.

sections.heading: Village life at Sandy Dunes and Pauloff Harbor

paragraphs.text: Sanak’s Sandy Dunes preserves repeated settlement beside an old pond. Small round or oval houses had hearths along one side. Shell middens protected food remains, and tools made from distant stone connect household life to travel across the island chain. Far later, the shore at Pauloff Harbor held buildings for a commercial cod fishery. Bunkhouses, sheds and stores supported the work of catching, salting and shipping fish. Cobb’s May 1912 photograph records the schooner Sequoia loading salted cod.

pages.title: Canada: many histories, one shared map
pages.intro: Explore eight regional histories in the area now known as Canada. The shared map lets you move between places at the same point in time, from early camps and houses to trade, community life and the effects of colonial rule.

sections.heading: Making a living on the Pacific coast

paragraphs.text: Footprints at Calvert Island preserve a brief moment on an early shoreline. Much later, stone-walled clam gardens enlarged productive beaches, while large houses anchored communities on the coast and in the Fraser interior. These histories make the coast a place of engineering, skilled work and political life long before European trading ships. At Yuquot, visitors entered a Mowachaht centre with its own authority and relationships. Forts, the fur trade and colonial government changed those relationships; the execution of Tŝilhqot’in leaders and the suppression of potlatches show the force behind that change.

sections.heading: Prairie histories beyond one way of life

paragraphs.text: The Prairie record includes ancient horse and camel hunting, places where people processed animal bodies, and later villages where maize was grown and stored. It is a history of different ways of using land, not a single timeless hunting society. Pemmican connected food production to continental commerce and Métis political life. Batoche began as a ferry and trading settlement before it became a battlefield in 1885. Treaty meetings and residential schools belong beside these places on the map: colonial expansion altered access to land, family life and the terms on which people could live together.

sections.heading: Northern tools and established trading worlds

paragraphs.text: A composite dart from southern Yukon reveals a carefully assembled tool made from wood, stone and binding materials. Centuries of northern history cannot be reduced to outsiders’ arrivals. Gwich’in, Inuvialuit, Tlingit and Tutchone relationships shaped the trading worlds that company posts entered. At Fort Selkirk, Chilkat traders challenged a company’s intrusion in 1852. The Klondike rush later brought another scale of pressure to Tr’ondëk Hwëch’in country. Moosehide’s history records a community’s move in that setting, while northern school and treaty histories expose the reach of colonial institutions.

sections.heading: Homes, sea mammals and authority in the Arctic

paragraphs.text: Arctic archaeology includes hunting tools, carefully built dwellings and settlements that differ across islands and centuries. The Rivendell evidence beside Lake Hazen and the houses at Qaummaarviit belong to local sequences; they do not describe one synchronized change across the entire north. At Qaummaarviit, house construction made warmth and access to hunting grounds part of everyday design. Later whaling stations relied on Inuit knowledge and labour. Missions, trading posts, courts and police brought new demands into places already inhabited. The regional guide follows those encounters through the early twentieth century without treating a new post as the beginning of local history.

sections.heading: Waterways join villages, work and diplomacy

paragraphs.text: Obsidian from a distant western source reached the Lake Huron region, and wooden fish fences survived beneath the Narrows at Mnjikaning. These findings reveal movement and collective work at very different times. Later longhouse villages brought households, food production and political relationships together. Revised dating at the Jean-Baptiste Lainé village changes where that community falls within contact-era history. Conflict in seventeenth-century Wendat country caused deaths and displacement, but community history continued elsewhere. Canoe commerce, the War of 1812, treaties and residential schools then changed the Great Lakes world in different, connected ways.

sections.heading: A river already full of communities

paragraphs.text: McDonald, Droulers and Mailhot-Curran preserve longhouses, food remains and everyday tools from St. Lawrence Iroquoian communities. Cartier’s visits entered a river world supplied and governed by its residents. Later French establishments depended on diplomacy as well as building. Wendake records community rebuilding; the Great Peace of Montréal records negotiations involving many nations. War reached both colonial towns and Indigenous homes, including Odanak in 1759. The nineteenth-century creation of reserves at Kitigan Zibi and Mashteuiatsh placed new administrative boundaries across older homelands rather than creating those peoples’ relationships with the land.

sections.heading: Many Atlantic histories at once

paragraphs.text: Debert’s stone tools, the coastal settlement at Phillip’s Garden and Norse woodworking at L’Anse aux Meadows belong to widely separated chapters. In the sixteenth century, Basque crews at Red Bay turned whales into an Atlantic commodity. Later fishing settlements, Mi’kmaq and Beothuk communities, Acadian farms and colonial forts coexisted around the region. British conquest brought forced departures from Grand-Pré and Île Saint-Jean. Nain’s mission history sits within Inuit Labrador, not outside it. The opening of Shubenacadie’s residential school in 1930 connects this regional history to the wider system that separated Indigenous children from families and communities.

sections.heading: Camps, gathering places and inland routes

paragraphs.text: Across the Shield, harvests brought families back to particular places. At Kamestastin in Labrador, quartz and charcoal mark ancient work beside a caribou crossing. At Kay-Nah-Chi-Wah-Nung on the Rainy River, sturgeon drew seasonal gatherings, and generations of people lived and raised mounds near the rapids. In later centuries, inland trade dealers, governments and missions used waterways already familiar to Indigenous families. Lac Seul shows what was at stake when a dam flooded homes, gardens, harvesting places and graves in the 1930s.

pages.title: Amaknak Bridge: houses built into the hillside
pages.intro: At Amaknak Bridge in Unalaska Bay, partly sunken houses once lined a knoll above the channel. Unangan builders laid stone walls against the slope, put hearths next to walls and ran narrow channels beneath floors. The houses overlapped as people repaired and replaced them. Those intersections reveal a village changing over generations.

sections.heading: A village built in stages

paragraphs.text: Excavations in 2000 and 2003 exposed houses on the knoll, and work in 2006 and 2007 examined most of what remained. The later team documented portions of at least 36 structures. At least 14 were complete or nearly complete, and excavators identified 17 hearths or channels. Some structures survive as little more than an inner curve of stones where the hillside sheltered the wall from erosion. Near the top of the knoll, deeper deposits preserve foundations that cut into or sit directly over one another. Excavation plans show the accumulation of these remains across time.

The builders dug pits roughly a metre deep and set stone around their edges. Most houses were round or oval and about three to four metres across. A few were rectangular and reached seven metres in length. Construction varied even within the settlement. Structure A was almost round, four metres across and built in courses of small stones above large uprights. One fragment called Structure 10 used horizontal slabs set into layers of sod. The surviving segment is just over three metres long. The complete outlines of many structures and the materials of their roofs remain uncertain.

sections.heading: An older structure beside a newer one

paragraphs.text: Structure 7’s main building measured about six by four metres. It had an east-wall hearth, a shaft rising about 1.5 metres through the wall and a channel branching beneath the floor. Stone slabs and whale vertebrae in lines were interpreted as bases for roof supports. The 2003 excavators interpreted three features on the west as rooms within this house, partly because they found step-ups toward the northwest and southwest spaces. The northwest and west features had their own distinctive construction. The west feature also contained a hearth and a pair of floor channels.

The 2006–2007 excavators returned to these intersections. They found a smaller hearth underneath the main building and older structures cut by its construction. On the north, the wall of Structure 7 and the adjoining northwest wall abutted and partly overlaid Structure A. The pressure had pushed Structure A’s south wall inward. Rogers favored reading the west and northwest structures as separately built, with the southwest feature also predating construction of the main room. The earlier team had already encountered a replacement south wall parallel to the collapsed one. Taken together, the observations establish an order for some rebuilding while leaving the pattern of shared rooms open.

sections.heading: Fuel, draft and work at floor level

paragraphs.text: The hearths sit between the stone walls and the center of household activity. In larger houses, a channel from the hearth sometimes branched into two arms, often under slabs. Structure 63 had two parallel paths from the hearth along its long axis. Structure V had a wall shaft and a channel system that split into smaller branches. The excavators considered how the channels might draw air to the fire or distribute warmth. Charcoal and hearths show that fires burned inside the houses. The buried parts of the installation leave room for different interpretations of how smoke, air and heat moved.

People also used the space under floors for storage. Structure 2 had a slab-covered storage pit alongside its hearth system, and Structure 3 preserved caches of cooking stones and a bundle of albatross long bones. The investigators thought the latter could have supplied material for needles. Within Structure 3, posts supported the roof near the center of the room. These floor traces show the labor of furnishing and maintaining a house in a setting where exposed wood and bone seldom keep their original form.

sections.heading: What the dates and animal remains show

paragraphs.text: Charcoal from Structure 7 West has a published calibrated range of 1950–1620 BCE. Charcoal from the main room has a range of 1280–820 BCE. Structure 2’s floor charcoal falls in 1770–1520 BCE, Structure 5’s in 1410–1010 BCE, and Structure 3’s hearth sample in 910–420 BCE. Floor, hearth and fill are different deposits. A branch could have died before someone burned it, while an already-empty pit could have filled with refuse. Crossing walls and overlapping floors offer an independent way to order events that charcoal alone cannot resolve.

Shell-rich refuse preserved bones of cod, seabirds, porpoises, seals and other animals. Some of the ringed seal bones were identified as belonging to recently weaned animals. Crockford and Frederick inferred access to seasonal pack ice in spring or early summer. Knecht and Davis also discussed open-water fishing and hunting, based on the animals present and their ages. Those seasonal signals show the range of waters and weather conditions residents had to know. The village’s stonework records another part of that knowledge, built into floors that people returned to, repaired and sometimes replaced.

pages.title: Iliuliuk and Unalaska: the village beside the harbor
pages.intro: The U.S. Coast Survey chart issued in 1875 shows Iliuliuk as a strip of buildings between steep ground and the water. A church appears among them. The chart records the village as surveyors found it in 1871 and 1872, during one period in a much longer Unangan history on Unalaska and the surrounding islands.

sections.heading: Reading the 1875 chart

paragraphs.text: Find the name Iliuliuk on the lower right of the chart. On the shore beside it, surveyors marked a church and a line of small building symbols. Other symbols follow the shore around the point. Close together on the page are two kinds of marks used for different purposes. Numbers in the water give measured depths in fathoms. Marks on shore help identify recognizable places. The survey made the harbor legible for mariners while leaving the names and activities of most households outside its purpose.

Across the water, the chart names Amaknak Island and locates an astronomical station used for the survey. Expedition Island lies within the harbor. The detail in the water reflects the time surveyors spent measuring it, including observations of tides described in the margin. The true north and magnetic variation markings help a reader orient the sheet. As a source for the nineteenth-century settlement, its strength is the relationship between shoreline, church and other visible buildings. The individually unnamed symbols cannot be matched to the households that lived and worked near the shore.

sections.heading: An earlier house on another bay

paragraphs.text: Reese Bay, west of Unalaska Bay, preserves evidence of coastal households from the early Russian period. Archaeologists mapped two large longhouses, smaller house depressions and older deposits. Longhouse 2 had a main floor extending about thirty metres east to west with smaller spaces off it. Archaeologists excavated part of it and recovered more than two thousand glass beads. Their size, shapes and colors helped place the use of that house in the early contact period, when glass beads had become part of exchanges between Unangan people and Russian traders.

Different parts of the floor yielded different concentrations of beads. The interpretation has to account for uneven excavation and for the fact that only part of the house was examined with water screening. Beads lost near a family work area or a well-lit entrance might remain in a floor, while cleaning could move others away. Historical accounts describe related families occupying shared houses and using spaces along their sides. The Reese Bay excavation makes the scale and some of the interior arrangement visible. The exact allocation of space among its residents remains uncertain.

sections.heading: Three generations of the Holy Ascension church

paragraphs.text: The first Holy Ascension church was built in 1826, in an existing community. Construction took place during Ioann Veniaminov’s years of missionary work in the region, when the church became associated with local teaching and the writing and translation of Unangam Tunuu. The shoreline village around the church provided the setting for both the new religious institution and continuing Unangan households. The earlier Reese Bay longhouse belongs to a different village and period, and offers another example of the skill and organization that people brought to building at the water’s edge.

A second church followed in 1858. It is the building phase that fits the church symbol on the Coast Survey chart. The chart was drawn from observations more than twenty years before construction of the standing church in 1894–1896. The later builders incorporated timber from earlier churches. Its cross-shaped building plan, bell tower and side chapels express a different spatial organization, even as reused material tied the building to its predecessors. The survey, building history and surviving building each give a different view of the village as it changed.

sections.heading: A settlement linked by water

paragraphs.text: William H. Dall’s field notes record sea otter, fox and seal skins traded at Iliuliuk from a number of islands, including Akun and Tigalda. His observations place the houses shown on the survey in a network of trade, transport and work. The same harbor that protected boats on their approach to the shore linked residents to more distant harvests and markets. Institutions visible to surveyors occupied only some of the waterfront. Its fisheries, small craft, landings and individual households matter to the history even where the survey leaves them unnamed.

The dates help hold these layers apart. Reese Bay’s beads describe one excavated contact-era house. The church records describe several generations of construction at Iliuliuk. The Coast Survey describes the harbor as it was observed in the early 1870s. Taken together, they show how a settlement can keep its relationship to water while buildings, materials and kinds of work change. Neither the church nor the harbor chart supplies a founding date for Unalaska’s Unangan community. Their more direct evidence is the location and form of nineteenth-century buildings within a much older inhabited landscape.

pages.title: Chaluka and Nikolski: a village beside its ancient mound
pages.intro: At Nikolski on Umnak Island, the Chaluka mound holds layers of ancestral houses and work areas accumulated through generations of village life. Across the bay, Ananiuliak Island contains an early toolmaking site and a distinct later village. Together their floors, depressions and buildings show several ways residents lived on the coast.

sections.heading: Two places on Ananiuliak

paragraphs.text: The early Core-and-Blade site holds deposits of discarded cores, long blades and the flakes left by shaping and maintaining tools. A recent lithic reassessment describes an approximate age range of 9,600–8,000 calibrated years before 1950, with the evidence from house floors and hearths potentially representing a much narrower span. The deposits include shallow house depressions as well as extensive stone-working debris. Researchers have debated how long people remained and how much of the site they used at one time. The shapes of the stone tools and their imported materials still give a direct view of decisions about work in this early coastal setting.

The National Park Service reports up to twenty-four house depressions at the distinct, younger Anangula Village site. They occur in three rows along a bluff, with smaller hollows interpreted as storage pits. The six houses excavators tested were partly sunken and roughly rectangular to oval. Fresh water ran down the bluff toward a narrow beach. The recorded rows establish a relationship among houses, high ground and access to water, while their individual spacing, dates and period of shared use remain unresolved. The landmark account mentions a smaller possible seasonal locality elsewhere on the island.

sections.heading: A house and its work areas at Chaluka

paragraphs.text: At Chaluka, the deep mound contains floors, discarded tools and accumulated remains from marine food gathering. One stratigraphic study compared excavations from 1938 to 1972 and distinguished eleven major natural and human events. The study reports reef and marine activity through the sampled sequence. Over time, houses were built and replaced and layers of activity accumulated. The excavated areas capture particular parts of the village. This is why the mound preserves a long history even though the layout of the entire settlement is hard to recover for any one date.

A house examined by Jean S. Aigner had an uninterrupted stone perimeter, a hearth lined in slabs and pits sunk beneath its floor. Floor deposits provide a closer view than the mound profile. Near the east corner, archaeologists found a cluster of small ovoid pebbles. Near several slab-lined and unlined depressions they found twenty-two awls and needles. Some pits had covers. Such concentrations can suggest tasks carried out in different areas, even when instruments were put down, stored or swept away in ways the surviving deposits cannot fully distinguish. These observations describe one excavated interior among several recorded walls.

sections.heading: Chapels and the standing church

paragraphs.text: The Historic American Buildings Survey dates construction of an early chapel directed by John Kriukov to 1806. A successor designed by Ivan Veniaminov was built of driftwood and consecrated in 1828. The church survey also mentions a possible later nineteenth-century church with an uncertain date and position. Driftwood makes the relationship between seafaring and building materials unusually clear. The earlier chapels and the standing church belong to distinct phases, even though no surveyed footprints for the early chapels are provided by those sources.

The standing St. Nicholas Church was erected in 1930. Its square front tower rises before a gabled narthex, a hipped nave and a gabled sanctuary. Intricate interior woodcarving records the work of Sergei Sovoroff and other local makers. The HABS account names Sergei and Joseph Krukoff as carvers of the royal doors. The survey photograph shows the church in the village decades after its construction. The shape it documents includes later work, including a ceiling altered after the atlas’s period.

sections.heading: Village work before 1934

paragraphs.text: The Aleutian Pribilof Islands Association records sea otter hunting at Nikolski in 1834 and the name Recheshnoe used in Russian records. A fox-farming boom began in 1920, and the Aleutian Livestock Company established a sheep ranch in 1926. Local people bought the vessel Umnak Native, which was wrecked in 1933. These ventures added movements of workers, animals and goods to a community with a much longer maritime history. The old mound, successive chapels and working shores mark different kinds of residence and work within the same village setting.

The local history follows named places at several scales. Ananiuliak’s early tools belong to an island locality. Its younger village has surviving rows of houses. Chaluka’s layered record contains one house with close evidence of activity, and nearby Nikolski has buildings documented in written records and photographs. Read together, they trace long residence around Nikolski Bay without assigning every generation to a single building layout. Community accounts also speak of ties between the island and Nikolski. Those ties belong in the story alongside the dates that archaeologists and building historians can establish.

pages.title: Canadian Shield — camps, waterways and inland communities
pages.intro: Lakes and rivers through the Canadian Shield brought people to places where they could find stone, intercept caribou, fish, gather and trade. Follow individual places from early hearths to the families whose homes and livelihoods were changed by the flooding of Lac Seul.

sections.heading: Early camps and stone working

paragraphs.text: At Cummins, a former shore of Lake Minong runs well inland from present Lake Superior. People worked jasper-rich taconite near an outcrop and left stone flakes, pits and hearths. The quarry was close to places where people camped and got food. Farther northwest, a piece of a quartzite projectile point from a terrace above Black Lake resembles Agate Basin points recovered elsewhere. Its find context had been disturbed, so its age comes from comparisons. Together the sites show how stone, shorelines and water helped shape where people stopped and what they did there.

On the other side of the Shield, people used the outlet of Kamestastin Lake where caribou crossed. At Shak Selma they left worked white quartz and charcoal beside a small fire. At Napeu Atik a bowl-shaped pit held a quartz tool and the debris of stone working. At Mistanuk across the narrows, the selected deposit contains much more Ramah chert. Burning bone and wood made it possible to date these contexts. The materials vary from one site to the next, even at the same lake. The deposits show choices about tools and work that would disappear if all three places were combined into one camp.

sections.heading: Working with copper, wood and fiber

paragraphs.text: At Renshaw near Thunder Bay, copper tools preserved traces of the materials once fitted to them. A barbed point still held part of its bark binding. Other finds retained grass cordage and wood. Copper corrosion helped preserve these organic materials, which often disappear from archaeological deposits in the Shield. A date measured on the bark places that object’s use in the fourth millennium BCE. Its maker needed both the metalworking skill to shape the point and knowledge of fibers that could hold it onto a shaft.

sections.heading: Where families fished, cooked and gathered

paragraphs.text: At Kay-Nah-Chi-Wah-Nung, the Place of the Long Rapids, spring sturgeon runs brought people together. People lived beside the rapids, and generations of mound builders made this a place of ceremony. Rainy River First Nations relates these earthworks to a living sacred landscape. The river also linked people to communities far beyond the rapids. Farther northwest at Wanipigow Lake, remains of wild rice and goosefoot survive with evidence of pottery-making traditions. The shore became a productive place to return to over many generations.

Pottery adds details about work that can be difficult to recover from camps in the forest. At Whitefish Lake, most of the pottery at Martin-Bird belongs to the Blackduck tradition. A re-excavation investigated food residues in the deposits and recorded other kinds of pottery as well. At Sipiwesk Lake, researchers compared potsherds with samples of sediment and fired experimental tiles. Some clay mixtures had a local character, while others occurred farther away. Households could carry a pot, collect clay from a distant place or make a vessel as they travelled.

sections.heading: Shared dwellings and routes through the interior

paragraphs.text: Excavations before the Caniapiscau Reservoir filled found small sites with rounded hearths. Other dwellings were six to twelve metres long with extended fires or a row of hearths. The excavators compare the longer homes to the Innu and Naskapi saaputuwaan, an arrangement in which more than one family could share space. The details help explain how people might organize hunting and divide food. At Ferguson Bay on Ashuanipi Lake, archaeologists found precontact hearths at separate levels. The older deposits and historical Innu traces show that families returned to the shoreline through very different periods.

At Mashteuiatsh on Lac Saint-Jean, Ilnu community members took part in discovering and excavating a site with fires and concentrated fragments of chalcedony. The stone was worked at the site. Two distinct features preserve activity separated by many centuries. At Waapushukamikw, on the Témiscamie River, traces of quarrying show how people obtained and prepared Mistassini quartzite. For the Cree of Mistissini the white hill and its cave also carry spiritual meaning. Camps, material sources and places of gathering belonged to the same travelled country.

sections.heading: Trade posts enter a country of established routes

paragraphs.text: Real buildings entered this waterway network in stages. A mission and trading post began at Métabetchouane in 1676, where a river route meets Lac Saint-Jean. Montréal traders set up at Obadjiwan in 1720, beside the narrows of Lake Timiskaming. At Norway House, a later depot was rebuilt near the Nelson River in 1826. Houses, warehouses, chimneys and mission buildings tell the stories of those institutions. Their locations also show a practical reliance on canoe routes, crossings and labour sustained by Indigenous people.

At Fort Resolution, a North West Company post stood offshore before the Hudson’s Bay Company built on the mainland in 1819. Violet Mandeville’s history records Indigenous guides hired there, including Akaitcho. Farther along the lake, remains of stone fireplaces at Old Fort Reliance reveal a kind of building later adapted by Dene craftspeople. Across the Shield, trade also had its own seasonal rhythm. When families gathered at Fort McKenzie, they brought meat and furs and acquired supplies before leaving again for their own winter camps.

sections.heading: Treaty-making, schooling and forced moves

paragraphs.text: Land and livelihoods came under new pressures. The Grand Council Treaty #3 preserves the Paypom account of the negotiations that led to the 1873 treaty. At Norway House two years later, the Treaty 5 text set out terms for land, annuities and a reserve for families who wanted to farm near Fisher River. At Tataskweyak in 1908, a later adhesion followed requests from northern Cree representatives for negotiation. These separate meetings make it possible to see that a treaty number can cover several stages of a relationship. At Sakitawak in 1906, officials heard English River and Clear Lake leaders’ requests for help in hard times, in a town also deeply shaped by Métis families and commerce.

The Naskapi Nation remembers a series of moves driven by the Hudson’s Bay Company. One took trade inland from Fort Chimo to Fort McKenzie in 1915. In northwestern Ontario, the residential school at Pelican Lake was operating by the late 1920s. The named children on the school memorial give a human scale to that institutional record. When reserve land at Lac Seul began flooding in 1930, families lost homes, gardens, wild rice beds and graves. Some moved to higher ground as what had been a connected shore became an island. The atlas ends in 1934, within a history that remained active for the people who lived it.

pages.title: Indigenous communities of Costa Rica and Panama
pages.intro: At Guayabo, stone channels carry water through a settlement built into the slopes of Volcán Turrialba. On a beach ridge in Bocas del Toro, fish bones, grinding stones and pottery tell another history of households drawing on a shoreline and trading with people inland. These places belonged to a region of distinct Indigenous communities connected by rivers, trails and coastal travel. Their histories are visible at different scales, from the traces of a meal to the design of a public plaza. The time slider puts this evidence in sequence. A dated grave shows a particular use of a place. Pottery styles can identify an earlier horizon of activity, and several dated deposits together can outline a period of building or settlement. People left all three kinds of evidence in Costa Rica and Panama. Sometimes they buried the dead in places where people had once lived.

sections.heading: Early activity on a shifting coast and inland foothills

paragraphs.text: Cerro Mangote is now well inland from the active shore of Parita Bay. When people were gathering shellfish and grinding plants at the low hill beside the Santa María River, the shore lay much closer. Shell accumulated alongside stone cobbles worn along their edges. The site also served as a burial ground in later periods. One adolescent’s remains date to 2476–2293 BCE, near the beginning of the already mapped Monagrillo pottery tradition. The burial and the accumulation of shell are evidence of different episodes in a long local history.

On the Caribbean side of Costa Rica, excavators at Las Mercedes-1 found early pottery deep beneath later deposits in the eastern part of the site. The sherds resemble pottery from the La Montaña complex, defined partly through research in the Turrialba valley. This comparison places the finds somewhere in a broad horizon ending about 300 BCE, with possible beginnings between 1500 and 800 BCE. The ceramics matter because they show activity long before the well-known stone buildings rose.

sections.heading: A river village, a highland house and kitchens

paragraphs.text: People at Sitio Sierra lived beside the Santa María River, upriver from the Pacific coast. A refuse deposit dated about 300–550 CE contained fish from the coast and estuary as well as freshwater fish. Nearby remains of deer and birds broaden the picture. Two cemeteries also preserve evidence from different generations. Comparing bone chemistry from the earlier and later groups suggests a changing balance of maize and other foods. The smaller samples behind these comparisons represent a few people and one part of the settlement’s many centuries.

In the Chiriquí highlands at Barriles Bajo, the outlines of a possible oval timber house remained as stains in the soil. Charcoal from one posthole dates to 541–680 CE. At Lomas Entierros, on a hill above Costa Rica’s lower Tárcoles River, traces are smaller still. Heated starch grains and burned shell point to cooking in Structure 13. Maize starch and the pattern of activity in Structure 44 suggest possible food storage. Imported pottery there links local domestic spaces to connections with Greater Nicoya.

sections.heading: How people honored the dead in Gran Coclé

paragraphs.text: At Sitio Conte and El Caño, within a few kilometres of each other on the Río Grande floodplain, some funerals brought together many people and large quantities of pottery and ornament. At Sitio Conte, the people who prepared Burial 11 surrounded twenty-three individuals with vessels. One person received much of the gold. At El Caño, the excavation of Tomb 7 documented successive acts of burial and offering. An infant’s ornaments prompted the excavators to consider whether some distinctions were passed down through families. The findings show unequal treatment of the dead. Assigning the mourners’ intentions and the causes of death requires additional evidence.

Along the La Villa River at Cerro Juan Díaz, a different set of burials provides evidence for the lives of people in the same broad archaeological region. Isotope measurements on bones and teeth suggest that diets and movements became more varied by about 700 CE. Much later, people buried children and adults across an earlier floor. In the excavated group, ornaments or other offerings were recorded with children alone. Similar attention to children in older graves gives the practice a local history across several centuries.

sections.heading: Streets, terraces and the movement of water

paragraphs.text: The stonework at Guayabo and Las Mercedes-1 shows how builders reshaped slopes and directed movement. At Guayabo, crews fitted stone retaining walls to changes in level, laid paved approaches and controlled water crossing the central space. Excavations place the most intense construction from about 850 to 1150 CE. Work continued in some parts of the settlement after that. The place was made through several stages of landscape alteration and building.

At Las Mercedes-1, charcoal beneath four foundations places major construction between 1000 and 1200 CE. Paths approached a plaza and raised platforms, and one wide ramp led toward a circular foundation. The site brings the scale of collective building into view. Later graves in some of the central spaces show that the community changed the uses of its built environment long after the main phase of construction.

sections.heading: Four sites in the Diquís Delta

paragraphs.text: The stone spheres make sense in relation to the places where people put them. At Finca 6, two spheres flanked the ramp to Mound 1, while groups elsewhere in the settlement formed lines in open spaces. A separate sample dates the ramp of Mound 2 to 1170–1280 CE. At Batambal, stone outlines and spheres occupied a hill visible across the delta. At Grijalba-2, builders faced artificial mounds with limestone and paved approaches with river cobbles. These differences help explain why excavators study the four settlements individually.

At El Silencio, the largest recorded Diquís sphere stands near a paved strip at the edge of a river terrace. Its granodiorite mass represents selection, shaping and placement on a striking scale. The dated sample from El Silencio belongs to earlier activity on the terrace, between 550 and 650 CE. Later pottery and the stonework give the place a second chapter whose exact construction dates remain open.

sections.heading: Connections across watersheds

paragraphs.text: Sitio Drago brings a Caribbean island into a history often told from Pacific river valleys. The residents of the village on Isla Colón drew fish from reefs, mangroves and waters farther offshore. Pottery recovered there includes material linked to central Panama, the Chiriquí–Diquís region and northern Costa Rica. Movement across water and between watersheds could involve several communities passing things along. Individual trips and exact paths remain hard to reconstruct.

The Spanish foundation at Panamá Viejo in 1519 introduces a new documentary record at one harbor. The archaeological sequence across the region had already recorded centuries of building, exchange and changes in the use of older places. Their histories continue at different places and scales into the era of Spanish colonization.
