pages.title: Atlantic Brazil: mounds, villages and exchange
pages.intro: Along Brazil’s Atlantic coast and eastern river valleys, people made strikingly different places to live, work and remember their dead. Shell mounds rose beside lagoons. Communities built houses on wooden piles in Maranhão’s wetlands, worked stone in Ceará’s coastal dunes and made large ceramic vessels in the inland valleys. Some pots cooked food before becoming burial urns. A green-stone pendant and graphite in pottery reveal connections beyond a single settlement. This history follows excavated places and dated episodes, from early coastal mounds to the villages of the centuries before European colonization.

sections.heading: Fishing grounds, forests and early mounds

paragraphs.text: Rio Caipora preserves an early shell mound in southern Santa Catarina. Charcoal from its base dates to the sixth millennium BCE. The modern coast lies well away from this mound, but geologists place it beside an earlier lagoon landscape. The species and sediments brought into the mound are clues to a shoreline that later shifted as lagoons changed and filled.

At Piaçaguera, near an ancient bay in São Paulo, burial groups used the same mound during overlapping periods. Chemical evidence from teeth and bones suggests that people relied heavily on marine fish while eating foods from other environments as well. Slight differences between burial groups are a reminder that neighboring families can share burial grounds and draw on different foods.

Farther south at Babitonga Bay, a directly dated object reveals another part of coastal life. A harpoon component recovered at Morro do Ouro was made from southern right whale bone. The find and a second dated piece from nearby Conquista support the case for people pursuing large marine animals. Later dated burials at Morro do Ouro provide a different perspective. Alongside fish, there is evidence of substantial plant consumption, with cultivation remaining an open question.

sections.heading: A sand core, a dry platform and a growing cemetery

paragraphs.text: The builders at Encantada III made a low mound with a sandy core and a thin shell-bearing cover. Burned material in the cover may have been brought in from elsewhere. The studied deposits contain few artifacts and no known graves. Its builders could have used the place for occasional processing or as a landmark. A much younger charcoal date near the surface may reflect a later visit.

Around the Saquarema lagoon in Rio de Janeiro, archaeologist Lina Maria Kneip found hearths and burials at Beirada and reported possible traces of temporary dwellings in this group of sites. In the Guapimirim wetlands at Amourins, people laid thick shells on mud to create a dry surface. The individual mounds they built were subsequently covered and joined. Excavated blocks from two graves preserve steps in the preparation of the places where people laid their dead.

Dates from shell mounds require attention to how the material arrived. At Tarioba farther northeast, researchers found evidence that shell layers contain material mixed over time and revised the chronology. At Cabeçuda on the Laguna shore, shell determinations date part of a mound that later rose to about twenty metres. Published calibrations differ, so the map retains the source and sample behind each range.

The water itself also matters to a radiocarbon date. A shell records carbon from the water where the mollusc lived, while charcoal records carbon from the atmosphere absorbed by a plant. Estuaries mix water from different sources, so two materials buried together can give different raw ages. At Cabeçuda, comparisons among shell, charcoal and bone help researchers judge how to convert those ages into a calendar range.

At Jabuticabeira II, southern Santa Catarina, older shell deposits alternate with darker layers where excavators uncovered hearths and clusters of graves. The positions of those features support an interpretation of a cemetery built in many episodes. Shell was a bulk building material. Deposits rich in fish bones, including croaker and sea catfish, sit among the traces of funeral gatherings. The excavated sequence shows how people made a monumental place through repeated acts of burial and remembrance.

sections.heading: Later ways of using the lagoons

paragraphs.text: Around the first centuries CE, later graves were added at Cabeçuda, while a dark deposit rich in fish bones accumulated over the older shell layers at Jabuticabeira II. Charcoal and partly burned material in the cap point to work that took place before the deposits were carried to the mound. The older burial layers already contain fish remains, so the contrast between shell and bone primarily shows a change in construction.

Several kinds of place were in use around the seventh century. People at Içara 01 buried their dead in the dunes, in some cases after cremation or other preparation. On the dune beside Lagoa dos Freitas, bones of estuary fish are abundant and excavators found no graves. Those bones record catching and gathering at a different sort of place. A separate upper layer dates to a much later period, with some ranges extending beyond 1500.

Galheta IV preserves a built funerary mound, animal-processing deposits and Itararé-Taquara pottery. Isotopes in sampled teeth are consistent with coastal lives, and the pottery closely resembles other coastal assemblages. These findings bring burial practice, fishing and ceramics into the same local story while leaving room for contact with people elsewhere.

By the later centuries of the guide, broken vessels from Riacho dos Franciscos II beside the Jaguaruna lagoon preserve compounds consistent with maize use. The pots belong to the Guarani ceramic tradition, and a dated context places use of the locality in the thirteenth or fourteenth century. Vessel residues show which foods people sometimes prepared in pots. Fish bones, when they survive, tell a complementary story of what people caught and ate. The histories of both practices can be read along the same shore.

At Galheta IV, some pottery preserved residues from aquatic foods. The contrast with the maize evidence at Riacho gives concrete examples of how people used vessels around the lagoons. Some substances leave more detectable traces than others, and many meals never go into a pot. The shape and chemistry of a vessel each answer different questions about what people made and did.

Farther north, builders at Sernambetiba raised small shell mounds on a natural shell bed near Guanabara Bay. Some of the mounds were later joined by broader layers. Excavators uncovered human burials and dark bands containing charcoal and fish bones. Charcoal from two depths dates separate deposits around the turn of the era and into the first centuries CE.

sections.heading: Fishing communities used the coast in different ways

paragraphs.text: On the coast southwest of Guanabara Bay, people fished and collected food around Guaratiba’s mangroves and tidal channels. At Zé Espinho, they also buried their dead among shell deposits. A dated context associated with one burial falls between 600 and 1222 CE. The shell mounds contain traces of repeated activity over a much longer period.

A cremation on Ilha do Cabo Frio was found near Una pottery. Its calibrated range reaches into the sixth century. Pierced shark teeth and cut marine shells came from other deposits on the island. The archaeologists considered the new burial practice a possible sign of contact with Una potters.

sections.heading: Potters lived on hills across the Zona da Mata

paragraphs.text: On hills near the Rio Novo and its tributaries, people made, finished and used clay vessels. The early pottery sample at Mata dos Bentes has a published age of 604–804 CE. Later dated pieces from Primavera and Poça show that similar skills were practiced at other hills. Flattened, textured, painted and polished surfaces preserve choices potters made for different vessels.

Charcoal and pottery were found together in a hearth deposit at Córrego do Maranhão near Carangola. Several measurements overlap from the late thirteenth century onward. At Teixeira Lopes and Emílio Barão, pottery samples place activity before 1500. These date ranges apply to particular deposits and pots, and later ages at the same places show how the record can accumulate through separate visits and settlements.

sections.heading: A cemetery and a village in the Paraíba Valley

paragraphs.text: People placed dozens of clay urns in the ground at Caçapava 1. Some were buried alone and others in groups. A dated urn context falls between 1040 and 1260 CE, while several later urns and a pit oven have overlapping ranges from 1280 to 1430 CE. The shapes link the vessels to the Aratu-Sapucaí pottery tradition.

Farther west at Santa Marina in Jacareí, archaeologists documented patches of dark earth with pieces of clay vessels and worked stone. Two charcoal samples date activity there to 1400–1475 CE. Some patches overlap, which suggests that work areas or houses changed as people used the site.

sections.heading: On a terrace above the Rio Preto

paragraphs.text: At Rio Preto Oeste near São Mateus, the field team found ceramic fragments, combustion features and an older vessel reused as an urn. Soot and finger marks survive on the pottery. The assemblage has features associated with the Aratu tradition, together with surface treatments that led the excavators to propose contact with Tupiguarani potters.

The report’s conclusion places the village tentatively in the fourteenth century. The authors flagged possible contamination in some charcoal samples, and a different part of their report prints conflicting ages. The mapped century follows their archaeological interpretation and remains provisional.

sections.heading: Burials along the Araruama lagoon

paragraphs.text: At Morro Grande, large clay pots and painted bowls were used in burial rites. Charcoal from an early urn reaches the sixth century, and charcoal from a hearth by a burial elsewhere on the site dates to a substantially later episode. The difference in ages and the position of the finds suggest that people returned to the locality after a long interval.

At Bananeiras, mourners placed a young woman in an urn with painted bowls and shell pendants. The latest published calibration of her bones gives 1500–1681 CE. An earlier calibration gave two possible ranges, 1420–1510 CE and 1600–1620 CE. Pottery residues from the site give independent evidence of sixteenth-century activity.

sections.heading: Fires in the dunes of western Ceará

paragraphs.text: At Jericoacoara, a dark soil layer held traces of hearths, charcoal and tiny shells. People chipped locally available stone into tools, changed their edges as they wore, and left fragments of bowls. Buried charcoal brings some of those visits into view as early as the fifth to sixth centuries CE. Other dates mark separate episodes later in the first millennium. Wind later exposed and shifted parts of the site.

sections.heading: Villages above the Maranhão wetlands

paragraphs.text: Hardwood posts preserve the outlines of communities along rivers and lakes that flooded seasonally. At Boca do Rio and Cabeludo, over a thousand surviving posts at each site form large central clusters with smaller groups nearby. Cooking vessels occurred most often around the likely houses. Figurines and more finely finished bowls concentrated near the centers. At Caboclo and Armíndio, the plans show clusters of much the same size.

The villages were spread across several river basins. Samples from Formoso include a timber dated within 441–637 CE and a distinct run of later dates on posts and soot. At Encantado, two wooden piles date broadly to the eighth through tenth centuries. A tree could grow for generations before its wood became part of a structure, so one piece of wood supplies one piece of the chronology.

A small, twice-perforated greenstone pendant from Boca do Rio points beyond the wetlands. Tests identified its material as nephrite, with no known occurrence in Maranhão in the study. The stone or the finished object traveled to the river settlement. Its starting place and the people who carried it remain unknown.

sections.heading: Potters and mourners in the interior

paragraphs.text: In western Bahia, groups of lidded clay urns at Praça de Piragiba preserve how people buried their dead along the Ribeirão Santana. In Alagoas, excavations on the Serra da Barriga found the living surface of an Indigenous village where potters made everyday vessels and forms used in burial. A date on pottery from that village belongs to the centuries before the ridge became central to Quilombo dos Palmares.

At Serra do Evaristo I in Ceará, excavation exposed eighteen large vessels, six with remains of people. In the drier country near Brejo Santo, mourners placed an adult in an internally painted bowl and covered it with a second vessel. Two teeth from that burial give separate possible ranges in the late thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. Archaeologists describe the ceramics at Evaristo as Aratu and the painted vessel at Brejo Santo as Tupiguarani.

sections.heading: Rock shelters in the Pernambuco Agreste

paragraphs.text: People returned to sandstone shelters in the Catimbau valley to bury their dead. At Alcobaça, woven plant fibres, potsherds and hearths are part of a long sequence of use. A directly dated burial from 992–1152 CE was distinct from earlier deposits of burned remains. At Pedra do Cachorro, excavators reconstructed how an adult's remains had been prepared for secondary burial. The cause of death is unknown.

sections.heading: Graphite in pots from southern Bahia

paragraphs.text: At Canaã, near the Rio Colônia, potters mixed graphite into some vessels and coated others with it. Bones of hunted animals, stone tools and pottery collected together suggest a place where people prepared food. One graphite-coated sherd dates to approximately 1306–1496 CE. Chemical tests on four other sherds found the strongest resemblance to a graphite sample from the Jequié area, roughly 130 km away. Other deposits remain possible, and the route the graphite traveled is unknown.

sections.heading: Conflict, injury and the treatment of the dead

paragraphs.text: At Pedra do Cachorro in Pernambuco, archaeologists found an adult man’s bones that had been cut, broken while fresh and gathered into a secondary burial. The excavators read these marks as deliberate treatment of the dead. They tell us what people did with the body, but do not establish how the man died. The map therefore shows this as a burial, with the bone evidence explained in its record.

At Zé Espinho, a ray spine near a woman’s ribs has been discussed as a possible injury. A later examination questioned its position, and the dated male burial shown here is a different individual. The case remains a research lead. Sixteenth-century accounts describe organized Tupinambá warfare, but those later accounts cannot locate an earlier battle at one of these villages. This pass has added the excavated settlements and burial evidence while leaving the dates and participants of unverified conflicts open.

pages.title: After Lapita in the Solomon Islands and Vanuatu
pages.intro: At Te Ana Tavatava in the Duff Islands, coral gravel accumulated each time people renewed the floors of their village. At Mafilau on Epi, the shells, potsherds and broken tools that people cleared away formed a mound taller than a person. These ordinary acts left two unusually deep records of life on islands whose settlements were often rebuilt, buried or moved. The map follows the communities that lived here after the first Lapita settlements. At times the clearest traces are farming soils or pots used in a kitchen. At others they are a shrine, a burial or a tool carried over open water. Looking at each place and its dated deposits shows how long connections persisted and how differently neighbouring islands used them.

sections.heading: The first coastal settlements

paragraphs.text: Nenumbo once stood near a shallow lagoon on Ngaua in the Reef Islands. Postholes and concentrations of stone and pottery suggest that people worked in different parts of a small hamlet. Plant traces recover a different part of their lives. Soil samples from the excavations contain banana phytoliths, microscopic bodies formed by plants. They give evidence for plant use alongside the shellfish and other reef foods left in the deposits.

In northern Vanuatu, plain and shell-impressed pottery at Matantas links the southeast shore of Big Bay to a late Lapita site at Port Olry. At Mafilau farther south, the people who built up the great mound on Epi made Early Erueti pots and worked shells into rings and drilled ornaments. Banana traces occur throughout the deposit. The mound grew by repeated dumping, and its contents combine cooking, coastal gathering, cultivation and craft.

sections.heading: Villages on shifting shores

paragraphs.text: Lakao has an uncommon record of prolonged activity in one place. Early users left fire pits and shellworking debris in the cave at Te Ana Tavatava. Later residents spread fine coral gravel on house floors in the open, building a thick layer through repeated resurfacing. The excavators identified village phases spanning roughly 400 BCE to 1000 CE. A cowrie-shell tool in their village deposits gives a clue to the processing of vegetable foods.

Across the sea, Malua Bay’s excavated surface appears to have been prepared by moving coral gravel onto beach sand. Charcoal and fire-cracked stones place people cooking near that sheltered landing place. Along the Santa Cruz coast on Nendö, excavations place the transition from using pottery to leaving pottery-free deposits around 100 BCE–100 CE. Some late settlements on Nendö had dance circles and craft-working evidence. Changes in pottery use document only one aspect of those histories.

sections.heading: Island pottery histories diverge

paragraphs.text: People at Sinapupu on Tikopia used incised vessels with strong similarities to Mangaasi pottery from central Vanuatu. Excavations recovered some of the distinctive sherds alongside shell arm ornaments. The fit between the two chronologies supports contact. How the pots reached Tikopia, and where individual vessels were made, are harder to recover from the sherds.

At Melarip on east Efate, weathered sherds with raised decoration and incised lines belong to the island’s last major ceramic phase. On Lamen Island off Epi, pottery remained in use much later. The Lamen pots show some likenesses to Malakula forms, and ash from nearby volcanic activity separates parts of the excavated sequence. On Tongoa, where the fifteenth-century Tombuk eruption transformed the island, the ceramic sequence changed again. The chronology follows where vessels are found and how they were made.

sections.heading: Living with rivers and slopes

paragraphs.text: At Ivanaud on Aneityum, excavators found stone-lined drains beneath later layers of flood sediment and garden soil. The lower and more closely spaced drains may relate to growers’ attempts to manage a wetter valley floor. Elsewhere on the island, a large furrow-irrigated system at Aname was rebuilt across two phases. The island’s food production depended on cultivation and on the work of managing water around it.

On Tikopia, a different form of land management can be traced through measurements on rat and pig remains. The chemical signals changed during the last major phase of island history before regular overseas contact. The excavators and isotope researchers relate these changes to how people used trees, soils and gardens. The samples sit within the Tuakamali sequence, which also brought changes in tool styles and contacts with the Banks Islands and Western Polynesia.

sections.heading: From inland shrines to the lagoon

paragraphs.text: Around 1200 CE, the Bao ridge above Munda acquired one of the earliest dated shrines in Roviana. People set a flat basalt slab above a paved area in front of a stone-faced platform. Roviana histories connect the inland ridge to the origins of communities that later held power along the lagoon. On Nusa Roviana, later shrine platforms with shell valuables and food offerings stood among settlements and within the fortified ridge. Lagoon traditions connect the ridge to named chiefs and to raiding.

In northwest Malakula, the relationship of village and ceremonial space took a different form. At Chachara, low platforms called nasara sit by concentrations of pottery and cooking debris. Such platforms are known from ceremony and grade-taking in northern Vanuatu. The midden beside the northern platform contains pig bone, shellfish and a shell adze as well as large quantities of a distinct late pottery style.

sections.heading: What travelled between islands

paragraphs.text: The places where tools ended up and where their materials formed can be far apart. A small flake from a fourteenth-century deposit on Sikopo in the Arnavon Islands matches obsidian in West New Britain. At Kahula on Taumako, two adzes found in early village layers came from Tutuila. On Emae, volcanic glass from Vanua Lava turned up in a midden. Each piece preserves a link across open water. The artifact and its geological source are the two securely shared points in the journey.

On Taumako, travel is also reflected in the Namu burial ground. Researchers compared strontium in tooth enamel, a record of where people lived when their teeth formed. They found patterns consistent with some women growing up elsewhere, including one with an especially distinct signature. Historic accounts of marriages between the Duff, Reef and Santa Cruz islands provide a context for interpreting the findings.

sections.heading: Roi Mata’s landscape

paragraphs.text: On the northwest coast of Efate, people laid stone walls around residential yards at Mangaas during its final settlement phase. In local tradition this was the residence of the last Roi Mata. Across the water on Lelepa, Fels Cave is associated with his death. The island of Artok holds the burial place where excavation uncovered a central grave with numerous accompanying burials. Archaeology and local accounts trace different aspects of that same landscape. Community and chiefly management have kept its customary restrictions in use.
